FOREWORD

# Foreword

The WAVE Country Report is our Network’s primary publication—a biennial, data-driven overview of the status of women’s specialist services in 46 European countries. As a key advocacy tool, the Country Report tracks progress, identifies persistent gaps, and measures the extent to which European countries meet the minimum standards set out by the Istanbul Convention, providing evidence for necessary legislative reforms and policy adjustments at the national and European levels.

The report focuses on women’s specialist services, including national helplines, women’s shelters, women’s centres, and specialist support for survivors of sexualised violence. Additionally, it provides insights into primary prevention work and femicide. For the first time, the 2025 edition also includes a chapter on the rise in technology-facilitated violence against women and girls (TFVAWG), and the strategies adopted by women’s specialist services to counter it. Women’s specialist services are operating in an increasingly complex and often openly hostile environment. Political backsliding, the rise of restrictive ‘foreign agent’ laws, and the spread of gender-neutral policies are eroding hard-won women’s rights and shrinking the democratic space in which feminist civil society can act. At the same time, TFVAWG is accelerating at an alarming pace, adding new forms of digital abuse to the already widespread physical, sexual, and psychological violence faced by women and girls. These developments are not isolated incidents – they reflect a broader backlash against women’s rights defenders and the fundamental European values of democracy and equality.

In the face of these significant challenges, women’s specialist services continue to demonstrate remarkable resilience, providing vital and life-saving support across Europe. There are also signs of progress. Since the last WAVE Country Report, the number of European Union (EU) countries operating helplines in line with the Istanbul Convention has risen from 19 to 21, and among non-EU countries, the figure has increased from 13 to 16. Yet, the provision of shelters and women’s centres has not improved, especially in non-EU countries, which were hit hardest by the recent cuts to USAID funding. These growing disparities highlight the urgent need for sustainable funding and genuine political commitment to ensure life-saving support for all women and girls, as well as to secure the long-term, effective prevention of violence against women and girls (VAWG).

## The rising challenge of tech-facilitated violence against women and girls

A fast-emerging and rapidly evolving challenge is TFVAWG. Digital technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) have opened new frontiers of abuse, with at least 40 forms of online violence now recognised – from cyberstalking and harassment to deepfake pornography<sup>1</sup>. Deepfake incidents alone increased by more than 550% between 2019 and 2023, disproportionately targeting women and forcing many out of digital and public spaces<sup>2</sup>. 20% of young women (18–29 years) in the EU have already experienced cyber-harassment.<sup>3</sup> Women human rights defenders,<sup>4</sup> journalists,<sup>5</sup> and politicians are subject to highly targeted online attacks designed to silence and discredit them. Perpetrators benefit from anonymity, lack of regulation, and the borderless nature of digital platforms – often acting with complete impunity. TFVAWG deepens existing structural inequalities, pushes women and girls out of online and offline public life, and ultimately threatens democracy itself.

Despite the scale of these harms, legal and institutional responses across Europe remain slow and systematically underfunded – leaving many women and girls exposed and unprotected. Addressing this crisis requires action from European governments and funders to invest in women’s and girls' safety and the protection of their human rights. This includes sustained funding for women’s specialist services responding to TFVAWG, comprehensive training for relevant government and justice-sector professionals, and urgent legal reforms backed by effective implementation and enforcement. At the same time, feminist advocacy must increasingly focus on reclaiming digital spaces – ensuring that technology becomes a tool for empowerment and safety, rather than one that fosters control, surveillance, and exclusion. Critically, however, states bear primary responsibility for protecting people and their data, regulating online spaces, and mandating safety-by-design standards for digital platforms. Any moves toward regulatory flexibility must not compromise Europe’s commitment to safety and digital rights protection. States need stronger enforcement mechanisms and greater commitment to maintaining high standards, rather than converging toward weaker frameworks that privilege platform interest over user safety.

### The importance of primary prevention

Despite the persistence of VAWG and the emergence of new forms of violence, institutional responses remain widely reactive – managing harm and the aftermath of violence after it occurs, rather than preventing violence in the first place. This must change.

WAVE continues to call for a fundamental shift towards long-term, transformative prevention strategies, with a particular focus on primary prevention: acting before violence happens and addressing the root causes of gender-based violence (GBV). Primary prevention is the most strategic and sustainable approach – not only to reducing harm, but to ending VAWG altogether. Achieving this requires sustained, cross-generational political will and financial commitment to dismantle the structural inequalities, harmful policies, and gender stereotypes that enable violence. Primary prevention of VAWG is not only a human rights obligation – it is an urgent economic and social necessity that must no longer be sidelined.

Violence against women costs the EU an estimated € 289 billion every year,<sup>6</sup> yet the evidence is unequivocal: every € 1 invested in prevention saves up to € 86 in long-term costs.<sup>7</sup> Despite this, prevention remains chronically underfunded and politically deprioritised. The gap between what we know and what we fund is no longer just a policy failure – it is a deliberate choice with profound human, social, and economic consequences.

Real change requires far more than political rhetoric or surface-level awareness campaigns. It demands sustained commitment and predictable, adequate funding for both primary prevention initiatives that address the root causes of VAWG and for feminist civil society organisations – especially women’s specialist services – that provide essential support to survivors.

This means supporting feminist civil society organisations doing this critical work on the ground, engaging genuinely with communities to transform the deep-rooted attitudes and norms that allow violence to persist. To be effective, these prevention strategies must be genuinely inclusive and intersectional, centring the voices and lived experiences of survivors – not as an add-on, but as the foundation of all policy and practice.

### Celebrating women’s specialist services

In closing, we pay tribute to the invaluable work of WAVE members, to whom this report is dedicated. Despite growing adversity and shrinking resources, women’s specialist services continue to show extraordinary resilience, innovation, and creativity. Whether operating under authoritarian

restrictions, providing shelters in conflict zones, running multilingual helplines, or pioneering digital advocacy, their work ensures that women’s voices, in their full diversity, continue to shape policy and decision-making on VAWG. For over three decades, the WAVE Network and its members have been at the forefront of efforts to secure women’s rights and build a future free from violence. Their courage, expertise, and solidarity inspire hope that a world without VAWG is possible.

This report is both a celebration of what has been achieved and a call to action. By documenting the current realities and identifying where progress is urgently needed, the WAVE Country Report aims to strengthen and unite women’s rights advocates across Europe in the shared task of building a safer, more just society for all women and girls.

Stephanie Futter-Orel (WAVE Executive Director) and Susana Pavlou (WAVE President)

Vienna, December 2025

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

# Executive summary

The WAVE Country Report 2025 provides an overview of women’s specialist services (WSS) in 46 European countries, covering national women’s helplines, women’s shelters, women’s centres, specialist services for survivors of sexualised violence, and primary prevention. It also includes a dedicated section on femicide and, new to this edition, technology-facilitated violence against women and girls (TFVAWG). The term ‘European countries’ in this context refers to the 46 Council of Europe member states represented in the WAVE Network, while recognising that this does not cover all states in geographical Europe. Data availability varies across countries, and where relevant, differences between EU Member States and non-EU countries are highlighted. A detailed description of data collection processes and limitations is provided in the methodology chapter.

The Council of Europe Convention on preventing and combating violence against women and domestic violence (the Istanbul Convention) remains the most comprehensive regional framework for assessing state responsibilities in the areas of prevention, protection, prosecution, and coordinated policies. It continues to serve as the main benchmark for evaluating the adequacy and quality of specialist services in Europe.

### Status of signatures and ratifications of the Istanbul Convention (as of November 2025)

* 44 countries have signed the Convention: Albania, Andorra, Armenia, Austria, Belgium, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Croatia, Republic of Cyprus, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Georgia, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Latvia<sup>8</sup>, Liechtenstein, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Republic of Moldova, Monaco, Montenegro, Netherlands, North Macedonia, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Romania, San Marino, Serbia, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Ukraine, United Kingdom.

* 39 countries have ratified the Convention: Albania, Andorra, Austria, Belgium, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Republic of Cyprus, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Georgia, Germany, Greece, Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, Malta, Republic of Moldova, Monaco, Montenegro, Netherlands, North Macedonia, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Romania, San Marino, Serbia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Ukraine, United Kingdom.

* One country has denounced and withdrawn from the Convention: Türkiye (effective 1 July 2021).

<sup>8</sup> On 30 October 2025, Latvia’s Parliament voted to withdraw from the Istanbul Convention, with 56 votes in favour and 32 against. As of December 2025, Latvia has paused its withdrawal from the Istanbul Convention following a parliamentary vote in October 2025, with the President returning the withdrawal bill for further review due to legal and human rights concerns. The process remains unresolved, with ongoing public debate and the possibility of a national referendum, while international organisations continue to express concern over the potential rollback of women’s rights protections.

* The European Union (EU) signed the Convention in June 2017 and acceded in June 2023.

Despite not being universal, the Convention remains the central reference point for assessing specialist service provision and broader state obligations across Europe.

### EU Directive on combating violence against women and domestic violence

A significant development in 2024 was the adoption of the EU Directive on violence against women and domestic violence (Directive (EU) 2024/1385), the first EU-wide legislation addressing violence against women (VAW). The Directive establishes minimum standards across Member States in the area of prevention, protection and support, including the criminalisation of female genital mutilation, forced marriage, and key forms of TFVAWG. Member States must transpose the Directive into national law by June 2027.

While recognising the Directive as a significant step forward, several gaps remain. Most notably, the Directive does not include a fully consent-based definition of rape, and its coordination model risks marginalising WSS within general victim-support systems. Furthermore, protections for particularly vulnerable groups remain insufficient, and negotiations led to weakened language in several areas.

The Istanbul Convention remains the main policy framework against which this report assesses regional progress and ongoing challenges in protecting women and girls from all forms of violence.

### National women’s helplines

National women’s helplines are one of the most important basic services for survivors of violence against women and girls (VAWG). Specialist helplines are essential because survivors frequently face disbelief, minimisation, or victim-blaming in broader society. A national women’s helpline, staffed by trained professionals or volunteers who believe survivors and understand the gendered dynamics of violence, offers the validation and solidarity that women need in order to seek support.

Article 24 of the Istanbul Convention, as well as the Directive (EU) 2024/1385, require state-wide, 24/7, free helplines that address all forms of VAW, and which are confidential, anonymous, and multilingual. Both instruments also require adequate and sustainable state funding (Istanbul

Convention, Article 8; EU Directive, Article 36). Without long-term investment, helplines cannot reliably function 24/7, train and retain staff, or expand accessibility.

For many women, calling a helpline is the very first step in seeking help. A free phone number, available 24 hours a day, helps them break the isolation and offers access to information and support. A national women’s helpline is also an entry point to the broader WSS network. Calls are often referred to local shelters, counselling centres, legal aid providers, or rape crisis centres (RCCs).

For decades, women’s NGOs have been at the forefront of establishing, running, and sustaining national helplines. Their expertise is rooted in direct work with survivors, feminist research, and international networking. They have developed standards of practice that reflect survivors’ real needs, and they have consistently advocated for states to recognise helplines as part of basic services. Helplines run by women’s NGOs differ fundamentally from generic services: they are survivor-centred, rights-based, and aware of the gendered structures underlying violence. Over the years, many helplines have become more professional and now receive state support or funding. However, their feminist roots remain essential, as they continue to guide the focus on survivors’ needs, safety, and rights.

## Overview of findings on national women’s helplines in Europe

By 2024, 39 of 46 European countries (85%) report having at least one national women’s helpline for survivors of VAWG. This means that seven countries (15%) still do not have a national women’s helpline. Of these, four are EU Member States, and three are outside the EU. In some countries, such as Armenia and Belarus, there is no state-wide service. In others, provision is fragmented or gender-neutral, as in Belgium, where separate helplines operate for Flemish- and French-speaking regions, of which one is for women and the other one is not exclusively for women, and in Latvia, where helplines exist but the 24/7 services are not women-specific and the specialised helpline does not operate 24/7.

In 2024, most European states continue to operate a single national women’s helpline, which is the recommended model. Twenty-nine countries (63%) follow this approach, giving women one well-known number that can be reached from anywhere in the country.

In summary:
* 29 countries operate one helpline
* Seven countries operate two helplines
* Two countries operate three helplines
* The United Kingdom has four helplines, one for each of its nations

By 2024, 37 countries (80%) meet the recommended standards for national women’s helplines: free of charge, available 24 hours a day, and grounded in a gendered understanding of VAW. This marks an increase from 32 countries in the 2023 report.

Language accessibility has continued to improve. In 2024, 29 countries (63%) report that their national women’s helpline offers multilingual support. Women’s NGOs run most national women’s helplines. A smaller number are operated by state institutions, and some countries use shared or changing models. Most helplines now receive at least some state funding, although seven countries still report having no state funding for their national services.

Across the 32 countries that provided figures or estimates, national women’s helplines received over 900,000 calls in 2024. This highlights the scale of demand and the central role helplines play in providing information, guidance and support.

Across Europe, many other helplines exist that do not meet the standards for a national women’s helpline but still provide information and support to women. These fall broadly into three categories:

* Specialist helplines offering support for specific groups of women or particular forms of violence (e.g. sexualised violence, trafficking, forced marriage, legal advice).

* Gender-neutral national gender-based violence (GBV) helplines, which provide support to all survivors and do not take a gender-specific approach.

* Helplines for related issues, such as homelessness, substance use, migration or asylum, which may intersect with women’s experiences of violence.

Alongside national services, there are many regional, local and specialised helplines. These may be linked to shelters, women’s centres or RCCs, or they may focus on particular forms of violence. They are especially important in countries without a national women’s helpline or where coverage is limited.

### KEY FINDINGS
* ~~85% of EU Member States and 84% of countries~~ outside the EU have at least one national women’s helpline.
* 39 out of 39 national women’s helplines in Europe operate free of charge.
* 37 out of 39 national women’s helplines in Europe are available 24/7.
* ~~37 countries (80%) meet the Istanbul Convention~~ standards – the helplines are both free of charge and available 24/7.

Recommendations are included at the end of the chapter on national women’s helplines.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

### Women’s shelters

Women’s shelters are a core part of any effective response to VAWG. For women whose homes are no longer safe because of fear, control, or physical harm, having access to secure accommodation can be lifesaving. Shelters are not only emergency places to stay; they are specialist services that protect women’s rights, dignity, and autonomy. They give survivors the chance to leave abuse, find safety, and start rebuilding their lives.

The first shelters were created by women’s grassroots initiatives, driven by solidarity and political awareness. Today, states have clear duties under international human rights standards to ensure that adequate shelter services exist for women survivors of violence. Article 23 of the Istanbul Convention requires states to establish appropriate, easily accessible shelters in sufficient numbers, offering safe accommodation and proactive outreach to survivors. The Convention’s Explanatory Report recommends one shelter place per 10,000 inhabitants. Although this is a minimum benchmark, evidence shows that actual demand often exceeds it, especially during periods of economic hardship, conflict, or broader social crises. Adequate funding, good geographic distribution, and high-quality support are as necessary as meeting the required number of beds.

The report distinguishes between women-only shelters and shelters open to women but not exclusively for them, and highlights the number of women-only shelters in each country. This distinction is important to track, particularly as WSS in some countries are losing funding or service contracts to gender-neutral or generic providers.

Research from across Europe consistently shows that women-only, feminist-run shelters offer more holistic and longer-term support. Their approaches focus on empowerment, self-determination, and rights-based advocacy. These shelters also play a key role in driving policy change and raising awareness about VAWG.

### Overview of findings on women’s shelters in Europe

Data from 46 European countries show that there are 3,224 shelters accessible to women, of which 2,365 are women-only shelters. Together, they provide 48,860 bed spaces for a population of more than 847 million people. This remains far below the Istanbul Convention’s minimum requirement of one family place per 10,000 inhabitants, with only 12 countries (26%) currently meeting this standard.

Compared with the WAVE Country Report 2023, the latest data show a modest increase in both shelters and bed spaces. The total number of shelters accessible to women rose from 3,087 to 3,224, and the number of available beds increased from 39,130 to 48,860. The number of countries meeting the Convention standard grew from 10

to 12. **Montenegro** now meets the minimum requirement following an increase in both shelters and bed spaces, and **Croatia** now exceeds the standard due to an expansion in capacity. **France** now meets the Istanbul Convention standards, although the consistent increase in bed spaces is also due to a different way of presenting data. On the contrary, **Liechtenstein** does not meet the Istanbul Convention standards, while in the previous report, it did. This is due to a difference in data collection: the previous reports erroneously included children's beds in the overall count.

In the EU, the number of shelters accessible to women increased from 2,232 to 2,371, and the number of bed spaces increased from 27,124 to 33,450. The number of EU countries meeting the benchmark rose from seven to nine. In non-EU countries, bed spaces grew from 12,006 to 15,410, though some of this increase reflects new data previously unavailable from **Russia** and **Ukraine**.

Women-only shelters are accessible around the clock in most European countries. Thirty-one of 46 countries (67%) report that all or most women-only shelters offer 24/7 access. Most women-only shelters continue to offer free services, but in 11 countries (24%), women are also asked to contribute financially for their stay, according to their financial capacities, or through access to municipal housing funds or other financing programmes.

Access remains uneven for women who face additional obstacles. Women with uncertain or undocumented residence status can access all or most shelters in 41% of countries. Accessibility for disabled women remains limited: only 37% of countries report that all or most shelters are accessible to women with mobility impairments, and 26% for women with sensory disabilities. Access for women aged 65+ is better, with 61% of countries reporting that all or most shelters accept them. Refugee women can access all or most shelters in 50% of countries, while homeless women can access all or most shelters in 46% of countries. Shelters are more inclusive for women with children with disabilities (43%), while access for women with older sons (14+) is lower (26%). Unaccompanied girls under 18 remain largely excluded, with only 20% of countries allowing them full or broad access.

Specialised shelter provision remains limited but present. Shelters for survivors of trafficking exist in 12 countries, and nine countries have dedicated services for LGBTQI+ survivors. Eleven countries report shelters for migrant and ethnic minority women.

Sustainable funding remains a significant challenge. Forty-four of 46 countries (96%) report some form of state or municipal funding, but **Belarus** has none. In **Moldova**, funding is available but does not extend to the **Transnistrian region**, where shelters rely entirely on international and private support. Many shelters still depend on short-term or project-based funding, affecting stability and long-term

**WAVE COUNTRY REPORT 2025**

**11**


---

planning. In contrast, a few countries, such as Sweden, Slovenia and Iceland, offer multi-year partnership models that provide greater security.

Women’s NGOs remain the leading providers of women-only shelters, running such services in 38 of 46 countries (82%). Other NGOs operate them in 20 countries (43%), faith-based organisations in 14 countries (30%), and state authorities in 17 countries (37%), as well as in the northern part of Cyprus. Four countries report other management models, including government-organised non-governmental organisation (GONGOs) or hybrid partnerships.

Women-only shelters are available across all regions in 16 countries (35%), while in 11 countries (24%), they cover most regions. In 13 countries (28%), they are concentrated mainly in major cities, and in Armenia, the northern part of Cyprus, and the Transnistrian region of the Republic of Moldova, they exist only in the capital. In addition, 36 countries (78%) report other types of shelters that can accommodate women survivors of violence, totalling 859 such facilities, including mixed-gender crisis centres, family shelters, anti-trafficking facilities, and shelters for vulnerable groups.

Women-only shelters remain essential for ensuring safe, specialist support for survivors. Their gender-specific approach cannot be replaced by generic or mixed services. As they are the leading providers in most countries, securing their long-term funding and availability is crucial so that all women can access protection when they need it.

## Women’s centres

Women’s centres are a vital part of specialist support for women and girls survivors of VAWG. They provide non-residential, gender-sensitive services that combine emotional support, legal information, practical assistance, advocacy, and empowerment. Rooted in feminist principles, women’s centres respond not only to survivors’ immediate needs but also work to challenge and change the social and institutional conditions that allow VAWG to continue. Their support is holistic, long-term and grounded in trust, prioritising women’s safety, dignity and autonomy. For the purposes of this report, the term ‘women’s centre’ includes all specialist, non-residential services that work predominantly or exclusively with women survivors of violence and their children.

Across Europe, women’s centres operate in varied contexts. Some are long-standing independent feminist NGOs, while others form part of coordinated networks or are connected to shelters and crisis services. Despite this diversity, their core purpose is shared: to offer safe, confidential, women-centred spaces where survivors are believed, supported, and empowered to rebuild their lives. They are often the first place where women seek help, especially when they are not ready or able to enter a shelter. Women’s centres are also key actors in prevention work, community outreach, awareness-raising, and policy advocacy, ensuring that survivors’ experiences shape national and local responses to violence.

The Istanbul Convention requires states to ensure accessible, well-funded and coordinated specialist services for women survivors of violence. Although it does not name women’s centres directly, the Convention’s guidance makes clear that such specialist, women-focused services are essential to fulfilling these obligations. It recommends one women’s centre offering non-residential support per 50,000 women to ensure adequate availability and access.

### Overview of findings on women’s centres in Europe

Women’s centres providing non-residential specialist support for survivors of VAWG were reported in 44 of 46 (96%) European countries. Only Belarus and Hungary remain without any such services. Across Europe, at least 3,401 women’s centres are operating: 2,510 in EU Member States and 891 in non-EU countries. This represents a decrease compared with the previous report, which reported a total of 4,085 women’s centres.

Out of the 3,401 women’s centres reported in 2024, 562 centres (16%) are run by women’s NGOs, 197 (6%) by other NGOs, 195 (6%) by state authorities, six by faith-based organisations, and seven by other or mixed entities. For 2,434 centres (72%), the managing organisation was not reported, highlighting persistent gaps in national statistical systems. Despite this, women’s NGOs remain the

12 **WAVE COUNTRY REPORT 2025**


---

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

leading providers of specialist support, while state-managed and mixed-service models appear to be increasing in some countries.

Women’s centres across Europe provide a broad range of support. Counselling and psychological services are the most widespread, available in 39 countries (85%), often through trauma-informed and empowerment-based approaches. Legal advice is offered in 38 countries (83%), while representation before courts, police or social services is available in 30 countries (65%). Support for social welfare, benefits, or financial issues is available in 29 countries (63%), and housing advice in 31 countries (67%), reflecting the importance of stability and safety for survivors rebuilding their lives. Employment-related support is reported in only 22 countries (48%).

Women’s centres also play a crucial coordinating role. Referrals and cooperation with other services are reported in 38 countries (83%), making women’s centres central actors within multi-agency responses. Emergency or short-term accommodation linked to women’s centres is available in 25 countries (54%), and in some cases, women’s shelters also function as centres, offering both residential and non-residential support.

Access to women’s centres for those facing additional barriers varies across Europe. About three-quarters of countries report that all or most women’s centres are open to specific groups such as migrant, refugee, disabled or older women, but gaps remain. Refugee women can access all or most centres in 29 countries (63%), and undocumented or insecurely documented women in 25 countries (54%). Accessibility for women with disabilities is uneven: 22 countries (48%) report full or broad access for women with mobility impairments, while 20 countries (43%) report similar access for women with sensory or cognitive disabilities. Older women (65+) have the best access, with 30 countries (65%) reporting all or most centres open to them. Access for transgender women varies significantly: 15 countries (33%) report that most or all centres are accessible. Only 15 countries (33%) report full or broad access for unaccompanied girls under 18.

Specialisation within women’s centres continues to grow. Centres focusing on trafficking in persons are the most widespread, present in 30 countries (65%). Many countries also report specialised services for other groups or forms of violence.

Reliable, sustainable funding remains essential. Thirty-six of 46 countries (78%) report that public funding is the primary source of support for women’s centres. However, funding remains inconsistent and often short-term in many contexts. Stable, multi-year arrangements, where they exist, remain the exception rather than the norm.

## Umbrella Specialist services for survivors of sexualised violence

Sexualised violence is one of the most widespread and harmful forms of VAWG. It covers a broad range of acts that violate women’s physical, psychological and sexual integrity and is overwhelmingly perpetrated by men against women and girls. At the centre of its definition is consent. The Istanbul Convention states that sexual violence, including rape, includes any sexual act carried out without a woman’s freely given agreement, and that consent cannot be assumed from silence, passivity or lack of resistance.

Although many countries have adopted consent-based legal definitions, survivors still face significant barriers in practice. The burden of proof continues to fall heavily on them, and harmful myths and stereotypes persist. Survivors are often questioned about their behaviour, credibility and character, and must frequently explain why their reaction during an assault did not amount to consent. These practices remain re-traumatising and obstruct access to justice.

Survivors of sexualised violence have immediate and long-term needs that require coordinated, specialist and trauma-informed responses. Immediately after an assault, women may need emergency medical treatment, crisis intervention and, where available, forensic examination. Longer-term needs include trauma counselling, peer support, legal information and advocacy to navigate institutions that can feel intimidating or unsafe.

The Istanbul Convention requires states to criminalise all non-consensual sexual acts (Article 36) and to ensure accessible specialist support through rape crisis centres (RCCs) or sexual violence referral centres (SVRCs) (Article 25). These services must be available regardless of whether a survivor reports the assault. The Convention also recommends at least one RCC or SVRC per 200,000

**WAVE COUNTRY REPORT 2025**
**13**



---

inhabitants, with services distributed across regions so that women in rural and remote areas can access them.

Specialist services take different forms. RCCs provide immediate, medium- and long-term emotional and practical support, grounded in feminist, survivor-centred principles. They offer counselling, therapy, advocacy and accompaniment in dealings with police, courts and other institutions, and many also run specialised helplines. SVRCs, often based in hospitals, focus on urgent medical and forensic care, crisis intervention and referrals. Other crisis or medical services provide emergency contraception, sexually transmitted disease prevention and trauma-informed psychological care. Specialised helplines offer confidential support, information and referrals, often serving as the first point of contact.

WSS for survivors of sexualised violence work on principles of belief, autonomy, confidentiality and empowerment. Their independence is essential, allowing them to advocate for survivors’ rights, challenge systemic shortcomings and press for structural change while maintaining cooperation with state institutions to ensure coordinated support.

**Overview of findings on specialised services for survivors of sexualised violence in Europe**

The 2024 data show a persistent and significant gap in the availability of specialist services for survivors of sexualised violence across Europe. To meet the Istanbul Convention requirement of one RCC or SVRC per 200,000 inhabitants, 4,248 centres would be needed in the 46 reporting countries. Only 633 centres are currently in place, leaving a gap of 3,615 services, or 85% of the total required.

In the 27 EU Member States, 2,243 services are needed, but only 334 exist, leaving 85% of required RCCs and SVRCs missing. In the 19 non-EU countries, 299 centres operate despite a need for 2,005, leaving an 85% gap.

Only four countries — Luxembourg, Iceland, Norway and Switzerland — meet or exceed the Istanbul Convention standard. Wales meets the standard, but the United Kingdom as a whole does not, with 65% of services missing. Norway and Switzerland exceed the minimum standard: Norway has 46 centres (compared with 28 required), and Switzerland has 63 centres (surpassing the 45 needed).

Across the 46 countries, the data show 208 RCCs, 221 SVRCs, 204 crisis or medical services and 50 specialist helplines. Provision remains uneven: 14 countries have no RCCs or SVRCs at all, and another 14 have only one or two. Countries with more developed provisions tend to prioritise either RCCs or SVRCs rather than both.

In countries without dedicated specialist centres, WSS often provide support. In Italy, for example, feminist women’s centres in the D.i.Re – National Women’s Network against Violence (Donne in Rete contro la Violenza) offer a full range of specialist services for survivors, including collaboration with forensic and medical services within the national health system.

A wide range of support is available across Europe. Forensic and medical care is reported in 29 countries (63%), and needs assessments are conducted in 31 countries (67%). Specialist psychological care is the most common service, available in 35 countries (76%). Advocacy and legal advice are provided in 27 countries (59%), and 28 countries (61%) report community awareness and prevention activities.

State funding is the main source of financial support for these services in 31 countries (67%), although many still rely on unstable or short-term funding arrangements. Twenty-two countries (48%) receive donations from foundations, trusts or individuals, and 12 (26%) countries report international funding.

Most specialist sexualised violence services are designed for women and girls. Thirty-two countries (70%) provide services for adult women, and 31 (67%) offer support to young women and girls under 18. Twenty-four countries (52%) also provide services for other groups, including men and boys, LGBTQI+ individuals and people with disabilities.

**KEY FINDINGS**

* ~~32 countries out of 46 (70%) have at least one~~ RCC, SVRC, or equivalent specialist service.
* ~~A total of 633 specialist centres (RCCs, SVRCs,~~ crisis or medical services) were reported across Europe.
* ~~In both EU Member States and countries outside~~ the EU, 85% of the necessary services are missing.
* Only four countries (Luxembourg, Iceland, Norway and Switzerland) meet the Istanbul Convention standard of one specialist centre per 200,000 inhabitants.

Recommendations are included at the end of the chapter on specialist services for survivors of sexualised violence.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

## Primary prevention

Primary prevention aims to stop VAWG before it occurs by addressing its root causes. At the same time, primary prevention also means creating the conditions for equality, safety and respectful behaviour in all areas of life. In its 2024 publication A Life Free from Violence, the WAVE Network identifies primary prevention as the most strategic approach to ending VAWG and achieving lasting gender equality. It works at several levels: by educating women, girls, boys and men; engaging communities, including activists, educators and civil society; and seeking change in policies, laws and institutions. Primary prevention can target different groups, such as survivors, potential perpetrators, bystanders, and professionals, through activities such as school-based workshops, feminist self-defence, peer education, and professional training. Together, these measures aim to shift attitudes, behaviours and wider social norms.

Research identifies several primary prevention measures with promising or proven results. Evidence supports school-based programmes that prevent dating violence and help children recognise abuse, as well as home-visitation and health outreach during pregnancy. Empowerment-focused and participatory approaches, including feminist self-defence and community-based initiatives that address structural gender inequality, have also shown positive effects. In contrast, some commonly used approaches, such as general awareness-raising campaigns or confrontational rape-prevention sessions, have not been shown to be effective primary prevention measures. It is essential to distinguish between primary, secondary and tertiary prevention, as these terms are often used interchangeably in state reporting. Primary prevention focuses on stopping violence before it occurs; secondary prevention targets early identification and intervention; and tertiary prevention addresses crisis response, recovery and long-term support.

Article 12 of the Istanbul Convention requires states to prevent VAW by promoting social change, particularly by eliminating the stereotypes and inequalities that sustain it. It calls for gender-sensitive and intersectional measures, attention to vulnerable groups, the promotion of women’s empowerment, the rejection of ’’honour’’-based justifications, and active engagement of men and boys in prevention efforts.

Despite strong evidence and cost-effectiveness, primary prevention continues to receive limited and inconsistent investment. Governments across Europe still devote far more resources to responding to violence after it has occurred than to preventing it. Without sustained funding for primary prevention, violence will continue to cause profound harm to women and children and impose high social and economic costs.

## Overview of findings on primary prevention

Survey responses show that 32 countries (70%) have an official document that includes primary prevention, such as a national action plan (NAP) or a strategy. This includes separate plans for three of the four nations of the United Kingdom, and for Belgium at both national and regional levels. Ten countries (22%) reported having no such document. In some cases, such as Norway, multiple action plans address different forms of violence, but only 18 countries (39%) include a clear definition of primary prevention. This indicates that even where plans exist, the concept is not always clearly understood or applied.

Funding for primary prevention remains limited and inconsistent. Only 16 countries (35%) reported having government funding for primary prevention activities, and where funding exists, it is often small-scale, regional, or linked to specific interventions. Even when funding is available, it is frequently unstable and insufficient for sustained, long-term work.

A wide range of activities are reported across Europe. Awareness-raising campaigns remain the most common, implemented in 39 countries (85%), despite evidence that they are not effective as a primary prevention tool. More promising approaches are also reported: 31 countries (67%) implement empowerment activities for women and girls, 29 (63%) run school-based primary prevention programmes, and 24 (52%) provide training for primary prevention practitioners. Feminist self-defence activities are present in 20 countries (43%), and 19 countries (41%) report programmes specifically targeting men and boys. Bystander intervention training and self-care activities (both implemented in 13 countries, 28%) are the least widespread. While the diversity of activities is encouraging, the current data do not show how far these interventions reach, and limited funding suggests that coverage is likely to remain modest.

Some governments also create barriers to primary prevention efforts, restricting the development or delivery of programmes. Monitoring and evaluation remain weak: only ten countries (22%) reported that public authorities collect data on primary prevention, and only four countries reported any publicly funded evaluation. In 28 countries (61%), no evaluation was conducted, and 21 (46%) provided mixed or unclear answers. This lack of systematic monitoring makes it difficult to assess effectiveness or identify gaps in provision.

## Technology-facilitated violence against women and girls (TFVAWG)

TFVAWG has expanded rapidly over the past decade as digital technologies have become embedded in everyday life. While online platforms offer opportunities for connection, information and activism, they have also become spaces where abuse can spread quickly and with significant impact. Women and girls are disproportionately targeted, and many forms of TFVAWG remain difficult to detect, prove or sanction, leaving survivors with limited protection.

TFVAWG includes any form of GBV carried out, enabled, or intensified through digital technologies or online environments. Its particular severity lies in its scale, reach and persistence: perpetrators can act anonymously, abusive content can be endlessly replicated and shared, and once online, it is often impossible to entirely remove. These dynamics multiply harm, amplify threats and may lead to further abuse both online and offline.

TFVAWG is closely connected to offline violence. Online abuse frequently escalates into physical harm, while violence that begins offline often continues digitally through the non-consensual recording or sharing of intimate images, digital surveillance or cyberstalking during and after abusive relationships. The combined impact can include fear, self-censorship, mental health harms and withdrawal from public or professional life. Women in public roles face particularly high levels of targeted online abuse aimed at silencing them.

GREVIO’s General Recommendation No. 1 (2021) confirms that the obligations under the Istanbul Convention

apply fully to TFVAWG. The Directive (EU) 2024/1385 criminalises the non-consensual sharing of intimate or manipulated material, cyberstalking, cyber harassment and cyber incitement to violence or hatred.

## Overview of findings on TFVAWG

Delegates’ responses show a marked rise in TFVAWG across Europe. Thirty-seven out of 46 countries (80%) reported an increase over the past two years. In nine countries, respondents were unsure, often because no official data is collected. Some noted that the rise may reflect increased visibility and willingness to report rather than an actual increase in incidents. Even so, the evidence points to growing levels of TFVAWG across most of Europe.

The most common forms of TFVAWG reported were cyberstalking, surveillance and spyware, identified in 30 countries (65%), and online harassment, hate speech and threats, also reported in 30 countries (65%). Image-based abuse, including non-consensual intimate image sharing, was reported as increasing in 26 countries (57%). Emerging forms are also becoming more visible: deepfakes and other AI-generated abuse were noted in 10 countries (22%), while sextortion and doxxing were each reported in nine countries (20%). Despite this, TFVAWG remains under-reported. Barriers include stigma, fear of institutional mistrust, and lack of awareness that specialised support exists. Marginalised groups such as migrant and minoritised women, as well as teenage girls, face even greater obstacles to reporting.

The data consistently highlighted that TFVAWG disproportionately affects women in public roles. Politicians, journalists, human rights defenders and feminist activists are frequent targets of coordinated online attacks intended to silence or discredit them. Young women and girls were also repeatedly identified as being at high risk, particularly from cyberbullying, grooming and image-based abuse.

Most countries reported new strategies from WSS to address TFVAWG. Thirty countries (65%) described concrete initiatives, while 12 countries (26%) indicated that they have no specific strategy yet. Innovation across Europe includes new apps, chatbots and digital safety tools. Examples include the Bright Sky app in Albania and the Czech Republic; the Viktoria WhatsApp chatbot in Poland; TinyCheck in Luxembourg for identifying stalkerware; Spain's 24/7 TFVAWG chatbots; and the SafetyNed digital safety service in the Netherlands. Many WSS have developed new safety protocols to address online monitoring, spyware, and coercive control carried out through digital means. Capacity-building efforts are also expanding, with WSS investing in staff training and developing new resources.

Prevention and awareness-raising initiatives have grown, and in several countries, WSS have directly shaped national legal and policy responses. Albania’s national helpline

**16**

Other work focuses on content removal and platform accountability, such as the support in Belgium for women seeking to remove non-consensually shared images.

### KEY FINDINGS
* 37 out of 46 countries (80%) reported an increase in TFVAWG over the past two years.
* The most common forms of TFVAWG were cyberstalking and digital surveillance (30 countries), and online harassment, hate speech and threats (30 countries).
* ~~Image-based abuse increased in 26 countries,~~ while emerging forms such as deepfakes, sextortion and doxxing were also reported.

### Femicide

Femicide refers to the gender-related killing of women and girls. There is still no single, internationally agreed-upon definition, and states, institutions, and researchers use the term differently, which makes comparisons difficult. In many countries, femicide is narrowly understood as the killing of a woman by a current or former partner. Feminist organisations and international mechanisms, including the UN Special Rapporteur on Violence Against Women and Girls, argue that this approach is far too limited and that femicide includes many forms of gender-related killings, including so-called honour killings, dowry-related murders, killings linked to witchcraft accusations, conflict-related deaths, killings connected to trafficking or sexualised violence, and cases where state institutions fail to protect a woman from known violence.

Reliable and comparable data on femicide remain extremely difficult to obtain. The lack of a shared concept affects how cases are recorded and classified. Most countries collect homicide data rather than femicide data, and when gender is documented, it is usually as a demographic detail rather than as a contextual or motivating factor. As a result, many gender-related killings of women never appear as such in official statistics. In some contexts, only intimate partner or family-related homicides are counted as femicide, while in others even these are recorded without reference to gender.

Across Europe, feminist organisations have taken the lead in documenting femicide. They gather and verify cases using media reports, legal records and information from WSS. Their work goes beyond counting deaths: they analyse patterns of coercive control, highlight systemic failures in state responses, and link individual cases to wider inequalities. Many publish reports, speak to the media, run campaigns and organise protests to draw attention to institutional shortcomings and the preventable nature of these killings. For many organisations, documenting femicide is a feminist act of remembrance and resistance, restoring visibility to women’s lives and demanding accountability.

At the international level, the UN Special Rapporteur on Violence Against Women and Girls continues to advocate for national femicide watches or observatories to be established in every country. These mechanisms are intended to record every case of gender-related killing of women and girls, analyse risk factors, identify institutional failures and strengthen prevention efforts.

### Overview of findings on femicide

Information provided by WAVE delegates from 35 out of 46 European countries indicates that at least 2,871 women were victims of femicide in 2024. Data were gathered from a mix of official statistics, media reports, research, and monitoring by WSS. This figure includes estimates from national experts and feminist organisations where official data were missing. No data were available from nine countries, and in several others, only partial or unofficial figures could be collected. Of the total number reported, 969 femicides occurred in EU Member States and 1,902 in countries outside the EU. In many cases, these numbers represent minimum estimates due to the continued lack of systematic monitoring across Europe.

Only 23 countries provided any disaggregated information, meaning that the figures below represent partial totals based on 1,120 cases where additional details were available. Among these cases, 843 women (76%) were killed by a current or former intimate partner, 217 women (19%) were killed by a family member other than a partner, 36 women (3%) by an acquaintance, and 24 women (2%) by other perpetrators, including strangers or unknown offenders.

Information on whether victims had previously received specialist support remains very limited. Of 46 countries, only 16 (35%) provided any information. Among these, 13 (81%) reported that some victims had received support, two (13%) reported that most had, and one (6%) reported that none had. Twenty-two countries reported not knowing, and eight provided no data. This means that in nearly half of European countries, there is no systematic information on whether women killed by men had prior contact with women’s services, shelters or other specialist support.

<page_footer>WAVE COUNTRY REPORT 2025
17
</page_footer>

---

Many women who were later killed had previously contacted state institutions. Out of 46 countries, 24 (52%) reported that some or most femicide victims had earlier sought help from authorities, most commonly the police. These cases highlight significant gaps in protection and follow-up when women report violence.

Recommendations are included at the end of the chapter on femicide.

Use of the term ‘femicide’ varies widely. It is officially used in nine countries (20%), under discussion or in development in four (9%), and utilised informally or mainly in public debate in 22 (48%). Respondents in 11 countries (24%) reported that state institutions do not use the term at all. In many cases, feminist NGOs and activists have driven the adoption of the term in public, academic and media discourse to highlight the gendered patterns behind the killings and to advocate for accountability.

Data collection remains inconsistent. Only six (13%) countries reported that the state officially collects femicide data. NGOs are the most active in documenting femicide, compiling data in 29 countries (63%), often through dedicated databases or reports. Police collect relevant data in 21 countries (46%), usually under general homicide statistics without identifying gender-related motives. Other state bodies collect related information in 19 countries (41%), though rarely under a specific femicide category. Media monitoring is a key source in 10 countries (22%), while academic research is a key source in 12 (26%).

Only a minority of countries have mechanisms to analyse femicide cases and identify lessons for prevention systematically. Twelve (26%) countries reported having such processes in place or under development, indicating early but uneven progress towards more coordinated and accountable responses.

### KEY FINDINGS

* There were at least 2,871 femicides in 2024, based on data and estimates from 35 of 46 countries.

* The term ‘femicide’ is officially used in nine countries, is under discussion in four, and appears mainly in public or academic discourse in 22 countries. In 11 countries, it is not used by state authorities.

* ~~In 29 countries, feminist NGOs are the primary~~ collectors of femicide data; police or other state agencies collect homicide data, but these statistics often do not identify gender-related motives. Many killings of women are recorded without reference to gender.

* Only six countries officially collect femicide data at the state level, and 12 countries have a femicide watch or similar mechanism, though most are not yet integrated into national prevention systems.

# Methodology

## Introduction

The WAVE Country Report is the primary publication of the WAVE Network, published biennially. The Country Report aims to survey the situation of women’s specialist servic- es (WSS) in 46 European countries and identify current progress and gaps concerning service provision, empha- sising five key areas: women’s helplines, women’s shelters, women’s centres, specialist services for survivors of sex- ualised violence, and primary prevention services. To do so, it draws on both quantitative and qualitative data to assess the number of services available in the surveyed countries and to provide insights into their characteristics and accessibility. Additionally, the Report provides a chap- ter on femicide, with insights into the related data collec- tion, and for the first time, a chapter about technology-fa- cilitated violence against women and girls (TFVAWG).

This approach is in line with relevant provisions on spe- cialist support services enshrined in the Council of Europe Convention on preventing and combating violence against women and domestic violence, also known as the Istanbul Convention. Not all countries assessed in the Report have

signed and ratified the Istanbul Convention. Nevertheless, its provisions are considered in this report to assess ser- vice availability across Europe and enable comparison across years and countries. Moreover, other legal instru- ments are referenced in the chapters, such as the Direc- tive EU 2024/1385 on combating violence against women (VAW) and domestic violence, and the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW).

The purpose of the WAVE Country Report is to depict the situation of WSS in Europe from a feminist civil society perspective and to reaffirm why WSS are best placed to provide support for women, their children and girls who are experiencing gender-based violence (GBV) and to pre- vent violence from happening. As the only report of its kind, the WAVE Country Report regularly collects and compares data, enabling monitoring of states’ compliance with inter- national standards for service provision and serving as a crucial tool for advocating improvements at the national and European levels and, eventually, for combating VAW in Europe.

**Research preparation**
* Regular consultations with different WAVE bodies
* Technical improvements of Data Collection Tool (DCT)
* Creation of questionnaire and pilot phase

**Data collection**
* Respondents: WAVE delegates
* Desk research and additional sources

**Data analysis**
* Validation of data
* Regular contact with delegates to confirm data

**Creation of WAVE Country Report**
* Writing country profiles
* Writing comparative chapters and tables
* Editing and feedback by different WAVE bodies

METHODOLOGY

# Research preparation

## A collective effort

Multiple WAVE bodies are involved in the development process of the WAVE Country Report.

The Editing Group was established in 2021 to support the WAVE team in the improvement of the WAVE Country Report and questionnaire and seeks to implement knowledge and expertise from WAVE’s diverse membership into the Country Report. The Editing Group involved in the research preparation of the Country Report 2025 comprises 12 members, including WAVE Advisory Board Members, Board Members, and WAVE Team Members. The members’ responsibilities include providing their expert advice and support on key decisions regarding the methodology and participating in the editing of the Report.

In 2023, the WAVE Country Report included, for the first time, a focus on primary prevention activities. In 2025, after evaluating the responses, the questionnaire section on primary prevention was further developed to improve data collection and reliability. This was done with the support of experts from the former WAVE Thematic Working Group on primary prevention, who provided feedback on the questionnaire and were involved in editing the related chapter.

Additionally, the WAVE Country Report is presented and discussed regularly with the WAVE Advisory Board during its in-person meetings. The Advisory Board consists of the same delegates and co-delegates who are responsible for the data collection at the national level. Presenting the latest published report and discussing its strategic aims help guide its development over the years, based on the experience and input of WAVE delegates from 46 countries. In May 2024 and May 2025, the Advisory Board met in Vienna, and sessions on the Country Report were held to present data from the previous report and gather input for the current one.

Lastly, the WAVE Board and management discuss key methodological and advocacy decisions as needed and guide the research and publications of the WAVE Network.

## The online Data Collection Tool

The Data Collection Tool (DCT) is an online platform run by the WAVE Network to collect data on WSS in Europe. It includes a questionnaire in English divided into a set of general questions and six core sections: national women’s helplines, shelters accessible to women, women’s centres, support services for survivors of sexualised violence, primary prevention activities, and femicide. In 2025, the general questions section also included two open questions on TFVAWG. The questionnaire consists of both closed- and open-ended questions, and collects both quantitative and

qualitative data. In 2025, the DCT was further developed to improve the quality of collected information, make it more user-friendly for respondents, and mitigate differences in support systems and data-collection processes. Each country included in the report has dedicated access to provide the data. Additionally, a number of countries complete multiple questionnaires to facilitate data collection in regions with specific forms of administration or where states do not exercise control over specific territories.

## Data collection process

## Pilot phase and data collection process

Before starting the data collection process for the current Country Report, the updated DCT was piloted by Editing Group members from five countries (Italy, Serbia, Romania, Russia, and the United Kingdom) in March 2025. The goal was to gather feedback and assess the DCT's user-friendliness, identifying areas for improvement. This pilot phase further improved the structure and conciseness of the questionnaire while ensuring comprehensive quantitative and qualitative data collection. The actual data collection took place between April and June 2025 and focused on data from 2024.

The data presented in this report were collected from WAVE member organisations across Europe, represented by one delegate and one co-delegate from each country. When filling out the questionnaire, country delegates were encouraged to consult with other WAVE Members in their countries and relevant government agencies as needed to provide reliable, verified data. The data in the report not only refer to services offered by WAVE members but also to all services available in each country.

The data collected through the DCT was complemented with desk research when, for example, information was lacking or the data provided was not precise. Additional sources also used to prepare the country profiles include Group of Experts on Action against Violence against Women and Domestic Violence (GREVIO) baseline evaluation reports, CEDAW periodic reports, and reports published by national statistical institutes.

## Countries included in the data collection

The data analysed in the report cover 46 European countries (27 European Union (EU) Member States and 19 European countries outside the EU) and were provided by WAVE delegates from each country, with support from WAVE Team members. In some countries, more delegates were involved in data collection, each providing data for their own region or nation. This is the case for the United Kingdom (UK), Belgium, Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Republic of Cyprus (including the northern part of Cyprus) and the Republic of Moldova (including the Transnistrian

Regarding the UK, delegates from each constituent country (England, Northern Ireland, Scotland, and Wales) completed a separate questionnaire. Country profiles were drafted for each of the UK countries; however, when examining service provision in Europe and in countries outside the EU, the UK was counted as a single entity. Two questionnaires were also completed by delegates from Belgium, one covering Flanders (the Flemish-speaking part) and another covering Brussels and Wallonia (the French-speaking part). One country profile was drafted for Belgium, covering the overall situation of service provision in the country and providing specific information for each of the two regions. Similarly, delegates from Bosnia and Herzegovina completed two questionnaires: one for the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the other for Republika Srpska. One country profile was drafted to illustrate the overall situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina and its specificities. In the case of the Republic of Cyprus, since the government does not exercise direct control over the territory of the northern part of Cyprus, administered by Turkish Cypriot authorities, two questionnaires were filled out by WAVE delegates; therefore, the country profile presents the data from the northern part of Cyprus in a different section, at the end of the profile. A similar approach was undertaken for the Republic of Moldova, where the government does not exercise direct control over the Transnistrian region. In this case, two questionnaires were collected, and the profile presents data from the Transnistrian region of Moldova in a separate section.

### Sources for population data

Population data presented in the country profiles and tables were retrieved from Eurostat's database and cover the year 2024,<sup>44</sup> unless otherwise specified. If 2024 data was unavailable for certain countries at the time this report was finalised, the latest year with available data was selected.

### Data analysis process

### Collaboration with WAVE delegates

Once WAVE received data from a country, the WAVE team reviewed the submission and compared it with the data

from previous Country Reports. In case of notable inconsistencies, the respondents were contacted to confirm the reliability of the information provided. Regular communication with them improved the quality of the information and the precision of the country profiles, which were corrected and approved by the respondents before publication.

### Methodological approach to collect and assess data

This report presents data and information on WSS for 2024. Where data for 2024 were unavailable, older data have been provided (referenced in the footnotes).

To assess the provision of national women’s helplines, the standards provided by Article 24 of the Istanbul Convention were applied. Specifically, a 24/7, free-of-charge national women’s helpline is necessary to meet the Istanbul Convention standards. Multilingual support is also strongly recommended and, therefore, included in the relevant tables. While Article 24 recommends that national helplines should provide advice in relation to all forms of violence, this report considers helplines offering support mainly or only in relation to domestic violence as meeting the standards for the provision of national women’s helplines. WAVE’s methodology aims at recognising helplines across Europe that provide a good and gender-competent service to survivors, even if limited to domestic violence, to welcome current promising practices, and eventually encourage states to ensure adequate helpline provision for survivors of all forms of violence.

When assessing the capacity of women’s shelters to accommodate women and their children, the standards provided by Article 23 of the Istanbul Convention were applied. For this methodology, one family shelter place is considered to be equivalent to one shelter bed space. When referring to family places, the Istanbul Convention and its Explanatory Report set a minimum requirement of one family place (covering two beds, one for a woman and one for a child) per 10,000 population.<sup>45</sup> This standard is a valuable tool for assessing the availability of beds in shelters accessible to women and for comparing data across countries, and it is applied in the related chapter and in the tables. Nevertheless, as the specific needs of each country may vary, as acknowledged in the Istanbul Convention Explanatory Report,<sup>46</sup> compliance with this standard is not included in the country profiles; rather, it is used to assess its availability at the European level.

The Country Report distinguishes between women-only shelters and shelters accessible to all survivors, including

METHODOLOGY

women. WAVE considers it essential to underscore the importance of shelters by and for women that apply a feminist, gender-specific approach and to monitor the availability of gender-specific services, as women’s NGOs providing specialist support are increasingly losing funding or contracts to gender-neutral or generic providers.<sup>47</sup> While the overall availability and gaps in beds availability at the European level include all shelters accessible to women, the quality and key aspects of shelters were analysed separately in the country profiles and shelters chapter. A separate column in the country profiles' table is included to record the number of women-only shelters in each country. When presenting information about other shelters that support not only women, the groups of survivors supported by these shelters are specified whenever respondents provide this information. These might include shelters supporting women, men, non-binary people, transgender people, or other specific groups of survivors.

Similarly, the availability of an adequate number of beds in a specific country does not necessarily reflect the accessibility of shelters for different groups of survivors. Therefore, respondents were asked if the shelters in their country are accessible to the following groups of survivors: women with uncertain residence status, undocumented women, refugee women, homeless women, women with physical, cognitive or sensory disabilities, women with substance abuse issues, older women, transgender women, women with older sons, women with children with disabilities and unaccompanied girls under the age of 18. Additionally, it was assessed if there are any shelters specialised in supporting particular groups, e.g., migrant/undocumented women, women with disabilities, Black and minority ethnic women, LGBTQI+ people, older women, or women survivors of specific forms of violence such as trafficking, ‘honour-based’ violence, forced marriage and female genital mutilation (FGM). This information, wherever available, is included in the country profiles in order to provide a clearer picture of the accessibility of shelter services in Europe.

The definition of **women’s centres** includes all women’s services providing non-residential specialist support to survivors and can encompass a broad range of women’s centres. Many women’s centres focus on counselling; however, WAVE recognises that not all women’s centres necessarily provide these services, e.g., some focus primarily or solely on prevention work and advocacy. The relevant tables of the Report include the proportion of the female population per centre, and highlight that in most cases, there are not enough centres to comply with the Council of Europe recommendation of one counselling centre for VAW survivors for every 50,000 women. Secondly, the tables relating to women’s centres indicate who the beneficiaries of such centres are, as in some cases they are women-only, in other cases they support all survivors of GBV; finally, the tables include a column to show whether centres are run by women’s NGOs, other NGOs,

the State, or other providers. This information is relevant because it indicates the general approach to service provision in each country. WAVE recognises that women’s NGOs mostly have a gendered understanding and analysis of VAW, and that their service provision is based on a feminist, gender-sensitive approach that aims to empower women.

As in the shelters section, additional accessibility information was gathered regarding women’s centres. Whenever available, the country profiles provide information on specialist support for particular groups of survivors and women survivors at risk of specific forms of violence. Article 25 of the Istanbul Convention makes specific reference to the provision of support for survivors of sexualised violence. The requirements are that states provide for the establishment of *“appropriate, easily accessible rape crisis or sexual violence referral centres”* for survivors, with the recommendation being one centre available for every 200,000 inhabitants. Therefore, data on the availability of women’s centres and **support services for survivors of sexualised violence** are presented in different sections of the Country Report. Although sexualised violence can also be a form of domestic violence, specialised services for survivors of sexualised violence should be analysed separately from domestic violence services. Importantly, sexualised violence can be committed irrespective of the relationship between the perpetrator and the survivor, in any setting, including but not limited to home and work. Another key feature of specialised sexualised violence services is holistic support for survivors of child sexual abuse and its long-term psychological and physical impact.

Some women’s centres provide support for women survivors of sexualised violence. However, this support is not always specialised and may therefore result in repeated referrals, as many survivors have unique needs, such as immediate forensic testing, complex trauma support and medical services, which general women’s centres supporting all survivors of VAW cannot necessarily provide. Services responding to survivors’ needs should ensure specific sexualised violence training and specialisation of service provision.

It is worth noting that different European countries have varied approaches to the provision of sexualised violence services. In some countries, women’s centres are offering specialised holistic support for all forms of VAW, including sexualised violence. The aim is to avoid multiple referrals and re-traumatisation, as well as ensure adequate and feminist support to survivors. Other countries have consolidated networks of rape crisis centres (RCCs), with trained staff offering immediate and long-term confidential survivor-led counselling and therapy and providing various services such as advocacy and prevention. To reflect these national differences, the questionnaire completed by WAVE delegates included the same multiple-choice
