WOMEN’S SHELTERS

# Accessibility of women’s shelters

## → 24/7 accessibility

Data collected for the WAVE Country Report 2025 show that women-only shelters are accessible around the clock in most European countries. In total, 67% of countries (31 out of 46) report that all or most women-only shelters offer 24/7 access, ensuring immediate availability for women escaping violence at any time. However, in 22% (10 countries), only some shelters provide 24/7 access, and two countries (4%), Belarus and Greece, report no round-the-clock access. In three countries, the situation remains unknown or unclear, often due to fragmented data or decentralised service provision.

This unevenness highlights a continued geographical and policy gap: while some states maintain comprehensive access, others restrict entry to office hours or rely on referral mechanisms that delay safety and protection.

Comments from the WAVE delegates who provided the data further reveal that 24/7 access often depends on interpretation and capacity. In several countries, such as **Finland** and the **Netherlands**, all shelters or emergency crisis centres provide full 24-hour access, ensuring immediate admission at any time. In others, including **Belgium (Flanders)** and **Iceland**, 24/7 accessibility refers primarily to the availability of hotlines or on-call staff, rather than guaranteed physical admission.

In countries like **Luxembourg**, **North Macedonia**, and **Poland**, shelters are reachable at night only through police or emergency referrals, which can create delays or exclude women who seek help independently. Some comments also noted that funding limitations or local administrative rules restrict night-time intake. In **Romania**, several categories of shelters exist, differentiated by the range of services provided and the duration of accommodation. Emergency reception centres offer immediate, short-term refuge for women survivors of violence. These centres are accessible 24/7 and typically accommodate women for a period of two to six months, providing essential services such as food, basic medical care, and psychological support. Recovery centres, on the other hand, provide a more stable and supportive environment with comprehensive assistance, including social services, legal counselling, and rehabilitation programmes. Their primary aim is to support women in regaining autonomy and rebuilding their lives free from violence, with stays lasting up to one year or longer, depending on individual needs.

## → Women’s shelters accessible free of charge

Across Europe, most women-only shelters continue to provide free accommodation and services, ensuring that survivors can access safety without financial barriers. However, the latest data show that 11 out of 46 countries (24%) report that women may be expected to contribute

financially for their stay. These countries are: **Belgium**, the **Czech Republic**, **Denmark**, **France**, **Germany**, **Ireland**, **Luxembourg**, the **Netherlands**, **Slovakia**, **Slovenia**, and parts of the **United Kingdom (Scotland and Wales)**.

In **Belgium** and the **Netherlands**, payment is systematically required, structured as a regulated co-payment model linked to income or social welfare rules. In both contexts, women are routinely expected to contribute a proportion of their accommodation costs, often calculated in accordance with municipal or social housing regulations. In the **Netherlands**, these costs are usually paid for through social welfare or benefits, which the women’s shelters help women apply for with the municipalities. Women who already have income from a salary or otherwise pay from this income. In no case are accommodation costs a barrier to accessing women’s shelters. In **Brussels** and **Wallonia**, women are expected to pay for their accommodation in the shelter, meaning undocumented women without sufficient income have limited access to women-only shelters, whereas in **Flanders**, accommodation is free for the first 12 weeks of a stay in a shelter with a secret address. After this twelve-week period, women are expected to cover the accommodation costs either through their own means or through a contribution from the Public Centre for Social Welfare.

In the remaining countries, payment is conditional or occasional. Women may be asked to contribute only if they have an income or receive social welfare benefits, while those without financial means are accommodated free of charge. In **Germany**, for instance, co-payment practices vary regionally depending on local funding arrangements. In **France**, it is based on the woman's income. In **Ireland**, women are expected to pay from approximately € 30–€ 60 per week, but the inability to pay is commonly considered by services. In **Denmark** and **Luxembourg**, shelters may apply small daily or weekly fees for women with income, which are waived in hardship cases. In **Slovenia**, shelters charge women 30% of the financial social assistance, but this can be adjusted according to income, whereas in **Slovakia**, accommodation is either free for the first few months or subject to only symbolic payments. Any contributions required later are typically adjusted based on the woman’s individual financial situation, including her income and essential expenses. In the **Czech Republic**, women are also expected to pay a fee for their stay. In **Wales**, he majority of the cost is met by Housing Benefit, but survivors also pay a minimal weekly service charge. In **Scotland**, women are expected to pay for their accommodation in shelters, but most do so through housing benefits.

By contrast, the majority of countries, 35 out of 46 (76%), confirm that shelter services are entirely free of charge. In **Russia**, church-affiliated shelters may ask women to help with domestic chores or community work, but no monetary payment is requested.

**WAVE COUNTRY REPORT 2025**

---

# Accessibility for diverse groups of women

Overall, inclusion has improved in recent years, but many women still face structural obstacles to accessing shelter services. Aggregated data show that across Europe, women with uncertain or undocumented residence status can access all or most women’s shelters in 41% of countries (19 out of 46), while 35% (16 countries) report partial access and three countries, **Bulgaria**, **Serbia** and **Russia** (7%) have no women’s shelters that can accommodate this group. These figures confirm that immigration and residency status remain among the strongest determinants of exclusion, particularly in states with ‘no recourse to public funds’ rules or restrictive welfare eligibility.

Refugee and homeless women encounter similar but slightly better conditions. Refugee women can access all or most shelters in 23 countries (50%), and they have partial access in an additional 12 countries (26%), while homeless women can access all or most shelters in 21 countries (46%). These proportions suggest that most shelters can accommodate women in unstable housing situations, but the absence of targeted support and the lack of long-term housing options continue to limit their safety and recovery.

Accessibility for women with disabilities remains inconsistent across Europe. Only 37% of countries report that all or most shelters are physically accessible to women with mobility impairments, while 41% report that some shelters are accessible. For women with cognitive or psychosocial disabilities, 26% of countries report all or most shelters being accessible, and 41% partial accessibility. Shelters designed or renovated without full consideration of accessibility standards often rely on ad hoc adaptations or the goodwill of staff rather than systematic provision. Accessibility for women with sensory disabilities (blind or deaf women) is similar, as 26% of countries state that all or most shelters are accessible and 48% report partial accessibility.

Women with substance abuse issues are among the most excluded groups, with only 17% of countries reporting all or most shelters being accessible, while 17% have no available shelters for this group, and in 48% of the countries, some shelters are available to them. Shelters often cite safety, limited staff capacity, and lack of addiction specialists as reasons for exclusion. This points to an ongoing tension between safety management and inclusivity, where rigid risk-assessment protocols may unintentionally exclude some of the most vulnerable survivors.

Older women (65+) have comparatively better access to shelters, with 61% of countries reporting all or most shelters being open to them, reflecting recognition that violence persists in later life and that ageing survivors require specific support. Older women don’t have access to shelters in only three countries (0.7%): **Belarus**, **Greece** and

**Russia**. Transgender women in 28% of countries have full or broad access, and 35% partial, while in 11% of the countries they are excluded. These disparities are often linked to policy ambiguity, inadequate guidance on inclusive practice, or resistance from funders or authorities to recognising transgender women as legitimate service users.

Shelters are generally more inclusive toward women with children with disabilities, wherein 43% of countries, all or most shelters accept them, and in 30% of the countries, some shelters accept them. Regarding women with older sons (14+), they have full or broad access to shelters in 26% of countries, and access to some shelters in 35% of countries. Unaccompanied girls under 18, however, remain largely excluded: only 20% of countries report that all or most shelters can accommodate them, while 24% provide partial access and 30% none. In most cases, unaccompanied minors fall under child protection rather than GBV frameworks, leaving a protection gap for adolescent girls exposed to violence.

According to the WAVE data, 23 countries report the existence of specialised shelters or accommodation programmes for particular groups of women, such as migrant or undocumented women, women with disabilities, LGBTQI+ survivors, older women, or women affected by specific forms of violence, including trafficking, forced marriage, or so-called honour-based violence. While these services represent essential steps toward inclusivity, they remain limited in number, unevenly distributed, and often dependent on short-term or project-based funding.

The most widespread form of specialised provision across Europe remains shelters for victims of trafficking, reported in 12 countries. In nine countries, there are dedicated services for LGBTQI+ survivors. In eleven countries, there are also shelters for migrant and ethnic minority women. In **Austria**, the women’s counselling centre ‘Orient Express’ in Vienna runs a shelter/emergency apartments, which can accommodate girls and women between the ages of 16 and 24 from all over **Austria**, who are affected by forced marriage.<sup>70</sup> In **Sweden**, there are specific shelters for women with substance abuse issues, women subjected to prostitution, pornography and trafficking, and women survivors of honour-based violence. Dedicated facilities for women with disabilities, older women, or women with substance abuse issues are comparatively rare and usually operate through partnerships between NGOs and specialised service providers rather than as stand-alone shelters. For example, in **Albania**, the Albanian Disability Rights Foundation offers specialised support, including technology-based tools and peer mentoring and partners with shelters to improve accessibility for women with disabilities. In **Slovenia**, there is one shelter specifically designed for women who have substance abuse issues and are survivors of violence.

70 In Sweden, prostitution is considered a form of men’s violence against women by law.

WOMEN’S SHELTERS

### Funding for women-only shelters

Reliable, sustainable funding remains one of the most critical determinants of whether women-only shelters can provide consistent, quality, and survivor-centred support. According to the data collected, 44 of 46 countries report state or municipal funding as a primary source, whereas there is none in Azerbaijan and Belarus. In Moldova, state funding is provided, but not extended to the Transnistrian region, where shelters rely exclusively on international and private sources.

In several Western and northern European countries, such as the **Netherlands**, **Denmark**, **Germany**, **Austria**, and **France**, shelters are integrated into public social protection systems and receive funding from national, regional, and municipal budgets. In **Austria**, women’s shelters are funded by the respective federal states and local governments, resulting in differing funding schemes across regions, and women are usually asked to enter shelters in their own area unless they are facing a high-risk situation. In **Finland**, for example, all three women-only shelters have been fully state-funded since 2015, following ratification of the Istanbul Convention. In **Denmark**, municipalities finance shelter accommodation at daily rates between DKK 1,000–3,000 (ca. €130–400), with 50% reimbursement from the state. However, in other contexts, public funding covers only basic operational costs, and shelters must actively seek supplementary resources to provide comprehensive support. In **Bosnia and Herzegovina**, for example, a 2025 amendment to the Law on Protection from Domestic Violence establishes a framework for funding shelters from federal, cantonal, and local budgets, but the exact financing percentages were removed, leaving implementation uncertain. Similarly, in **Serbia**, women-only shelters are financed from local government budgets, which mainly cover basic operations, but are also supported by donations from foundations and individuals. In **Slovenia**, the Ministry of Labour, Family, Social Affairs and Equal Opportunities is the primary funder of the 16 women-only shelters, covering around 70% of their costs.

Beyond state support, donations from foundations, private individuals, and trusts are among the primary funding sources in 31 countries. Donations remain particularly important for feminist NGOs, which use them to cover staff salaries, rent, utilities, and emergency assistance when state funding is delayed or insufficient. In **Armenia**, for instance, state funding typically covers only 10% of women’s shelters' budgets, with the remainder coming from foundations, international donors, and individual contributions. International funding was reported in 16 states, and additionally in the northern part of Cyprus. It plays a vital role in sustaining shelters in non-EU countries when domestic resources are limited. Examples include support from UN agencies, foreign embassies, and private foundations, often providing lifelines for independent women’s NGOs that cannot access national funding. In **Türkiye**, for instance, the Mor Çatı Women’s Shelter Foundation operates the

only independent feminist shelter, financed exclusively through donations and international projects.

Religious institutions contribute to shelter funding in nine countries: **Albania**, **Germany**, **Italy**, **Malta**, **Portugal**, **Romania**, **Russia**, **Switzerland**, and **Ukraine**. In most cases, this support is provided through church-affiliated charities or faith-based NGOs, rather than feminist women’s organisations. In **Russia**, for example, some shelters run by the Orthodox Church provide accommodation and basic aid, though not necessarily gender-specific or rights-based services.

A particularly detailed report from **Albania** shows an expanding network of state-funded services. In 2024, the Ministry of Health and Social Protection financed 11 services for victims of violence, including six multifunctional emergency centres, three shelters for victims of violence and trafficking, one national counselling line, and one day residential service for women and girls in vulnerable situations, reaching over 4,000 beneficiaries with a budget increase from 51.8 million ALL to 79.4 million ALL (€ 515,000 to € 789,000.). Crowdfunding was also reported as an emerging supplementary source in some contexts.

Despite progress, funding remains fragmented, project-based, and precarious in much of Europe. Many shelters operate under annual budget renewals or competitive tenders, which undermine long-term planning and the ability to retain experienced staff.

In contrast, a few countries, such as **Sweden**, **Slovenia**, and **Iceland**, offer multi-year, partnership-based agreements between the state and women’s NGOs, which guarantee stability and preserve independence.

### Entities running women-only shelters

The data collected show that women-only shelters across Europe are most frequently operated by women’s NGOs with a gender-specific or feminist approach. Such organisations run shelters in 38 out of 46 countries, confirming that the women’s movement continues to form the backbone of protection and support for women and their children escaping violence. In addition, 20 countries report women-only shelters operated by other NGOs, while faith-based organisations provide such services in 14 countries. State authorities run women-only shelters in 17 countries, as well as in the northern part of Cyprus, and four countries report that shelters are managed by other entities, such as government-organised non-governmental organisations (GONGOs) or hybrid partnerships between public and private actors.

In total, WAVE delegates reported 760 shelters run by feminist women’s NGOs, 180 by other NGOs, 181 by faith-based organisations, and 449 by state institutions. These figures should be interpreted with caution, as several countries were unable to provide disaggregated data or

**WAVE COUNTRY REPORT 2025**

**49**


---

could only offer estimates. In some contexts, data are not systematically collected at the national level, and in others, shelter management is decentralised, with responsibilities shared between local authorities and contracted service providers. This makes it difficult to establish an exact breakdown of shelter operators, particularly in countries with mixed or hybrid models.

Despite these challenges, the data clearly demonstrate that women’s NGOs continue to play a leading and irreplaceable role in ensuring that women-only shelters operate in line with feminist principles and international standards. However, the growing involvement of state and non-feminist actors marks an important structural shift. In several countries, the expansion of state-run and faith-based services has been accompanied by a reduction in the influence of feminist NGOs, often linked to competitive funding models or changes in policy frameworks that favour gender-neutral or welfare-oriented service provision. There has been an increase in the proportion of shelters run by private, profit-driven actors in **Sweden**. In 2012, only 8% of shelters were run by private, profit-driven actors. This figure rose to 37% in 2019, and in the latest mapping report, it stands at 47%. At the same time, the proportion of non-profit shelters has decreased from 54% in 2019 to 46% in the first quarter of 2024.

Examples from national contexts illustrate the diversity of organisational models. In **Albania**, a mixed system exists in which seven shelters are run by NGOs, including Edlira Haxhiymeri, Different and Equal, Woman to Woman, and Vatra, while others are operated by faith-based organisations (*Papa Giovanni XXII* in Shkodër and *Rozalba Home* in Lezhë), and by the state (including the National Centre for the Treatment of Victims of Domestic Violence and the shelter for victims of human trafficking). In **Austria**, the long-established Association of Austrian Autonomous Women’s Shelters (*Autonome Österreichische Frauenhäuser – AÖF*) continues to provide gender-specific support, although some shifts have taken place, such as in Salzburg, where the former women’s shelter was replaced by a mixed model jointly managed by Association VIELE and Jugend am Werk. In **Finland**, several municipal and national agencies operate shelters, but *Turvakoti Mona*, run by a women’s NGO focusing on cultural and ethnic diversity, remains an example of feminist practice within a publicly funded framework. In **Moldova**, *Casa Mărioarei* remains the only feminist-run shelter, offering empowerment-based, trauma-informed support to survivors and representing a model that should be expanded nationwide. In **Slovenia**, feminist organisations such as SOS Helpline for Women and Children, the Association for Nonviolent Communication, and *Ženska svetovalnica* operate alongside state and faith-based services. In **Türkiye**, the Ministry of Family and Social Services runs 112 shelters, municipalities manage 35, and the Directorate of Migration oversees two, reflecting a highly centralised, state-led model.

## Geographical coverage

The data collected by WAVE show that women-only shelters are available across all regions in 16 countries, while in 11 countries, they cover most regions (over 50%). In 13 other countries, shelters are concentrated in major cities; in Armenia, the northern part of Cyprus, and the Transnistrian region of the Republic of Moldova, they are located only in the capital. For five countries, no information was provided.

This distribution highlights persistent regional disparities in access to safe accommodation for women and their children. In several countries, particularly those with centralised or urban-based service networks, women living in rural or remote areas continue to face significant barriers to reaching protection.

Comments from WAVE delegates underline that these gaps are not merely geographic but also reflect broader inequalities in resource allocation and local governance capacity. In federal or decentralised systems, such as those in **Austria** and **Spain**, regional authorities have varying levels of responsibility and funding for shelter provision, resulting in uneven coverage. In smaller countries like **Slovenia** or **Denmark**, the concentration of shelters in urban centres is partly offset by well-developed outreach and referral mechanisms, while in others, such as **Poland** and **Serbia**, large regions remain without any women-only shelter.

The WAVE data reveal considerable variation in how long women usually stay in women-only shelters across Europe. In eight countries, the average length of stay is limited to up to three months, while in 15 countries, women remain for three to six months. In 12 countries, stays of up to one year are possible, and in three countries, women may stay for more than a year, often in transitional or reintegration shelters designed to support longer-term recovery. In some countries, shelters offer varying lengths of stay. Some shelters have a fixed length of stay, sometimes connected to funding models, while others are more flexible. Eight countries did not provide any data on this question.

These figures suggest that while most countries provide mid-term accommodation (up to six months), only a smaller group offers the extended stays necessary for survivors to rebuild stability and autonomy. In practice, the duration of stay often depends on the type of shelter: emergency shelters typically accommodate women for a few weeks to several months, while reintegration or recovery shelters may allow stays of one year or more. For example, in some systems, emergency shelters provide accommodation under court-issued protection orders, after which women are referred to long-term reintegration services, though these remain limited in number.

WOMEN’S SHELTERS

# Data on the provision of services in women’s shelters

According to data collected for the WAVE Country Report 2025 on the three most common forms of violence reported by survivors accommodated in women-only shelters, domestic violence remains by far the most common form of violence, cited by 35 countries. This broad category encompasses various overlapping forms of abuse, most frequently physical and psychological violence, which were reported by 32 and 23 countries, respectively.

Other forms of violence were reported less frequently as one of the three most common forms. Sexualised violence was identified in nine countries, while economic violence and violence directly or indirectly affecting children were mentioned in five and seven countries, respectively. Stalking and technology-facilitated violence against women and girls (TFVAWG) were rarely captured, reported in only three and two countries, reflecting both their underreporting and the absence of systematic data collection in shelter services.

The most common forms of in-house support are counselling and psychological assistance, reported in 41 countries, and referrals or collaboration with other services, reported in 39 countries. These findings underline the dual role of shelters as both safe spaces and coordination hubs within national support systems.

Casework, which includes safety planning, risk assessment, and individual support plans, is available in 39 countries, demonstrating that most shelters work through structured, personalised approaches tailored to each survivor’s situation. Practical advice on housing, social benefits, healthcare, or employment is offered in 35 countries, reflecting the recognition that long-term independence requires economic and social reintegration.

Finally, legal advice is provided in 33 countries, often through partnerships with women’s rights NGOs or legal aid providers. Access to legal counselling remains uneven, however, with some shelters relying on external referral systems rather than in-house expertise.

When it comes to declining referrals, the most frequently cited reason was no space or capacity to support the survivor, reported in 31 countries, followed by survivors being ineligible for support (for example, the woman was an undocumented migrant, or the woman did not experience VAW) in 21 countries. Insufficient capacity to accommodate women with children was cited as a reason for declining referrals in 16 countries. Shelters in 23 countries also reported having to decline referrals because they were not adequately equipped to meet the specific needs of some survivors, for instance, women with physical or mental disabilities, or those requiring specialised accessibility adaptations.

Qualitative comments reveal that capacity shortages remain a significant obstacle across Europe. In some countries, such as Austria and Moldova, shelters operate at or near full occupancy year-round, leaving many women unable to find a place when they need it. For example, in Austria’s AÖF network, approximately 58% of women declined in 2023 could not be accommodated due to a lack of space. The situation is particularly acute for women with children, as many facilities have limited family rooms.

In addition to capacity issues, several WAVE delegates reported that infrastructural barriers and restrictive admission criteria contribute to a decline in referrals. Shelters often lack facilities for women with disabilities or mental health conditions, and in some cases cannot accommodate women with substance use issues or severe psychiatric disorders due to safety and staffing limitations. Accessibility is further constrained where shelters operate in privately rented buildings that cannot be modified for physical access.

## Findings on other shelters

Across Europe, 36 out of 46 countries reported the existence of shelters other than women-only facilities that can accommodate and support survivors of VAW. In total, these countries identified 859 such shelters. The range of services and target groups varies widely, reflecting differences in welfare systems, funding structures, and national approaches to violence prevention and protection.

These shelters include mixed-gender crisis centres, family shelters, anti-trafficking facilities, faith-based safe houses, and centres for specific vulnerable groups, such as LGBTQI+ individuals, teenage mothers, or people with substance abuse issues. In several countries, including Belgium, Poland, and Albania, such facilities are run by local authorities or large social welfare organisations, while NGOs often complement their work by providing specialised counselling or referral services.

However, many of these mixed or general shelters lack the specialised, gender-sensitive approach necessary for addressing the specific needs of women survivors of violence. For example, in Belarus, survivors may share accommodation with men, including potential perpetrators, or may be housed in facilities without confidentiality safeguards. Others are placed in ‘crisis rooms’ or temporary accommodation units under social welfare systems, which do not always ensure safety, privacy, or trauma-informed care.

Among the 36 countries reporting the existence of mixed or non-specialised shelters, the majority indicated that these facilities are open to multiple gender groups and survivor categories. According to the WAVE delegates, 23 countries confirmed that such shelters accommodate cisgender women, 19 accept cisgender men, 17 include

**WAVE COUNTRY REPORT 2025**

51


---

transgender women, 15 accept transgender men, and 16 are open to non-binary people. Additionally, 11 countries noted that shelters also support other groups of survivors, such as people with disabilities, refugees, and survivors of trafficking and those affected by homelessness.

While these figures suggest a growing trend toward inclusivity, several delegates emphasised that the mere openness of shelters does not necessarily ensure safety or gender-competent care. In many cases, the shelters do not apply gender- or trauma-informed approaches, nor do they have trained staff or infrastructure to meet the specific needs of LGBTQI+ individuals or survivors with disabilities. In some countries, admission is formally unrestricted, but services remain de facto gender-neutral, meaning that women survivors of male violence may lack adequate protection, confidentiality, and support tailored to their experiences.

Moreover, respondents highlighted that data on access for transgender and non-binary people are rarely disaggregated or systematically recorded, and that many facilities assume inclusivity without explicit policies or safeguards. Out of the 36 countries that reported the existence of other shelters supporting survivors of VAW, only six countries stated that all such shelters offer 24/7 access, while three reported that most do. In eight countries, only some shelters are available around the clock, and in one country, Belarus, it was indicated that none of their mixed or general shelters provide continuous access.

# COUNTRY EXAMPLE: Croatia

Croatia’s network of women’s shelters has a long feminist history rooted in the activism of the women’s movement. The first shelter was opened in 1990 by the Autonomous Women’s House Zagreb (AWHZ), marking the beginning of organised, rights-based protection for women survivors of violence. Throughout the 1990s and 2000s, six additional autonomous women’s shelters were established by women’s NGOs across the country. In 2024, Croatia reported 26 shelters accessible to women.

The shelter system operates under a mixed model, combining women’s shelters run by feminist NGOs with state, church, city, and county-run homes that accommodate survivors of domestic violence.

Funding for autonomous women’s shelters has deteriorated over time. In the early years, the state, city, and county governments jointly financed around 90% of their annual budgets, each contributing approximately 30%. Today, funding is provided through three-year contracts following public tenders, but each of these authorities now covers less than 30% of operational costs.

Concerns have also been raised about the inclusion of religious organisations in state tenders for shelters. For example, the St. Michael shelter, operated by the Association Betlehem, a faith-based organisation known for its opposition to abortion and sexual and reproductive rights, received state funding under the same mechanism as feminist-run shelters. This raises questions about value-based consistency and adherence to women’s human rights principles in state-funded service provision.

Overall, Croatia’s shelter system reflects both the legacy of feminist leadership in establishing life-saving support for women and the increasing institutionalisation and bureaucratisation of these services. Safeguarding the feminist model that built Croatia’s first shelters remains critical to ensuring that protection services uphold survivors’ rights, empowerment, and safety.

# Conclusion

The latest WAVE findings confirm what the feminist shelter movement has long known: women-only shelters are indispensable, life-saving, and rights-affirming services, and Europe still lacks enough of them. Across 46 countries, 3,224 shelters accessible to women offer 48,860 bed spaces for a population of 847 million, far short of the Istanbul Convention’s recommendation of one place per 10,000 inhabitants, which corresponds to 84,732 beds needed. Only 12 countries (as well as Northern Ireland) currently meet this baseline. Capacity gaps are compounded by uneven geographic distribution, with many rural and remote areas lacking timely access and partial 24/7 availability, which can be the difference between safety and grave risk.

The Council of Europe Quality Guidelines and Article 23 of the Istanbul Convention are clear: shelters must be safe, confidential, survivor-centred, free of charge for women without means, staffed by trained women professionals, and available for as long as needed. Yet practice remains inconsistent. Many countries report co-payment regimes or ad-hoc fees; women with undocumented status, disabilities, substance use needs, or older sons face structural barriers; and unaccompanied girls are frequently excluded due to system silos. The most common reasons for declining referrals are a lack of space and an inability to meet specific needs, revealing gaps in capacity and accessibility. The data also underscore the irreplaceable role of feminist women’s NGOs: they operate shelters in 38 countries and anchor survivor-centred, empowerment-based methodologies. However, procurement and gender-neutral service models risk displacing women’s NGOs with generic providers, diluting expertise and trust.

# HOUSE-USER Recommendations

* States should establish clear minimum quality standards for women’s shelters in line with the Istanbul Convention and the Council of Europe’s Quality Guidelines for Shelters for Victims of Violence against Women and Domestic Violence. These should cover safety, confidentiality, staffing ratios, survivor participation, and accountability mechanisms.

* Governments must guarantee adequate, long-term, multi-year core funding for women’s shelters and their umbrella organisations to ensure long-term sustainability and reduce dependence on short-term grants or competitive procurement systems that undermine continuity and autonomy.

* States should establish or strengthen coordination between women’s shelters and other key sectors such as law enforcement, justice, health, social welfare, housing, and employment services, ensuring survivors can access adequate support through integrated referral mechanisms, including long-term and affordable housing for survivors after leaving shelters.

* Governments must create or strengthen national databases and monitoring systems to track the number, capacity, and occupancy of women’s shelters, ensuring data are disaggregated by gender, age, disability, and residence status while maintaining confidentiality.

* Women’s shelters must be accessible to all women, including women with disabilities, older women, migrant and refugee women, queer women, and those with substance-use or mental-health needs, supported by staff trained in inclusive and intersectional practice. Access to women’s shelters should be possible irrespective of whether women are undocumented or have a precarious migrant status.

* States must ensure adequate geographical distribution of women’s shelters, including in rural and remote areas, and promote public awareness on the right of women to access safe accommodation and available services through accessible, multilingual information.

* Governments should integrate women’s shelters into national emergency-response protocols and crisis-response plans. These protocols should be incorporated into National Action Plans on VAWG and ensure continuity of protection and access

to shelters for women and children during crises, conflicts, displacement, and natural disasters.

* States should protect the feminist, survivor-centred character of women’s shelters by prioritising WSS with proven gender-specific expertise in policy frameworks. Regular consultation with survivors and women’s NGOs must be institutionalised, ensuring that those directly affected shape shelter policies and monitoring mechanisms.

* Women’s shelters must be staffed by professionals who have received adequate training on how to prevent and respond to VAWG and must put the survivor and her needs at the centre of all interventions. Ongoing training and support for shelter staff, including mental health advice, must be guaranteed to ensure that they can provide the best care to survivors and manage the emotional toll of their work.

# Women’s centres

icon: decorative flower-like symbol

## Introduction

Women’s centres are a cornerstone of specialist support for women and their children survivors of violence against women and girls (VAWG). They provide non-residential, gender-sensitive services that combine emotional, legal, and practical support with empowerment and advocacy. Rooted in feminist principles, these centres not only respond to the immediate needs of survivors but also work to transform the social and institutional conditions that sustain gender inequality and VAWG.

Across Europe, women’s centres operate in diverse contexts, some as independent feminist NGOs, others as part of integrated service systems or networks connected to shelters. Despite this diversity, their fundamental mission is consistent: to offer safe, confidential, and women-centred spaces where survivors are believed, supported, and empowered to rebuild their lives. Women’s centres are also key actors in prevention, awareness-raising, and policy advocacy, ensuring that women’s lived experiences inform national and local responses to violence.

According to WAVE’s methodology for this data collection, the term ‘women’s centre’ includes all women’s services providing non-residential specialist support to survivors, serving only or predominantly women survivors of violence and their children (if any). These centres provide empowering short and long-term support, based on a feminist and gender-specific approach to violence and focusing on the human rights and safety of survivors. The following services are subsumed under the term:

* Women’s counselling and women’s crisis centres supporting women survivors of all forms of gender-based violence (GBV)

* Services offering support to survivors of sexualised violence

* Regional crises centres on domestic violence centres

* Pro-active intervention centres serving victims as a follow-up to police interventions

* Specialist services for particular groups such as Black and minority ethnic women, migrant and refugee women survivors of violence

* Outreach services

* Services providing independent domestic or sexual violence advisors

* Other newer types of services

These centres usually provide information, advice, advocacy and counselling, practical support, court accompaniment, proactive support, outreach, and other services.

Since the WAVE Country Report 2023, the landscape of women’s centres has continued to evolve under the combined pressures of gender equality backsliding, austerity measures, and increasing institutionalisation of services. In many countries, feminist NGOs face shrinking funding opportunities, competition from gender-neutral or state-run services, and challenges in sustaining their autonomy and quality standards. At the same time, the demand for specialist, long-term, and trauma-informed support remains high, particularly among women facing multiple forms of discrimination or displacement.

## International obligations

The Istanbul Convention sets out clear obligations for states to ensure that services for women subjected to all forms of violence are accessible, adequately funded and well-coordinated. Article 18 provides the overarching framework, requiring states to establish a comprehensive and effective network of general and specialist services to protect and assist survivors and their children.<sup>71</sup> It emphasises that all measures must be based on a gendered understanding of violence, respect women’s human rights, and prioritise their safety and empowerment. Article 22 builds on this by requiring immediate, short-term and long-term specialist support services for all women survivors of violence and their children. Although the Convention<sup>72</sup> does not explicitly refer to women’s centres, the Explanatory Report makes clear that such specialist women’s services, providing counselling, legal and practical assistance, advocacy and empowerment support, are central to meeting these obligations.<sup>73</sup> It also recommends that one women’s centre providing non-residential support should be available for every 50,000 women in the population, ensuring adequate coverage and accessibility. Women’s centres, therefore, represent a key pillar of the Convention’s implementation, putting its standards into practice at a community level.

The European Union (EU) Directive 2024/1385 acknowledges the importance of women’s specialist support services in its Preamble (paragraphs 58–59), emphasising their role in providing targeted, integrated support tailored

WOMEN’S CENTRES

to survivors’ needs. However, the Directive's framing prob- lematically positions these services as optional add-ons to general victim support rather than as essential, auton- omous pillars, and the Preamble lacks the binding legal status accorded to specialist services under the Istanbul Convention and in line with WAVE standards. Article 25 perpetuates this ambiguity by suggesting specialist ser- vices can form part of general services, blurring the clear distinction established by the Istanbul Convention, and merely references women’s support services as potential referral points rather than as foundational systems of sup- port. This limited recognition fails to align with Article 22 of the Istanbul Convention, which asserts that specialist women’s support services, best delivered by women’s or- ganisations rooted in feminist principles and survivor-cen- tred approaches, are independent and critical for effective- ly addressing GBV.

The UN Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW), in its General Recommendation No. 35 on gender-based violence against women (2017),<sup>74</sup> calls on States to ensure that survivors have access to shelters, counselling, legal aid, and support from women’s organisations. This establishes a clear expectation that States should fund and enable women-led, gender-sensi- tive services, including women’s centres, as part of com- prehensive protection systems.

### WAVE framework for data collection on women’s centres

This chapter provides an updated overview of women’s centres in Europe in 2024, based on data and qualitative input from WAVE members. Respondents provided data on the number and type of women’s centres in their coun- try, distinguishing between those working only with wom- en survivors of violence against women (VAW), those open to all survivors of GBV, and other forms of provision. The questionnaire also collected information on the range of services available, including counselling and psycholog- ical support, legal advice, advocacy, and practical assis- tance such as housing or employment support. It explored accessibility for diverse groups of women, the existence of specialised services for survivors of specific forms of violence, management and funding structures, and geo- graphical coverage.

This comprehensive approach enables comparison across countries and identifies progress and remaining gaps in meeting the Istanbul Convention’s standards for specialist support. The 2024 data reaffirm the central role of feminist women’s centres in ensuring effective, survivor-centred re- sponses to VAWG.

<sup>74</sup> See CEDAW Committee (2017) General Recommendation No. 35 on gender-based violence against women, updating General Recommendation No. 19, paras. 31(b) and 32.

## Findings on the situation of women’s centres in Europe

Women’s centres providing non-residential specialist sup- port for survivors of VAWG were reported in 44 of the 46 European countries covered by WAVE. Only Belarus and **Hungary** remain without any such provision. According to data from WAVE members, at least 3,401 women’s cen- tres operate across Europe: 2,510 in EU member states and 891 in non-EU countries. This represents an overall de- crease compared with the previous report, which reported a total of 4,085 women’s centres (2,995 in the EU, 1,090 in non-EU countries).

Applying the Council of Europe’s recommendation of one counselling centre for every 50,000 women, the current figures indicate a continued gap. Across Europe, there is approximately one women’s centre per 129,329 women, meaning that provision still falls far short of the minimum standard, and 61% of the women’s centres recommended at the European level remain missing. While many coun- tries report progress in maintaining or expanding their net- works, significant geographical gaps persist, particularly in rural or remote areas.

The women’s centres across Europe differ in their scope and target groups, reflecting different national policy frameworks, funding models and feminist traditions. Based on the data collected, most countries distinguish between four broad categories of provision:

* Centres serving women survivors of VAW – explicitly women-only and feminist in orientation

* Centres serving all survivors of GBV or domestic violence – open to women, men and sometimes children

* Other centres – including general victim support services or centres without a defined gender focus

* Undefined – where no information was provided on the primary target group

Across Europe, 1,425 centres (42%) work with women survivors of VAW and their children. According to the data, 710 centres (21%) are open to all survivors of gender-based or domestic violence, while a smaller group of 43 centres (1%) provide other forms of support not directly connected to VAW, and for 1,223 centres (36%), the target group was not specified in the data available.

In the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, all eight women’s centres provide support specifically for women survivors of violence, offering counselling, legal assistance, and representation at courts and other institutions.

The same is true for Greece, where all 44 centres operate as services for women, although this data is for state-run women’s services, while data for NGO services is not available. In Estonia, all 19 identified centres follow this model, providing specialist, women-only support.

In Scotland, 36 out of 37 women’s centres work only with women survivors, while in Wales, all 20 centres are women-only. These services are deeply rooted in feminist practice and provide comprehensive, gender-specific support, including counselling, legal advice and advocacy, often delivered through national women’s aid networks.

In Switzerland, among the 24 women’s centres, the majority serve only women survivors, with a small number open to all survivors of GBV. Each canton has a state-funded information centre for survivors of violence and gender-related issues, alongside NGO-run counselling centres specifically for women.

Of the 710 centres open to all survivors of gender-based or domestic violence, some are run by the state and some by women’s NGOs. In Finland, Denmark, Poland, Norway, Türkiye and Azerbaijan, state-run or mixed centres provide assistance to all survivors. In Slovakia, women’s NGOs have been legally required to offer services to all domestic violence survivors to obtain accreditation. In Germany, the network includes both feminist women’s counselling centres and mixed-gender support organisations.

In Albania, there are twelve women’s centres. Five work with women survivors of violence, and five support all survivors of GBV, while the remaining two mainly engage in advocacy activities. The women-only centres, many of which are part of the Albanian Women Empowerment Network (AWEN) or the Monitoring Network Against Gender-Based Violence, provide legal, psychological, and social support grounded in feminist practice. Centres open to all survivors, such as the Psycho-Social Centre Vatra, provide counselling, reintegration and advocacy services. Two other centres operate within broader social service or gender equality frameworks.

In Denmark, six women’s centres operate nationwide: four work with women only and two are open to all survivors. ”The Mother’s Aid – Out of the Shadow of Violence“ programme supports women and their children after leaving abusive relationships, offering counselling, legal advice and reintegration services. The Joan Sisters Centre provides peer-led, trauma-informed counselling for women affected by sexual violence, while Tell Someone offers individual and group counselling for survivors of partner violence and their families.

In Finland, there are 28 women’s centres, most of which are run by the Federation of Mother and Child Homes and Shelters. Under state accreditation rules, 24 centres are open to all survivors, though women make up the vast

56

**WAVE COUNTRY REPORT 2025**

---



WOMEN’S CENTRES

majority of those they work with. This system reflects Fin- land’s integrated, gender-neutral approach to responding to violence.

In **Austria**, 65 counselling centres for women and girls op- erate within the national Network of Austrian Counselling Centres for Women and Girls, along with 17 independent centres. All are feminist and state-funded, providing legal, psychological and practical support across all nine feder- al states. In addition, 32 Violence Protection Centres work with all survivors of GBV, with women representing about 80% of those supported.

While different services can play an important role in en- suring geographical coverage, they often lack a gendered understanding of violence. WAVE members continue to express concern that gender-neutral approaches risk eras- ing women’s specific experiences of male violence and weakening specialist feminist provision of services.

In the group of centres that provide other forms of sup- port not directly connected to VAW, there are general ‘cri- sis rooms’ or ‘violence prevention centres’ that provide casework and referrals but are not specialised in VAW. In **Bulgaria**, services for survivors of violence mainly focus on domestic violence. The law defines victims broadly, including both women and men. Women’s NGOs provide counselling and other support to all survivors of domestic violence, though their work primarily focuses on women. In **Hungary**, there are non-residential services for the sup- port of survivors of domestic violence, which are called ‘crisis ambulances’. Currently, there are seven crisis ambu- lances in the country, with regional spread. Most of them are operated by the Hungarian Interchurch Aid. These ser- vices, however, do not categorise themselves as women’s centres; they are not operated by a feminist approach to violence. NANE and PATENT Associations provide in-per- son victim support services with a feminist approach, but they do not operate as centres; their scope and outreach are determined and limited by available human and finan- cial resources. The ‘Integrated Client Service’ – a joint NANE-PATENT initiative – offers trauma-aware support to survivors: legal assistance, psychological and social counselling, provided by a team of experts who regularly consult with one another to ensure balanced and coordi- nated cooperation. The ‘Helper's Network’ – also a joint NANE-PATENT initiative – was operational in 2024 and provided victims/survivors with technical and practical support for legal and administrative processes, in a trau- ma-informed and victim-centred manner.

### Entities running women’s centres

Women’s centres across Europe are managed by a diverse range of entities, reflecting national policy frameworks, funding systems and institutional traditions. According to WAVE’s data collection for this report, five main types of service providers operate across the region: women’s

NGOs, other NGOs, state-run services, faith-based organi- sations, and other or mixed providers.

Out of a total of 3,401 women’s centres reported in 2024, 562 centres (16%) are run by women’s NGOs, 197 centres (6%) by other NGOs, 195 centres (6%) by state authorities, six centres by faith-based organisations, and seven cen- tres by other or mixed entities. For 2,434 centres (72%), no information was provided on the managing entity.

Women’s NGOs remain the leading providers of women’s centres across Europe. They manage more than half of all identified centres and are the leading providers in **Austria**, **Croatia**, **Italy**, **Portugal**, **Slovenia**, **Spain**, **Serbia**, **North Macedonia**, and **Kosovo**, where services are defined as feminist, women-only and survivor-centred. In these coun- tries, women’s NGOs offer integrated services that com- bine counselling, legal and practical support, and advocacy and empowerment. For instance, the Austrian Association of Autonomous Women’s Shelters and the Central Infor- mation Office of Autonomous Women’s Shelters (*Zentrale Informationsstelle Autonomer Frauenhäuser, ZIF*) in Germa- ny both reported operating extensive non-residential coun- selling and outreach services led by feminist professionals.

In **Germany and Sweden**, a mix of women’s NGOs and larger social welfare organisations operate centres, re- flecting the decentralised structure of service provision. Respondents indicated that women’s NGOs often provide specialist, feminist services within these broader systems. State-run services account for 603 centres (18%) across Europe. These are most common in **Finland**, **Denmark**, **Poland**, **Türkiye and Azerbaijan**, where governments have established national networks of crisis response, violence prevention or family support centres. Respondents from these countries confirmed that such centres usually serve all survivors of violence and are managed by public au- thorities such as ministries or municipal social services. In **Türkiye**, for example, the state network of Violence Preven- tion and Monitoring Centres (ŞÖNİMs) operates in every province, while in **Finland and Denmark**, crisis centres are largely coordinated through local municipalities.

icon: flower

Faith-based organisations manage six centres in **Albania**, **Romania and Slovenia**. A further seven centres are oper- ated by other or mixed entities, including four such centres in Iceland.

For the majority of centres (72%), the managing entity was not reported, reflecting ongoing limitations in national data monitoring systems. The 2024 findings indicate that while feminist women’s NGOs continue to lead the provision of gender-specific, survivor-centred support, there is also a growing presence of state-managed and mixed-service models. This diversification expands geographical cover- age but can create challenges in maintaining gender com- petence and consistent quality standards across Europe.

# Services provided by women’s centres

Women’s centres across Europe provide a wide range of specialist, non-residential services that address the diverse needs of survivors of VAWG. Data collected for the WAVE Country Report 2025 show that most countries have at least one women’s centre offering counselling, legal and practical support, crisis intervention and community outreach. Although the level and quality of provision vary, women’s centres remain central to ensuring survivors’ safety, empowerment and recovery.

It is important to note that the figures below refer to the existence of women’s centres providing these services within each country, not to the proportion of all individual centres that offer them. In other words, a ‘Yes’ response means that the service exists in that country, not that every identified women’s centre in the country provides it.

Table 10: Services provided by women’s centres

According to the 2024 data, counselling and psychological support are available in 39 countries (85%), making this the most widespread service provided by women’s centres. Both individual and group counselling are provided, often grounded in trauma-informed and empowerment-based approaches.

Legal advice is provided in 38 countries (83%) by at least one women’s centre. Representation at court, police or social services is available in 30 countries (65%). Financial and social welfare support or advocacy services exist in 29 countries (63%), while housing advice is provided in 31 countries (67%), reflecting the importance of women’s centres in helping survivors achieve safety and stability after leaving violent situations. Employment-related support

is reported in fewer than half of countries (22, or 59%), usually in the form of job counselling, skills development, or referrals to employment services.

Women’s centres also play an important coordinating role. Referrals and collaboration with other services are reported in 38 countries (83%), underscoring their central role in multi-agency response systems. Residential support services, such as emergency accommodation linked to non-residential women’s centres, are available in 25 countries (54%), demonstrating how integrated service models can provide continuity of care across the crisis and recovery stages. In some cases, women’s shelters also act as centres and so offer both residential and non-residential support services.

The latest data collection also captured information on how many women’s centres in each country provide specific services. While this level of detail was not reported consistently across all countries, the available information offers valuable insight into how services are organised and where strong integrated models exist.

In **Austria**, for example, women’s centres report providing a comprehensive range of support. Counselling and legal advice are available in all centres, while many also offer advocacy, outreach and housing advice. Several Austrian centres combine individual and group counselling with longer-term empowerment programmes and play an active role in prevention work and in coordinating with local institutions.

In **Italy**, the Anti-violence centres (*centri antiviolenza*) reflect one of the most developed national networks. They provide psychological counselling, legal advice, housing and employment assistance, and proactive contact with survivors referred by the police or social services. Many centres also offer empowerment and reintegration programmes for women rebuilding their lives after leaving violent relationships.

Similarly, **Spain** has a broad and well-coordinated system of Women’s Centres (*centros de la mujer*) operating at regional and municipal levels. Almost all centres offer psychological and legal counselling, and many extend their services to include institutional mediation, childcare support and awareness-raising initiatives. Coordination between local women’s centres and shelters ensures that survivors receive continuous support from crisis response to long-term recovery.

In many other countries, even where detailed quantitative data are not available, descriptive information confirms that counselling, legal assistance, and practical advocacy remain the backbone of support provided by women’s centres across Europe.

The data from 2024 shows encouraging progress in mapping the diversity of women’s centres and the scope of

their services. Future WAVE data collection will build on this foundation, aiming for even greater consistency and comparability in reporting. This will help strengthen the evidence base for assessing compliance with Article 22 of the Istanbul Convention, which calls for immediate, short- and long-term specialist support services for survivors of VAWG.

## CASE STUDY: Austria – integrated and specialist network with stable public support

Austria represents one of the most comprehensive and well-established models of women’s specialist service provision in Europe. The country has a nation-wide network of counselling centres for women and girls, combining state funding with the autonomy of feminist NGOs. As of 2024, the Network of Austrian Counselling Centres for Women and Girls includes 65 centres operating in all nine federal states, with at least 17 additional independent women’s counselling centres.

Women’s centres in Austria provide a wide range of services including counselling, psychological support, legal advice, social welfare assistance, employment counselling, housing advice and referrals to other services. Many also provide representation before courts and social institutions. Services are confidential, free of charge and available in person, by phone or online. Several centres also provide residential support or collaborate closely with shelters.

Austria’s women’s centres play an active role in prevention, awareness-raising and advocacy. They conduct empowerment workshops, school-based programmes and community campaigns against VAWG, often in partnership with local authorities. A new National Action Plan currently being developed includes specific funding lines for prevention.

Specialisation is another defining feature of the Austrian model. Many centres have developed expertise on specific forms of violence or particular groups of survivors. For instance, Orient Express and LEFÖ in Vienna support women affected by forced marriage and trafficking; DIVAN in Graz focuses on survivors of honour-based violence; and the African Women Organisation operates the ‘Bright Future’ project addressing female genital mutilation. The centre Ninlil provides counselling for women with cognitive and physical disabilities, while several centres explicitly welcome transgender and non-binary survivors.

Accessibility and inclusion are enshrined in Austrian legislation: since 2016, all recognised women’s centres must be barrier-free.

Funding for women’s centres comes primarily from the state and local governments, complemented by donations and small-scale international or faith-based support. Although funding is sometimes project-based and bureaucratic, the overall model ensures institutional stability and national coverage.

## Accessibility for groups of women at the intersection of multiple forms of discrimination

Women’s centres across Europe are founded on the principle of equality and non-discrimination, aiming to ensure that all women survivors of VAWG can access specialist support. Data from the WAVE Country Report 2025 show that women’s centres in most countries are open to a wide range of women, although the degree of accessibility and inclusivity varies across groups.

Most countries report that women’s centres are accessible to women with different backgrounds and needs. Across the 46 reporting countries, about three-quarters indicate that all or most women’s centres are open to specific groups such as migrant, refugee, disabled or older women. However, barriers remain in ensuring equal access for women with disabilities, undocumented women, transgender women and unaccompanied girls, whose needs often require specialised responses or additional institutional coordination.

Access for refugee women is relatively covered, with 29 countries (63%) reporting that most or all women’s centres are accessible to them. Women with uncertain residence permits or undocumented women also have some degree of access in the majority of countries, though only 25 countries (54%) confirmed that all or most centres provide support without restrictions.

icon: decorative flower

In many cases, access depends on legal or funding frameworks. For example, in Italy and Spain, services are available to all women regardless of residence status, and staff receive training on supporting migrant and refugee survivors. In contrast, some countries provide access through specialised centres or by cooperating with NGOs supporting migrants, rather than through all women’s centres.

Women with physical disabilities have access to most or all centres in 22 countries (48%), while accessibility for women with sensory disabilities (e.g., blind or deaf women) and women with cognitive disabilities (e.g., intellectual and/or psychosocial impairments) is reported at slightly lower levels (20 countries, 43%).

These differences often reflect physical barriers in older buildings, limited availability of sign language interpreters, and insufficient resources for tailored support. Nonetheless, several countries, including Austria, Germany, and Sweden, report targeted efforts to improve accessibility.

**WAVE COUNTRY REPORT 2025**
59


---

through structural adaptations, accessible communication tools, and partnerships with disability organisations. Access for older women (aged 65 and above) is the most comprehensive among all groups. Thirty countries (65%) report that all or most women’s centres are accessible to older survivors of violence. This reflects growing awareness of violence against older women and recognition that they may experience specific barriers, such as dependency on family members or economic vulnerability. In **Portugal and Finland**, for example, awareness campaigns and outreach programmes have been developed to reach older survivors through community services and health systems.

Access for transgender women varies significantly between countries. About one-third (15 countries, 33%) report that most or all centres provide support to transgender survivors. Some centres are open to everyone but do not have the training or clear procedures needed to meet different survivors’ needs, while others refer transgender survivors to general victim support or LGBTQI+ organisations.

For unaccompanied girls under 18, accessibility depends largely on national child protection frameworks. Around a third of the countries (15, or 33%) report that all or most women’s centres can support unaccompanied girls, often in collaboration with youth services or guardianship systems. In **Spain and North Macedonia**, for example, coordination between women’s centres and social welfare institutions ensures that adolescent survivors of violence receive both protection and psychosocial support.

### Specialised centres for specific forms of violence

Specialisation within women’s centres reflects efforts to address the complex realities of intersecting forms of VAWG and discrimination. The 2024 WAVE data indicate that across Europe, there is a growing network of women’s centres offering support based on dedicated expertise on specific forms of violence or with particular groups of survivors.

Centres specialised in trafficking in persons are the most prevalent, reported in 30 countries (65%). These centres often combine individual counselling, legal aid, and reintegration support, and many work in collaboration with law enforcement or national anti-trafficking coordinators. Strong examples come from **Austria, Romania, and Serbia**, where women’s NGOs lead comprehensive anti-trafficking services, often with specialised shelters or safe houses. Specialised services for undocumented and refugee women are present in less than half the countries, in 18 (39%) and 20 (43%) countries, respectively. In **Italy and Spain**, for instance, national women’s networks have developed expertise in migration-related violence, providing language support, legal advice on residence status, and access to safe accommodation. In **Germany and Sweden**, feminist organisations offer targeted counselling and

advocacy for refugee and asylum-seeking women affected by sexualised and domestic violence, often in cooperation with refugee support agencies.

Centres addressing forced marriage, honour-based violence, and female genital mutilation remain less common but significant. Twenty-two countries (48%) report specialised centres for survivors of forced marriage, while 19 (41%) have services addressing honour-based violence, and 15 (33%) for survivors of female genital mutilation. These forms of violence are most frequently addressed in Western and Northern Europe, where migration patterns have prompted targeted policy responses. In **France, the Netherlands, and Belgium**, women’s centres work in partnership with migrant women’s organisations to provide culturally sensitive and rights-based support.

Specialised services for Black and minority ethnic women are reported in 15 countries (33%), reflecting a continued need for intersectional approaches that address racism and structural exclusion alongside VAWG. In the **United Kingdom, Germany, and Finland**, Black and minority ethnic and migrant women’s organisations have been instrumental in developing community-based advocacy and counselling that combine feminist and anti-racist frameworks.

According to the data collected, 16 countries (35%), as well as **England and Northern Ireland**, have women’s centres specialised in supporting women with physical disabilities, while 15 countries (33%) report specialised services for women with cognitive or sensory disabilities. These centres often focus on accessible counselling environments, adapted communication tools and coordination with disability services. Examples include **Austria**, where specialist counsellors receive training in disability-sensitive approaches, and **Germany**, where there are women’s centres specialised in supporting women survivors with physical, cognitive and/or sensory disabilities.

Centres for older women (65 years and above) are available in 18 countries (39%) as well as in **Northern Ireland and Wales**, which report dedicated services. In **Portugal and Finland**, for instance, some women’s centres have integrated elder abuse prevention into their programmes, combining community outreach with support for older survivors within existing counselling services.

There is also growing recognition of the need for age-appropriate, gender-sensitive services for girls under 18. Eighteen countries (39%), as well as **Wales**, report specialised centres or programmes for girls, often linked to broader child protection systems. In **Spain and Croatia**, women’s NGOs operate dedicated counselling and prevention projects targeting adolescent girls affected by dating violence or sexual abuse. In **Moldova**, there are 10 centres specialised in supporting girls under 18.

Specialisation for transgender women and non-binary people remains more limited, though it is expanding. Fourteen

**60**
