WOMEN’S CENTRES

countries (30%), as well as Wales, have at least one women’s centre with specific training or protocols to support transgender survivors, and ten countries (22%), as well as Wales, report initiatives inclusive of non-binary people. These centres often collaborate with LGBTQI+ organisations to ensure safe and informed support. In **Sweden** and **Belgium**, feminist organisations have introduced inclusive training and adapted intake procedures to respond sensitively to survivors’ gender identity and lived experiences of discrimination.

Although these specialised services remain unevenly distributed, their presence across more than half of reporting countries represents progress towards meeting the Istanbul Convention’s requirement to ensure equal access to protection and tailored support. However, as in previous years, the availability of such centres is often dependent on project-based or international funding, raising concerns about their sustainability and national recognition within state frameworks. At the same time, countries should aim to go beyond the minimum requirements of the Istanbul Convention by strengthening specialised and intersectional service provision, ensuring that support effectively reaches all women, including those facing multiple and intersecting forms of discrimination.

### Specialist support for survivors of sexualised violence

Sexualised violence remains one of the most underreported and traumatising forms of VAWG, and the availability of specialist, trauma-informed services is a critical indicator of compliance with the Istanbul Convention’s Articles 22 and 25. European countries vary in their approach: in some cases, women’s centres offer specialised holistic support for all forms of VAW, including sexualised violence, while others maintain consolidated networks of RCCs with trained staff providing immediate and long-term survivor-led counselling. To reflect these national differences, the WAVE questionnaire included the same multiple-choice question about types of sexualised violence support in both the women’s centres and the sexualised violence support services sections. This section presents the results about the support provided by women’s centres to survivors of sexualised violence.

Data collected for the WAVE Country Report 2025 show that women’s centres in most countries provide at least some form of specialist support for survivors of sexualised violence, though the scope and quality of these services vary significantly. The most widely available service is specialist psychological care, reported in 30 countries (65%). This includes trauma therapy, counselling, and peer support groups provided by trained professionals. Countries such as **Austria**, **Germany**, **Italy**, and **Spain** have developed strong networks of rape crisis and sexual violence counselling centres integrated within broader women’s NGO structures. In **Austria**, the women’s helpline (*Frauenhelpline*) and women’s shelters (*Frauenhäuser*) collaborate

with regional crisis centres to provide long-term trauma counselling, while in **Spain**, regional crisis centres (*centros de crisis 24 horas*) offer 24/7 emergency psychological and legal assistance.

Specialist advocacy services for survivors of sexualised violence are reported in 23 countries (50%), and often include accompaniment to medical and legal appointments, court support, and coordination with police and health services.

Legal advice related to sexualised violence is available in 29 countries (63%), often as part of comprehensive support packages offered by women’s centres. Legal services typically include assistance in filing complaints, representation in court, and support in obtaining protection measures. However, only 10 countries (22%) report that women’s centres provide specialist forensic or medical care, which remains primarily the responsibility of state or hospital-based services. In some contexts, such as **Ireland** and **Finland**, partnerships between women’s NGOs and hospital-based sexual assault units ensure coordinated survivor care.

Needs assessment mechanisms, such as evaluating survivors’ entitlement to special measures in court or in asylum processes, are in place in 20 countries (43%). These services are crucial in ensuring that survivors’ safety and psychological well-being are prioritised throughout legal and administrative procedures.

Finally, community education and prevention work related to sexualised violence is conducted in 26 countries (57%). Many women’s centres engage in prevention campaigns, often targeting young people and professionals. Examples include the ‘No is No’ (*No es No*) campaign in **Spain**, and school-based sexual violence prevention programmes implemented by women’s centres in **Croatia** and **Italy**.

icon: asterisk

Despite these positive examples, the overall picture shows that comprehensive sexual violence response systems remain uneven. Many countries lack integrated forensic and medical services linked to feminist counselling centres, and the sustainability of specialist psychological and advocacy services is often dependent on short-term funding. Ensuring a consistent, nationwide network of trauma-informed, survivor-centred services, therefore, remains an urgent priority for compliance with the Istanbul Convention’s standards.

### Funding and geographical coverage of women’s centres

Women’s centres across Europe continue to rely on a combination of state funding, donations and international funding to sustain their work. The data collected show that the majority receive some form of state funding, whether from national, regional or local authorities. In 36 out of 46 countries, public financing represents the main source

**WAVE COUNTRY REPORT 2025**

61


---

of support. In several countries, including **Austria**, **Spain**, **Italy**, **Portugal** and **Finland**, such funding has enabled the development of stable national or regional networks of women’s centres. However, even where state funding is well established, it is often project-based or short-term, requiring frequent reapplication and limiting service continuity and staff retention.

Donations and international funding continue to play an important role, with 34 of 46 countries reporting receiving donations and 25 receiving international funding. This is particularly important for feminist NGOs operating in political or financial environments that restrict public funding for gender equality. In the Western Balkans, Eastern Europe and the South Caucasus, many women’s centres rely on grants from the European Union, United Nations agencies or private foundations. This is especially the case in **Serbia**, **Kosovo**, **Georgia** and **Armenia**, where international support has been crucial in maintaining feminist service provision in the absence of adequate state backing.

Only a small number of countries report funding from religious institutions, notably **Albania**, **Austria**, **France**, **Germany**, **Portugal**, **Switzerland** and **Ukraine**.

Overall, the funding landscape reveals a clear imbalance: feminist NGOs that offer the most specialised, gender-specific and empowerment-based support are often the least financially secure. Meanwhile, larger state-run or generic providers tend to benefit from more stable public budgets, even when their services are less specialised or gender-sensitive.

The geographical distribution of women’s centres remains uneven across Europe, creating persistent disparities in women’s access to specialist support. Seventeen countries (37%) report that women’s centres are available in all regions, a situation found mainly where there is a strong national coordination mechanism or statutory funding model, as in **Austria**, **Spain**, **Italy**, **Sweden** and **Portugal**, but also in smaller countries such as **Croatia** and **Montenegro**. In a further group of thirteen countries (28%), women’s centres operate in most regions, while in ten countries (22%) the centres operate only in major cities or only in the capital city in the case of **Cyprus**.

In many parts of Eastern and South-Eastern Europe, provision is concentrated in major urban centres, leaving survivors in rural, island or mountainous areas without in-person access to counselling or legal assistance. A few smaller or more centralised states report that women’s centres exist only in the capital city, which severely limits accessibility, particularly for women who face financial or mobility constraints, or who need to maintain confidentiality when seeking help.

While the overall network of women’s centres continues to expand, geographical inequalities persist. Several countries are attempting to address these gaps through mobile outreach, online counselling and local referral mechanisms. Examples include **Finland**, **Croatia**, and **Spain**, where women’s NGOs have developed regional outreach models and worked with local authorities to expand access for women outside major cities. However, without stable, long-term funding and decentralised service planning, achieving genuine national coverage remains difficult.

### CASE STUDY: Serbia – feminist-led provision sustained through international support

Serbia provides an instructive example of a feminist NGO-led system functioning with limited state involvement and significant reliance on international and donor funding. As of 2024, there are 42 women’s centres in Serbia, of which 32 are run by women’s NGOs and 10 by other NGOs. Among them, 25 serve women survivors of violence, while 17 provide services to all survivors regardless of gender.

Women’s centres in Serbia offer counselling and psychological support, referrals and coordination with other services, legal advice, and advocacy. Some also provide representation before courts and social services, as well as financial or social welfare support. Specialist services for survivors of sexualised violence are available in a small number of centres, including needs assessment, psychological care and advocacy.

The network is geographically uneven: most centres are concentrated in cities, while some regions have no centres at all. This urban concentration reflects the absence of systemic state funding and coordination. Instead, women’s NGOs sustain their work largely through international donors and project-based grants. The principal funding sources are international foundations, UN programmes and bilateral donors, with only minimal state contributions.

Despite financial insecurity, women’s centres in Serbia demonstrate strong feminist principles and survivor-centred approaches. They offer essential support in a context of limited public infrastructure, bridging the gap between institutional systems and women’s actual needs. Many centres also engage in prevention and empowerment activities, including running workshops, awareness campaigns, and advocating for policy reform.

A few centres provide specialist or intersectional services, including to women with uncertain residence permits or undocumented women, women with physical and sensory disabilities, and Black and minority ethnic women and survivors of forced marriage. Some centres also support refugee women, transgender women, non-binary people and girls under 18, though in very small numbers.

62
**WAVE COUNTRY REPORT 2025**



---



WOMEN’S CENTRES

Women’s centres in Serbia have a crucial role in a system where public services often lack the necessary gender competence or accessibility. However, without state-backed financing or national coordination, sustainability remains a major challenge.

## Conclusion

The data collected for the WAVE Country Report confirm that women’s centres remain the cornerstone of specialist, non-residential support for survivors of VAWG in Europe. Despite diverse governance models, their defining feature is the provision of gender-specific, feminist and empowerment-based services. Across 46 countries, women’s centres continue to ensure that survivors are believed, supported and empowered, yet their reach, sustainability and recognition vary considerably.

Progress since 2023 is visible in the gradual expansion of networks, especially in countries with stable public funding frameworks such as Austria, Spain, and Italy. The persistence of feminist NGO-led provision in regions such as the Western Balkans demonstrates the resilience and expertise of civil society, even where state involvement is limited. However, the overall availability of centres still falls short of the Council of Europe’s recommended standard of one counselling centre per 50,000 women, with coverage remaining uneven and rural areas particularly underserved. The findings highlight an ongoing tension between the institutionalisation of services and the preservation of feminist principles. While state-run or mixed models have improved geographical reach, they often lack gender-specific understanding and survivor-centred methodologies. Feminist NGOs, which provide the most comprehensive and empowering forms of support, continue to face precarious, project-based funding, limiting their ability to retain staff and maintain quality standards.

The data also reveal growing diversification in the services provided. Counselling, legal support and advocacy remain universal, but more centres now offer specialist services for survivors of sexualised violence, trafficking, forced marriage and other intersecting forms of discrimination. There is visible progress in accessibility for women with disabilities, migrant and refugee women, and older women, though significant gaps remain for undocumented and transgender women as well as unaccompanied girls. Overall, women’s centres continue to bridge the gap between survivors and institutions, translating the principles of the Istanbul Convention into practice. Their future sustainability depends on stable and adequate funding, state recognition of feminist expertise, and continued advocacy to ensure that every woman in Europe has access to specialist, rights-based, and survivor-centred support.

## ARROWS-TO-DOT Recommendations

* Women’s specialist services should develop a shared definition for ‘women’s centres’ grounded in feminist, gender-specific, rights-based and survivor-centred principles and methodologies. A shared definition would aid clarity and consistency in data collection and facilitate a more accurate representation of specialist services in line with the Istanbul Convention.

* Governments should guarantee institutional, multi-year core funding for feminist women’s centres to ensure long-term sustainability, staff retention and high-quality support. Public funding should be prioritised for feminist NGOs applying gender-specific, survivor-centred methodologies, and procurement systems should include gender competence and feminist principles, not only organisational size or administrative capacity.

* States must strengthen cooperation and partnerships between public authorities and women’s NGOs. Efforts should focus on expanding the provision of specialist services for women survivors and their children, particularly in countries or regions where such centres are absent or limited.

* States must establish and maintain comprehensive, national data collection systems that capture available women’s centres and service providers, geographical coverage, target groups, and number of survivors supported, ensuring public accessibility and reducing the burden on under-resourced feminist civil society organisations.

* The availability of adequate specialist services for minoritised and marginalised groups must be ensured, including support for survivors of forced marriage, honour-based violence, female genital mutilation, human trafficking, and for refugee, migrant and undocumented women, which remains non-existent or very limited in many countries.

* States must establish comprehensive geographical coverage of women’s centres, including coordinated outreach in rural, remote and island areas where in-person services are scarce.

* States should promote the integration of intersectional and trauma-informed approaches in service provision through training, quality standards and monitoring in order to strengthen gender-specific and survivor-centred practice.

# Specialist services for survivors of sexualised violence

icon: umbrella

## Introduction

Sexualised violence is one of the most pervasive and harmful forms of violence against women and girls (VAWG), causing deep and lasting trauma to women and girls across Europe and beyond. It encompasses a continuum of behaviours that violate physical, psychological, and sexual integrity. It includes rape and sexual assault, coerced or unwanted sexual acts, sexual harassment, sexual exploitation, forced or non-consensual sexual touching, non-consensual image sharing, online sexual abuse, stalking with sexual intent, grooming, and child sexual abuse. It can occur in intimate relationships, within families, in workplaces and institutions, in public spaces, online, and in situations of conflict, displacement, or detention.

The prevalence of sexualised violence in Europe remains alarming. According to the latest European Union gender-based violence (EU GBV) survey, around 30% of women in the EU (one in three) have experienced physical and/or sexual violence since the age of 15, and approximately 17% of women report having experienced sexual violence (including rape and other unwanted sexual acts).<sup>75</sup> Sexualised violence is often experienced at an early age: one in four women reports some form of sexual harassment before the age of 15, and young women are disproportionately affected by online and image-based abuse. These figures are alarming, yet despite its gravity and the long-term traumatic consequences for survivors, sexualised violence remains among the most underreported of all crimes. Shame, fear of disbelief, stigma, and distrust in institutions frequently prevent survivors from seeking help or justice.

Sexualised violence is not a random or private act but a deeply gendered violation that reflects and reinforces unequal power relations. It is in the overwhelming majority of cases committed by men against women and girls. On a societal level, it functions as a mechanism of control, intimidation, and subordination. Feminist research has long shown that the threat and reality of sexualised violence shape women’s daily lives by restricting their freedom of movement, limiting participation in public life, and undermining equality. Liz Kelly’s concept of the *continuum of sexual violence* further demonstrates that women’s experiences of sexualised aggression, from seemingly minor acts of harassment to rape, are connected through the same structures of male power and control. This framework

exposes how everyday intrusions and coercive behaviours sustain an environment in which more severe forms of sexualised violence can occur.<sup>76</sup>

Central to the issue of sexualised violence and its definition is the concept of consent. The Istanbul Convention defines sexual violence, including rape, as any sexual act without the freely given consent of the victim. Consent must be given voluntarily, as the result of free will, assessed in the context of the surrounding circumstances. It cannot be inferred from silence, passivity, or lack of resistance.<sup>77</sup>

Despite notable legislative developments, international standards, and case law emphasising the need to integrate consent-based definitions and adopt an affirmative consent approach (the yes-means-yes model), in practice, the presumption of innocence continues to place a heavy burden of proof on the prosecution, and indirectly on the survivor. Whereas the focus once lay on proving active resistance, survivors are now expected to demonstrate the absence of consent. This requirement remains challenging, often humiliating, and re-traumatising for survivors of sexualised violence. The situation is further exacerbated by persistent myths and stereotypes surrounding sexualised violence, which lead to intrusive questioning of survivors’ behaviour, credibility, and character. Although the phrasing of such questions may have evolved since the introduction of consent-based definitions, their underlying implications of blame remain unchanged. Consequently, the responsibility continues to fall on the survivor to prove that their reaction during an assault did not constitute consent, and ultimately to demonstrate their own victimisation.

Understanding the centrality of consent means recognising that survivors often do not resist physically, as trauma and fear can trigger freezing or dissociation responses. Legal and institutional responses that fail to understand these dynamics risk reproducing myths and stereotypes that blame survivors for violence perpetrated against them. The move towards consent-based legal definitions across Europe represents progress in aligning law with lived experience. Yet this must be matched by specialist services that support survivors holistically, uphold their autonomy, and ensure that consent and bodily integrity are respected in all interventions. Survivors of sexualised violence have a range of immediate and long-term needs that require coordinated, specialist, and trauma-informed

SPECIALIST SERVICES FOR SURVIVORS OF SEXUALISED VIOLENCE

responses. Immediately after an assault, women may need urgent medical care, psychological first aid, and forensic examination, where available. In the long term, many require trauma counselling, peer support, specialised legal information, and advocacy to navigate systems that often re-traumatise or intimidate them.<sup>78</sup>

Above all, survivors need to be believed, supported, and treated with dignity.<sup>79</sup> When survivors receive insensitive or discriminatory responses from police, prosecutors, medical staff, or family members, they may experience secondary victimisation, which deepens the trauma of the original assault. Specialist services are designed to prevent this by offering informed, survivor-centred, and gender sensitive support. Survivors also need systems that are accessible to all, including women living in rural areas, migrant and refugee women, women with disabilities, Roma women, and other marginalised groups.<sup>80</sup>

According to WAVE definitions, specialist services for sexualised violence include several types of provision, each addressing different aspects of survivors’ needs.

**Rape crisis centres (RCCs)** are specialist services offering immediate, medium-, and long-term support to survivors of rape, sexual assault, or any form of sexualised violence. Their work is rooted in feminist, survivor-centred principles. They provide counselling, therapy, advocacy, and accompaniment throughout legal proceedings and in contact with other institutions. RCCs also engage in community education, awareness-raising, and inter-agency cooperation to improve institutional responses and prevent sexualised violence. Many operate specialised helplines that provide counselling, information on rights, and referrals to other services.

**Sexual violence referral centres (SVRCs)** usually focus on the immediate aftermath of an assault. Often based in hospitals, they provide emergency medical and forensic care, evidence collection and storage, crisis intervention, and referrals to longer-term community-based services such as RCCs.

**Crisis or medical services** offer urgent medical treatment, emergency contraception, prevention of sexually transmitted infections, and trauma-informed psychological support.

**Specialised helplines** for sexualised violence provide confidential, accessible, and immediate emotional support, information, and referral. They are often the first point of contact for survivors who are not yet ready to engage in person.

Many women’s centres also provide counselling, advocacy, and accompaniment to survivors of sexualised violence as part of a broader holistic response to VAWG. In countries where RCCs or SVRCs do not exist, these centres often fill critical gaps, even without formal recognition or funding.

Historically, specialist services for sexualised violence were pioneered by women’s organisations grounded in feminist theory and activism. They were created not as extensions of state systems but as acts of resistance to a culture that silenced survivors and normalised male violence. The feminist model sees survivors not as passive recipients of aid but as agents in their own recovery. It understands sexualised violence as a social and political problem rooted in gender inequality, and its aim is not only individual healing but systemic transformation.

Key principles of feminist specialist services include belief, autonomy, confidentiality, and empowerment. They use trauma-informed methods that understand the complexity of trauma responses and the importance of restoring control and trust. They provide both direct support and advocacy for structural change. It is essential for feminist services to maintain independence to fulfil this role effectively. While cooperation with state institutions is necessary to ensure coordination and funding, independence allows them to criticise systemic failings and defend survivors’ rights without political or institutional pressure.

## International obligations

The Council of Europe Convention on Preventing and Combating Violence against Women and Domestic Violence (the Istanbul Convention) establishes that all non-consensual sexual acts must be criminalised (Article 36) and that states must provide accessible, specialised support through RCCs or SVRCs (Article 25). These services must be available regardless of whether survivors report the crime, ensuring that support and justice are not conditional on legal action. It further recommends that at least one RCC or SVRC should be available per 200,000 inhabitants and that they should be geographically distributed to ensure accessibility, including for women in rural and remote areas.<sup>81</sup> Despite these standards, the current provision across Europe remains far below the recommended level, with significant disparities in access, quality, and sustainability. The Group of Experts on Action against Violence against Women and Domestic Violence (GREVIO), in its midterm horizontal report, found that while immediate medical and trauma care for sexual violence is generally well developed across parties, long-term psychological counselling remains insufficient. Yet such long-term services are essential, as many victims do not seek help immediately due to stigma, shame, guilt, fear of not being

believed, or the emotional difficulty of disclosing sexual violence. As a result, the effects of trauma often surface weeks, months, or even years later, making sustained psychological support crucial for recovery and for addressing the long-term consequences of sexual violence.<sup>82</sup>

The Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW) has played a defining role in framing sexualised violence as a violation of women’s human rights. In its General Recommendation No. 35 on gender-based violence against women, the Committee explicitly requires States to ensure that sexual assault, including rape, is recognised *“as a crime against the right to personal security and physical, sexual and psychological integrity and that the definition of sexual crimes, including marital and acquaintance or date rape, is based on the lack of freely given consent and takes into account coercive circumstances”*.<sup>83</sup>

As recognised in the Directive (EU) 2024/1385 on combating violence against women and domestic violence, *“the traumatic nature of sexual violence, including rape, requires a particularly sensitive response by trained and specialised staff”*. The Directive further underlines that *“victims of sexual violence need immediate trauma support combined with immediate forensic examinations for the safe-keeping of evidence needed for future prosecution”*. It calls on Member States to ensure that *“rape crisis centres or sexual violence referral centres should be available in sufficient numbers and adequately spread over the territory of each Member State, taking into account the geography and demographic composition of the Member State concerned, and notes that such centres can form part of the existing healthcare system in the Member State”*.<sup>84</sup> These provisions reaffirm the obligation of EU Member States to provide accessible, specialist, and survivor-centred services for all women and girls survivors of sexualised violence. The Directive emphasises accessibility for survivors with disabilities, migrant and refugee women, and those in rural areas, and underlines that services must be available irrespective of whether survivors report the crime. It is important to note, however, that while the Directive indeed establishes an important framework, significant gaps remain, specifically the absence of a consent-based definition of sexual violence and insufficiently detailed requirements on the nature and scope of support services. While the Directive broadens access to general victim services, it risks relegating specialist women’s services to a subordinate role rather than ensuring direct access to long-term, tailored support.<sup>85</sup>

## WAVE framework for data collection on sexualised violence services

For the 2025 report, WAVE gathered information on specialist services for survivors of sexualised violence, asking whether services for women and girls survivors of sexualised violence exist in each country, and which types are available, including RCC, SVRC, crisis or medical services, and specialised helplines. Respondents were asked to provide the number of each type, their availability, and their location. The questionnaire also explored the kinds of support these services offer, including medical and forensic care, trauma counselling, advocacy, legal advice, and community awareness work.

Information was also collected on how services are funded, where they are distributed geographically, and which groups of survivors they support, including women, girls, and other affected groups. Respondents could add comments about country-specific systems, such as whether women’s centres offer support to survivors of sexualised violence or where forensic evidence is collected. This allows for consistent comparison between countries while recognising national differences in service models.

## Findings on the situation of specialist services for survivors of sexualised violence in Europe

The data show a severe shortage of specialist services for women and girls survivors of sexualised violence across Europe. To meet the Istanbul Convention standard of one RCC or SVRC per 200,000 inhabitants, 4,248 services would be required across 46 countries. However, only 633 centres are currently reported, leaving a shortage of 3,615 services, or 85% of the total required.

In the 27 EU Member States, 2,243 centres are needed, yet only 334 exist. This leaves a shortage of 1,909 centres, meaning that 85% of the required services are not in place. In the 19 European countries outside the EU, there are 299 centres compared to the 2,005 required, leaving an 85% gap. Data on the availability of sexual-violence-specific services remain incomplete, as not all countries were able to provide figures, meaning the actual number of services is likely higher. This is particularly evident in contexts such as Germany, where services exist but no comprehensive data could be obtained; however, these gaps do not substantially alter the overall finding of a significant shortage of specialised support.

Table 11: Overview of findings on service provision – sexualised violence support services

These figures reveal a severe and consistent failure to meet international standards for service provision. In practical terms, this means that most women and girls in Europe do not have access to an RCC or SVRC in their area. The data underline the urgent need for states to prioritise the establishment, expansion, and sustainable funding of specialist, feminist services so that survivors everywhere can receive the support, safety, and justice they are entitled to under the Istanbul Convention.

Of the 46 countries covered by the data collection, only **Luxembourg**, **Iceland**, **Norway**, and **Switzerland** meet or exceed the required level of one RCC or SVRC per 200,000 inhabitants. This represents just four out of 46 countries (9%). In addition, **Wales** meets the standard within the **United Kingdom**, although when the United Kingdom is considered as a whole, it falls short, with 65% of the services missing. Both **Norway** and **Switzerland** significantly exceed the Istanbul Convention standard. Norway operates 46 centres, compared with the 28 required by its population, while **Switzerland** has 63 centres, far surpassing the 45 needed to meet the minimum standard.

RCC or SVRC have not been established in **Austria**, **Cyprus**, **Hungary**, **Latvia** and **Türkiye**. On the other hand, **Greece**, **Italy**, **Slovakia**, **Azerbaijan**, **Belarus**, **Georgia**, **Kosovo**, **Liechtenstein**, and **Montenegro** have no specialist sexualised violence services at all. This means that nine out of 46 countries (20%) provide no support through specialist sexualised violence services. However, in these countries, other women’s specialist services (WSS) provide support to survivors of sexualised violence.

## Types of sexualised violence services

Across Europe, the data show that provision of specialist services for survivors of sexualised violence remains fragmented and uneven. A total of 208 RCCs and 221 SVRCs were reported across 46 countries. In addition, there are 204 crisis or medical services and 50 specialised helplines providing support to survivors. The distribution of these services is uneven across Europe: 14 countries have no RCCs or SVRCs, and another 14 have only two or fewer. Both Norway and Switzerland exceed the number required by the Istanbul Convention. In **Norway**, there are 22 Sexual Assault Reception Centres (*Overgrepsmottak*) and two Rape Clinics (*Voldtektsmottaket*), located within hospitals across the country. These centres function as RCC or SVRC, providing immediate medical care, psychological first aid, and forensic examination. Additionally, there are 21 Centres for Victims of Incest and Sexual Abuse (SMI-SO/NOK), which offer long-term psychological and peer support for survivors of incest, sexual abuse, and rape, as well as for their relatives.

Among countries with larger numbers of services, most have prioritised the development of either RCCs or SVRCs, rather than both. In **Switzerland**, there is one RCC, around 60 SVRCs, and two crisis/medical services. In **Belgium**, there is also one RCC and 10 SVRCs. WAVE delegates explained that the classification of services “does not entirely fit the reality on the ground.” The NGO SOS Viol in Brussels provides long-term counselling and support for survivors, while the state-run Sexual Assault Care Centres in **Brussels** and **Wallonia**, and the Sexual Violence Care Centres (*Zorgcentrum na Seksueel Geweld* – ZSG) in **Flanders**, offer 24/7 comprehensive medical, forensic, and psychological care. These hospital-based centres represent a strong integrated model, although the NGO-led RCC remains the only one offering long-term therapeutic support independent of the health system.

In **Finland**, there is one RCC and 25 SVRCs. The SERI Support Centres form a coordinated, state-funded national structure providing immediate medical, forensic, and psychological support, regardless of whether survivors choose to report to the police. Experts describe this as a coherent and trauma-informed national model integrated into the healthcare system. In **Lithuania**, five major regional hospitals are responsible for providing specialised services, including medical care, forensic services, evidence storage, and crisis intervention. However, the system is still in the process of formation, and many hospitals do not yet provide all necessary services. While survivors receive treatment for physical injuries and prevention of sexually transmitted diseases and pregnancy, psychological support is limited, especially during nights and weekends. The Specialised Complex Assistance Centres (SKPC) also offer psychological and intermediary assistance to survivors of domestic and sexualised violence, and there are 14 organisations running these centres across the country. In **North Macedonia**, three SVRCs operate in Skopje, Tetovo, and

67


---

Kumanovo. They operate within the general healthcare system and lack dedicated state funding. They provide medical, psychological, and legal assistance but face significant challenges in accessibility and sustainability due to insufficient funding. In **Romania**, Intervention Centres for Victims of Sexual Violence were established in 2021 and are based in hospitals, where survivors can receive medical services and forensic evidence collection. Access begins through emergency units, after which the coordinator activates a multi-agency response, including the police and social services. Survivors can then access free psychological and legal counselling, temporary accommodation, and social support. In practice, however, the system remains bureaucratic, inconsistent, and often depends on the initiative of individual professionals. In **Serbia**, five SVRCs provide medical, psychological, and legal support, while women’s organisations deliver longer-term counselling and advocacy.

Several countries have opted for developing more RCCs. For example, in **Spain**, by June 2025, 54 RCCs operating 24/7 were expected to be established nationwide. According to NGO sources, at least 23 centres are currently operational. **Estonia** has five RCCs located in regional hospitals, providing primarily specialist forensic and medical care for survivors of sexualised violence. The **Netherlands** has 16 RCCs operating as Sexual Assault Centres, offering comprehensive support that includes specialist forensic and medical care, psychological services, advocacy, legal advice, and prevention activities. At these centres, multidisciplinary teams of medical, psychological, social, and law-enforcement professionals work together to provide coordinated specialist care to survivors.

**England**, on the other hand, has taken an approach to develop both RCCs and SVRCs, albeit still in insufficient numbers. It provides a relatively wide network of sexualised violence services, with 35 RCCs and 48 SVRCs (SARCs) across the country. SARCs handle forensic and medical care and work in coordination with police and women’s services, while RCCs and other organisations offer psychological support, advocacy, legal guidance, and prevention activities. Despite the range of services, provision varies significantly between regions, and support for children and rural areas remains limited.

In countries where there are no reported RCCs, SVRCs or even specialist sexualised violence services, WSS still provide them. For example, **Italy** has a longstanding tradition of feminist women’s centres which provide a full range of specialised services for survivors of all forms of VAW. The centres belonging to D.i.Re – National Women’s Network against Violence (*Donne in Rete contro la Violenza*) are able to offer full support to sexualised violence survivors, including cooperation with the national health system’s forensic and medical care procedures, as required by law. In **Italy**, survivors are referred to the local women’s centres that are run by women’s NGOs and provide specialist and competent support for cases of sexualised violence.

Women’s centres can accompany women during medical procedures and judicial proceedings, offer needs assessment, specialist advocacy services and community awareness and education for prevention. Specialist forensic and medical care is provided in medical services. In the case of **Liechtenstein**, which has a total population of about 40,000 inhabitants, women survivors of sexualised violence are referred to facilities in **Switzerland**. In **Hungary**, there are no RCCs or SVRCs. Women survivors of sexualised violence can access basic support through general crisis centres or feminist NGOs, such as NANE and Patent, which offer information, legal advice, and emotional assistance. Forensic examinations are conducted in hospitals upon police request, without dedicated or trauma-informed structures. In **Greece**, there are no specific services, so while women’s centres can provide counselling to survivors of sexualised violence, they do not provide specialist support.

### CASE STUDY: Ireland

Ireland offers a comparatively strong and evolving model of support for survivors of sexualised violence, with 17 RCCs and six sexual assault treatment units (SATUs) providing a broad range of specialist services. RCCs deliver psychological support, advocacy, legal information, and prevention work, while SATUs ensure high-quality, state-funded clinical and forensic care. Survivors can access RCC services anywhere in the country, reflecting a flexible, survivor-centred approach, even as regional differences in resources and capacity persist.

A notable strength of the Irish system is its integration of formal and community-based supports, including vital grassroots organisations that reach marginalised groups. National helpline provision is robust, with a 24/7 state-funded service complemented by regional and specialist NGO helplines. While challenges persist, particularly in rural accessibility and the uneven availability of court and police accompaniment, the overall structure demonstrates a strong commitment to comprehensive, survivor-centred care and represents a good practice model for further development.

Across Europe, few countries provide the full range of integrated support required under the Istanbul Convention. Twenty-nine countries (63%) reported offering specialist forensic and medical care, and 31 (67%) conduct needs assessments, for example, in relation to protection measures or court procedures. Specialist psychological care is the most common form of support, available in 35 countries (76%), while 27 (59%) provide sexualised violence advocacy services and legal advice. Twenty-eight countries (61%) reported engaging in community awareness and prevention activities.

SPECIALIST SERVICES FOR SURVIVORS OF SEXUALISED VIOLENCE

Regardless of whether countries have prioritised RCCs, SVRCs, or other models, those with specialised sexual violence services generally offer a similar range of support. All six key service types are available simultaneously in 15 countries (33%), including those with a stronger focus on RCCs, such as **France**, **Ireland**, and **the Netherlands**, as well as those that primarily operate SVRCs, such as **Belgium**, **Denmark**, **Switzerland**, and **Sweden**. In **Germany**, forensic evidence is collected in specialised violence protection clinics (*Gewaltschutzambulanzen*) or hospitals, depending on regional availability. The nationwide network BAG FORSA coordinates feminist counselling centres that deliver psychological care, advocacy, and prevention work, though medical and forensic services are often separate.

In **France**, Women’s Houses (*Maisons des Femmes*), university hospitals, and women’s rights centres jointly deliver services including medical and forensic care, psychological counselling, and legal information. However, long-term support remains limited, as most interventions focus on acute cases. In **Malta**, the Care for Victims of Sexual Assault (CVSA) operates 24/7 within the main hospital, providing medical care, counselling, and legal guidance. In **Moldova**, pilot centres integrate forensic, medical, psychological, legal, and advocacy support, offering a holistic and trauma-informed approach. However, access is limited to urban areas, and there is an ongoing need for sustainable funding and expanded outreach.

### Funding of sexualised violence services

Across Europe, state funding remains the primary source of financing for sexualised violence services, reported by 31 countries (67%). However, reliance on unstable and short-term funding sources remains widespread. Twenty-two countries (48%) reported using donations from foundations, trusts, or individuals, while 12 (26%) reported receiving international funding. Only one country, **Ukraine**, reported receiving support from religious institutions, while two countries, **Spain** and **Ukraine**, identified additional or mixed funding sources.

In many countries, state funding is limited to covering basic operational costs and is often project-based rather than sustainable. This leaves services vulnerable to political and economic fluctuations. For example, in **Germany**, RCCs and counselling services such as Wildwasser rely heavily on donations to compensate for inadequate institutional funding. Similarly, in **Scotland**, RCCs are primarily funded by the national government, but this model is under threat as authorities consider shifting to localised, commission-based funding.

In contrast, some countries have developed more stable and structured funding models. In **Belgium**, the establishment and expansion of Sexual Assault Care Centres (*Centres de Prise en Charge des Violences Sexuelles* – CPVS) are supported by federal funding from the Secretary of State for Equality and by the national lottery. The 2024 law on

CPVS formalised state responsibility for funding. In **Lithuania**, the five designated hospitals providing forensic and medical care for survivors are financed by state funds. The Ministry of Social Security and Labour also supports the specialised assistance centres (SACs), ensuring continuity of psychological and social support services. However, there is no separate funding stream specifically for sexual violence services.

Several countries continue to depend heavily on international donors. In **Moldova**, for instance, specialised services receive significant support from the European Union, UN Women, UNFPA, and USAID, which fund infrastructure, training, and capacity building. Similarly, projects in **Serbia** and **Romania** have been supported through international grants such as Norway Grants and the UN Trust Fund to End Violence against Women.

At the same time, gaps in public investment remain a significant obstacle to comprehensive service provision. In **North Macedonia**, **Romania**, and **Poland**, centres often operate without dedicated state funding or rely on healthcare institutions’ limited budgets, leading to inconsistent or interrupted service delivery. Survivors who are uninsured or lack documentation may face additional barriers to medical assistance when specific funds are not allocated.

### CASE STUDY: Germany

Germany has a broad but decentralised system of services for survivors of sexualised violence, combining feminist counselling centres, RCCs, medical and forensic support, and national helplines. Although the overall provision remains uneven across regions, Germany’s model demonstrates how long-standing feminist expertise has shaped public and institutional responses to sexualised violence.

Specialised services available to survivors include RCCs, SVRCs, crisis and medical services, and a specialised helpline. These services provide forensic and medical care, psychological counselling, legal advice and advocacy, and community awareness and prevention activities. In addition, around half of Germany’s women’s centres offer counselling and support related to sexualised violence, extending the reach of assistance beyond specialist facilities.

icon: T

The development of SVRCs is currently being expanded through a federal initiative coordinated by an RCC in Hesse. This effort aims to ensure more consistent availability of trauma-informed, interdisciplinary services across all federal states. Meanwhile, the Sexual Abuse Helpline (+49 800 2255530) provides free, anonymous support to children, family members, and professionals concerned about sexual abuse, offering both emotional support and practical guidance.

**WAVE COUNTRY REPORT 2025**
69



---

A key coordinating structure is the Federal Working Group of Feminist Organisations against Sexual Violence against Girls and Women (*Bundesarbeitsgemeinschaft Feministischer Organisationen gegen Sexuelle Gewalt an Mädchen und Frauen e.V.*, BAG FORSA). Representing 22 member organisations, BAG FORSA promotes a feminist, society-wide approach to combating sexualised violence and supports local centres in their development and sustainability. It works closely with the German Association for Prevention and Intervention (DGPI) and the Federal Coordination of Specialised Centres (BKSF), ensuring coherence across diverse service providers.

## Geographical coverage of sexualised violence services

Geographical access to specialist services for survivors of sexualised violence remains uneven across Europe. Seven countries (15%) reported that services are available in all regions, while 10 (22%) indicated that coverage extends to most regions. In contrast, 11 countries (24%) reported that services are available only in major cities, and seven (15%) that they exist solely in the capital. The remaining countries did not provide information.

In **Belgium**, 10 Sexual Assault Care Centres ensure that every region, including more remote areas such as Arlon and Genk, has access to 24-hour, survivor-centred care. Similarly, in **Finland** and the **Netherlands**, hospital-based models ensure national coverage through coordinated networks. In **Spain**, each autonomous community maintains at least one crisis centre or hospital-based unit operating 24/7, though rural areas remain without such services. Countries such as **Ireland**, **Germany**, and **Scotland** also have relatively broad coverage. In **Ireland**, RCCs exist in 17 of 26 counties, and in **Scotland**, centres are present even in remote island regions through outreach and digital support.

Many countries in Central and Eastern Europe continue to face serious accessibility gaps. In **Lithuania**, forensic and medical care is available only in five major cities, while local centres primarily support survivors of domestic violence. **North Macedonia**, **Moldova**, and **Serbia** report that specialised centres are concentrated in capitals or a few large cities, leaving survivors in rural areas with limited or no access. In **Moldova**, mobile outreach initiatives attempt to fill this gap, but complete forensic and counselling services remain urban-based. Similarly, in **Romania**, **Montenegro**, and **Poland**, survivors outside urban centres often rely on general hospitals or non-specialised services.

## Groups of survivors supported by sexualised violence services

Most sexualised violence services in Europe are designed to support women and girls, in line with their primary

mission to address VAWG. Thirty-two countries (70%) reported providing services specifically for adult women, and 31 (67%) offer support to young women and girls under 18. In addition, 24 countries (52%) indicated that services are also available to other groups, such as men and boys, LGBTQI+ individuals, and persons with disabilities.

In several countries, services that were initially established for women have expanded to include other groups. In **Belgium**, the Sexual Assault Care Centres (*Centres de Prise en Charge des Violences Sexuelles* – CPVS) provide support to women, men, transgender people, and children, although women account for over 90% of those using the services. In **Finland**, Sexual Violence Referral Centres are open to survivors over the age of 16, while the NGO-run RCC *Tukinainen* offers support to women and girls of all ages. The **Netherlands** similarly allows access to all survivors, regardless of age or gender.

In many other countries, services remain primarily oriented towards women and girls but have developed the capacity to support other groups within the same framework. In **Ireland**, RCCs are open to survivors regardless of sex, gender or sexuality. In **Scotland**, for example, twelve centres support survivors of all genders, and three centres provide support only to women survivors of sexualised violence, with most RCCs supporting survivors from the age of 13. In **Germany**, **Serbia**, and **Spain**, feminist and women’s organisations continue to serve women as their primary target group but collaborate with other agencies to ensure that men, boys, and other survivors can receive appropriate care elsewhere. In **Lithuania**, legislative amendments have enabled five designated hospitals to assist women, men, and children. Since the full-scale invasion, **Ukraine** has expanded its support system for survivors of conflict-related sexualised violence, establishing additional services specifically tailored to the needs of women affected by wartime abuses. Delegates also noted the emergence of a small number of services for male survivors, primarily focused on addressing sexualised violence linked to war trauma.

## Conclusion

The findings of this report reveal a persistent and alarming gap in the provision of specialist services for women and girls survivors of sexualised violence across Europe. Despite clear obligations under the Istanbul Convention, the vast majority of countries do not fulfil the required standard of one RCC or SVRC per 200,000 inhabitants. Only four countries meet or exceed this requirement. This means that millions of women and girls in Europe still do not have access to specialist, trauma-informed, and gender sensitive services for survivors of sexualised violence.

Where services do exist, they are often underfunded, unevenly distributed, and concentrated in urban areas. Even in countries with more established systems, long-term

**70**
**WAVE COUNTRY REPORT 2025**



---



SPECIALIST SERVICES FOR SURVIVORS OF SEXUALISED VIOLENCE

psychological counselling and independent feminist advocacy remain limited compared to acute, hospital-based care. The sustainability of services is further undermined by unstable funding structures, with many relying on short-term projects, donations, or international aid rather than secure, institutional financing.

While some countries have broadened access to include all survivors of sexual assault, WSS remain the cornerstone of an effective, long-term feminist response. These services are grounded in the understanding that sexualised violence is a form of structural gender inequality and that survivors need not only medical or legal help but also safety, belief, and empowerment. Their independence is essential to holding institutions accountable and to ensuring that survivors’ rights and autonomy remain at the centre of all interventions.

Equally important is the sustained provision of long-term psychological and advocacy support. Many survivors come forward months, years, or even decades after the violence occurred, particularly those who experienced sexualised violence as children, and require stable, trauma-informed services that can accompany them through their healing at their own pace. Ensuring consistent, long-term support across the life course is therefore essential to addressing the full impact of sexualised violence and enabling survivors to rebuild their lives with dignity and autonomy.

To comply with international standards and meet the real needs of survivors, states must urgently invest in expanding, coordinating, and sustainably funding feminist specialist services. Without such commitment, sexualised violence will continue to be met with silence, fragmented care, and systemic neglect rather than justice, healing, and equality.

## Umbrella Recommendations

* European states must prioritise the establishment of sufficient RCCs and SVRCs in all regions, according to the Istanbul Convention standard of one centre per 200,000 inhabitants and guarantee specialist, trauma-informed, gender-specific support.

* National governments and EU institutions should provide sustainable, multi-year funding for specialist sexualised violence services to ensure long-term operational stability, prioritising remote, rural and underserved regions as well as minority and marginalised communities.

* States must strengthen cross-sector cooperation, including healthcare, law enforcement, legal services, and women’s NGOs, based on equal partnership and recognition of women’s NGOs as

independent, specialist actors, ensuring coordinated and comprehensive referral pathways for survivors of sexualised violence.

* States should develop and maintain national coordination mechanisms and data collection systems on sexualised violence, including sex-disaggregated and intersectional data on prevalence, reporting, access to services, and justice outcomes, in line with the Istanbul Convention. This should include regular quality assurance and monitoring to evaluate the effectiveness of sexualised violence services and guide policy development, in collaboration with women’s NGOs and survivor representatives.

* Accessibility of sexualised violence services should be guaranteed for all survivors, with particular attention to those from marginalised groups, such as women with disabilities, migrant and refugee women, Roma women, LGBTQI+ survivors, and those living in rural areas.

* States must adopt and enforce affirmative consent-based definitions and legislation on sexualised violence, developed in collaboration with WSS, requiring voluntary, informed and ongoing affirmative consent.

* States must invest in sustained public awareness, educational programmes and prevention campaigns to counter myths, victim-blaming and harmful gender stereotypes associated with sexualised violence, highlighting men’s collective responsibility to challenge the norms that enable such violence.

* Gender-specific, survivor-centred, and rights-based methodologies should be embedded across all specialist sexualised violence services, including free-of-charge long-term recovery programmes such as trauma-informed therapy, empowerment groups, and economic reintegration support.

icon: umbrella

* States must establish systematic, initial and continuous training for all relevant professionals (including police, judiciary, healthcare and education) on gender-informed responses to sexualised violence and workplace harassment prevention.

# Primary prevention of violence against women and girls

icon: hand

## Introduction

Violence against women and girls (VAWG) is one of the most pervasive violations of human rights across all societies. It is rooted in gender inequality and power imbalances between women and men, and it is predominantly perpetrated by men against women and girls.

Although its prevalence and manifestations vary across the world, the underlying cause and intent are the same: to exert power and control over the lives of women and girls.

Under pressure from civil society, particularly women’s movements, many countries across Europe and worldwide have developed structural responses to this issue by providing protection to survivors and ensuring the prosecution and punishment of perpetrators. Most countries have developed policies and legislation, as well as specialised support services, mainly through the involvement and advocacy efforts of women’s NGOs. While these efforts represent significant progress, the prevalence of VAWG remains alarmingly high and continues to pose a grave challenge.

Besides strengthening protection, prosecution, and the provision of services to women who have experienced violence, it is equally necessary to place greater emphasis on the prevention of VAWG. Without challenging and transforming the underlying attitudes, norms, and structures that legitimise gender inequality and violence, it will not be possible to achieve a lasting reduction in violence. This is where primary prevention plays a crucial role, as it seeks to stop violence before it occurs by addressing its root causes and creating the social conditions in which equality and non-violence can thrive.

## What is primary prevention, and why is it important?

Primary prevention means *stopping VAWG before it occurs* by addressing its root causes: unequal distribution of power and resources between women and men, discriminatory norms, stereotypes and harmful attitudes that enable and validate violence, and a lack of prevention skills

in professionals and the general public. At the same time, primary prevention involves promoting gender equality, prosocial behaviour, and safety across all areas of life.

In its 2024 publication *A Life Free from Violence: Primary Prevention as the Key to Eliminating Violence Against Women and Girls*,<sup>86</sup> the WAVE Network emphasises that primary prevention is the most strategic and transformative approach to ending VAWG and achieving lasting gender equality. According to this report's findings, primary prevention operates at several interconnected levels. It targets women, girls, boys, and men through education and awareness-building. It also works with groups and communities, such as activists, educators, and civil society organisations, as well as at the structural level by influencing policies, laws, and institutions. It addresses different audiences: women survivors of violence and discrimination, potential perpetrators, bystanders, professionals who can intervene, and institutions or individuals who sustain patriarchal systems. Activities can take various forms, such as school-based workshops for children, feminist self-defence for women and girls, peer education programmes, and workshops for professionals. These interventions are needed at all levels of society to create systemic change.

Research has identified several proven or promising primary prevention strategies. Evidence shows that school-based programmes to prevent dating violence and teach children how to recognise and avoid abuse, as well as home visitation and health outreach during pregnancy, can be effective in preventing VAWG.<sup>87</sup> Empowerment and participatory initiatives addressing structural gender inequality, together with feminist self-defence for women and girls, have also demonstrated positive impacts, remarkably when grounded in feminist and community-based approaches.<sup>88</sup> In contrast, some commonly used approaches, such as general awareness-raising campaigns or confrontational rape prevention sessions, have been shown to be ineffective as forms of primary prevention.<sup>89</sup>

It is important to distinguish primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention, especially as states tend to conflate the three when presenting their prevention efforts and reporting on VAWG prevention. This distinction was first promoted by the World Health Organisation (WHO) in relation to diseases, accidents, and disabilities and then adapted to

### THREE-PRONGED APPROACH to prevention of VAWG

**Primary prevention:** Stops violence before it starts by tackling root causes like gender inequality and stereo- types. Actions may include community organising for gender equality and against VAWG, school-based pro- grammes on preventing child abuse or dating violence, feminist self-defence, and programmes challenging harmful masculine behaviour and attitudes.

**Secondary prevention:** Early action and response to violence when it starts, to stop escalation. Activities include helplines, risk assessments, early police or health interventions, and safety planning.

**Tertiary prevention:** Addressing the consequences after violence has occurred, supporting recovery and prevent- ing recurrence. Examples include shelters, counselling and therapy, economic empowerment, and perpetrator programmes.

Empowerment lies at the heart of primary prevention. Un- like traditional support approaches, which often reinforce dependency and maintain existing power imbalances, em- powerment seeks to restore control, agency, and collective power to survivors. Self-awareness and self-care are also central to feminist primary prevention. Feminist activism often emphasises responding to crisis, leaving little space for reflection, rest, or regeneration. Yet slowing down, re- storing self-awareness, and connecting with one’s own sensations and emotions are essential acts of resistance against patriarchal conditioning that teaches women to ignore their instincts and sensitivity to injustice. Feminist self-defence exemplifies this principle by combining phys- ical, psychological, and verbal techniques that enhance women’s confidence, safety, and agency. Research shows that self-defence training not only reduces fear and avoid- ance but also strengthens general self-efficacy, support- ing women’s participation in all areas of society.

Despite the evidence of success and cost-effectiveness, primary prevention remains underfunded and often ne- glected in favour of secondary and tertiary responses that deal with violence after it has occurred. Governments continue to invest more in crisis management than in pre- vention, even though prevention is far cheaper and more

effective in reducing both human suffering and econom- ic costs. For instance, one French study found that every euro invested in prevention saves up to eighty-seven euros in costs, including direct expenses.<sup>91</sup>

Ultimately, primary prevention allows us to imagine and build a society without violence. It shifts the narrative from counting survivors to celebrating those who will never ex- perience violence. It focuses energy on transformation, empowerment, and collective freedom. By prioritising pri- mary prevention, we can redirect resources and attention from managing the consequences of patriarchy to con- structing a safer, fairer, and more equal world for everyone.

### International obligations

International frameworks recognise prevention as an es- sential component of states’ human rights obligations. The Istanbul Convention, which has been ratified by 38 Council of Europe member states, was also formally ac- ceded to by the European Union (EU) in June 2023, en- tering into force across member states in October 2023. This added significant weight to its provisions and implies broader applicability, especially in countries that have not ratified it individually. In its opening preamble, the Istan- bul Convention recognises that “violence against women and girls stems from historically unequal power relations and harmful gender norms”.<sup>92</sup> While it does not distinguish between primary, secondary and tertiary prevention, it un- derlines the importance of prevention by dedicating Chap- ter III of the Convention to this issue. Article 12 explicitly addresses states’ obligations to take measures to prevent violence against women (VAW) through social change, thereby enshrining the states’ obligation to engage in pri- mary prevention.

More specifically, Article 12 obliges states to eliminate stereotypes and inequalities that sustain VAW, using legislation and other preventive measures grounded in a gender-sensitive and intersectional approach. Special attention should be given to vulnerable groups, including women with disabilities, minority women, refugees, and displaced persons. States must also promote women’s empowerment, reject ‘honour’ as a justification for vio- lence, and engage men and boys in primary prevention.<sup>93</sup>

The General Recommendation No. 35 on gender-based violence against women to the Convention on the Elimi- nation of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CE- DAW) strengthens the focus on prevention. It defines gen- der-based violence against women (GBVAW) as “one of the fundamental social, political and economic means by which

**WAVE COUNTRY REPORT 2025** 73

---

the subordinate position of women with respect to men and their stereotyped roles are perpetuated”,<sup>94</sup> calling for comprehensive responses addressing systemic causes. It recommends integrating gender equality, non-violent masculinities, and evidence-based, age-appropriate comprehensive sexuality education into curricula at all educational levels.<sup>95</sup>

The WHO’s RESPECT Framework, an interactive ecological model of the primary prevention of VAW, organises risk factors on the different levels at which they occur (societal, institutional, community/family, and individual).

The framework outlines seven strategies to prevent VAW (RESPECT):<sup>96</sup>

◾ R – Relationship skills strengthened

◾ E – Empowerment of women

◾ S – Services ensured

◾ P – Poverty reduced

◾ E – Environments made safe

◾ C – Child and adolescent abuse prevented

◾ T – Transformed attitudes, beliefs, and norms

To encourage implementation, WHO and UN Women released the RESPECT Implementation Package in 2020,<sup>97</sup> a collection of practical resources that includes strategy briefs for each RESPECT pillar, programme examples, mini briefs on enabling environments, a monitoring and evaluation brief, and a workbook for national prevention planning.<sup>98</sup>

Since the last WAVE Country Report in 2023, the new Directive (EU) 2024/1385 on combating violence against women and domestic violence was adopted on May 14, 2024, and entered into force on June 14, 2024. Although WAVE has been critical of the final adopted text, having consistently advocated for a stronger instrument that would classify gender-based violence (GBV) as an Eurocrime,<sup>99</sup> the Directive still represents a significant step forward. For the first time, a broad range of measures to combat VAWG has become an official part of EU law, providing a binding framework for Member States. This binding international legal document explicitly states that Member States must adopt a comprehensive approach to address violence, including primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention measures, making it the first international instrument to use this language. Member states’ primary prevention obligations under the Directive include public awareness campaigns and integrating primary prevention into formal education

(e.g., improved sexuality education, empathy-building, and healthy relationships).<sup>100</sup>

Taken together, these international and regional instruments clearly establish that states’ obligations extend beyond responding to violence once it occurs. They require governments to address the root causes of VAWG by transforming harmful norms, eliminating structural inequalities, and promoting gender equality in all areas of life. Prevention is therefore not an optional policy choice, but an essential human rights obligation.

## WAVE framework for collecting data on primary prevention

This is the second time that WAVE has collected, with its members' help, data and insights on primary prevention of VAWG. Since there is no unified formal definition of primary prevention, with international documents focusing on different components and aspects of all three types of prevention, WAVE has focused on what has been shown to work and what is aligned with the priorities of women’s specialist services (WSS), based on recommendations from the WAVE Primary Prevention Working Group. Therefore, the data collection focused on promising primary prevention strategies to address VAWG, the existence of National Action Plans (NAPs), definitions of primary prevention, and the funding of these programmes at the national level.

## Findings on primary prevention in Europe

In its 2025 survey, WAVE collected information from 46 countries:<sup>101</sup>

◾ NAPs or other national provisions on primary prevention – if and how prevention is included in official strategies

◾ Funding for primary prevention activities

### National Action Plans

NAPs are an efficient way to ensure that VAWG is ad- dressed through holistic measures that include primary prevention. The EU Directive 2024/1385 mandates under Article 39 that Member States must establish NAPs to pre- vent and combat VAW and domestic violence by 14 June 2029.<sup>102</sup> According to a UN Women analysis of its global database on VAWG from July 2025, 34% of UN Member States have not adopted a dedicated NAP to address VAWG.<sup>103</sup>

Based on information from WAVE members, the last WAVE Country Report from 2023 listed 31 countries with some form of NAP or a similar policy document. In this round of data collection, we specifically asked if there was an official document on primary prevention, such as a NAP or other provisions. Responses indicate that 32 countries (70%) reported having an official document on prevention, such as a NAP or a strategy, although it is not known whether they specifically address primary prevention. This includes separate plans for three of the four nations in the **United Kingdom**<sup>104</sup> and in **Belgium**, which has a national as well as two regional plans.<sup>105</sup> No NAP or similar doc- ument defining primary prevention was reported in ten countries. **Azerbaijan** and **North Macedonia** both had a NAP, but they expired at the end of 2023, and a new one hasn’t been passed yet. **Austria** is developing a new NAP that will include primary prevention, but the exact defini- tion and measures are not yet known. Some countries do not have an official NAP, but they do have other strategic documents. For example, the **United Kingdom**’s approach to addressing VAWG will be set out in the Tackling VAWG Strategy 2025. In the **Netherlands**, primary prevention is listed as one of the four pillars of the Stop Femicide! plan, with numerous activities outlined by different ministries.

Some countries, such as **Hungary**, **Greece**, and **Moldova**, rely on NGOs and EU projects rather than a national strat- egy to develop primary prevention programmes. Some countries have multiple NAPs covering different forms of VAWG, such as **Norway**, which has a NAP on domestic

violence, rape, forced marriage, female genital mutila- tion, and online sexual abuse. These include preventive measures, but they are not defined within a single nation- al framework of primary prevention. In these cases, pre- vention is carried out operationally through measures and activities, but it is not defined conceptually, and there is no holistic, coordinated primary prevention approach, de- creasing the efficacy of individual measures.

### Defining primary prevention

The existence of a NAP is often used as an indicator of a country’s commitment to implement an integrated policy and a strategic, holistic approach to addressing and elimi- nating VAWG. However, the findings of the WAVE data col- lection for the Country Report 2025, similar to the 2023 report, show that the existence of a NAP does not guar- antee that it provides a comprehensive, gender-sensitive strategy and a primary prevention framework.

When asked if there is a definition of primary prevention of VAWG in their country’s NAP or elsewhere, 18 WAVE country delegates (39%) responded that there is such a definition. Among the countries that responded yes to this question, there is variation in the detail provided in the definitions of primary prevention, and it could not al- ways be verified whether the definitions were specifically about primary prevention or only about prevention. Some countries have very clear definitions (the **Netherlands**, **Italy**, **Scotland**, and **Albania**), while others only refer to prevention in terms of general awareness measures or international standards. Many countries take their defini- tion of prevention directly from the WHO or the Istanbul Convention, while others create their own national defini- tions based on education or on removing stereotypes. For countries that responded that they do not have a defini- tion of primary prevention in an official document, a com- mon theme is that prevention exists but is implemented through activities such as awareness-raising, education, and campaigns.

For countries that do have a definition of primary preven- tion in their NAP, some explicitly align it with internation- al definitions. For example, **Belgium** quotes the WHO’s health-prevention framing and applies it to VAWG. Some countries have more detailed and specific descriptions of primary prevention. For example, the **Netherlands** defines it as:

“eliminating root causes of violence against women. Pre- venting gender-based violence (including femicide) can be achieved largely by eliminating gender inequality as a cause of the violence. We want to promote gender equality and equality between individuals and drive a societal culture change. This
