# Femicide

icon: shoe

## Introduction

Femicide is the gender-related killing of women and girls. These crimes are most often perpetrated by men and are rooted in stereotyped gender roles and historically unequal power relations between women and men, which instil a sense of possessiveness and superiority among men toward women. The term highlights that women are not killed as a matter of chance or coincidence, but within the context of unequal power relations, misogyny, and discrimination. The word was first used publicly by feminist activist Diana Russell in 1976 as "*the killing of females by males because they are female*".<sup>148</sup> Understanding femicide helps to make visible the structural nature of violence against women and girls (VAWG) and the continuum that connects everyday forms of harassment, control, and abuse with the most extreme outcome, the killing of women.

There is still no uniform or internationally agreed-upon definition of femicide. States, international organisations, and researchers use the term in different ways, making comparisons difficult. Many countries where it is used limit its meaning to the killing of a woman by her current or former intimate partner. Feminist NGOs and international mechanisms, including the United Nations Special Rapporteur on Violence Against Women and Girls (UN Special Rapporteur), have long argued that this is too narrow. The UN Special Rapporteur’s report on gender-related killings of women<sup>149</sup> identified a wide range of forms that femicide can take, including so-called honour killings, dowry-related deaths, killings linked to witchcraft accusations, conflict-related killings, those connected to sexualised violence or trafficking, and cases where a woman’s death results from state failure to protect her from known violence. The report also recognised indirect femicides, such as suicides following domestic or sexualised violence, deaths caused by unsafe abortion or maternal neglect, and other harmful practices. Each of these deaths reflects the continuum of VAWG and the structural discrimination that women experience throughout their lives.

According to the most recent global estimates published by the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) and UN Women in November 2024, around 140 women and girls were killed every day in 2023 by an intimate partner or family member.<sup>150</sup> The report shows that homes remain the most dangerous place for women, and that the real number of femicides is likely much higher due to poor data and underreporting. At the European level, the

European Institute for Gender Equality (EIGE) notes that women make up 87% of victims of intimate partner homicides and 60% of victims of domestic homicides.<sup>151</sup> However, differences in definitions and data systems between countries mean that these figures are incomplete and cannot yet show the whole picture.

Femicide is not an isolated crime. It is the most visible and irreversible expression of the system of male violence that limits women’s freedom and equality in all areas of life. Naming it, documenting it, and understanding its patterns are crucial steps in preventing future killings and achieving justice for all women whose lives have been taken by gender-based violence (GBV).

Feminist organisations have been central to naming, documenting, and politicising femicide. Long before official data collection began, women’s rights groups exposed the scale and patterns of gender-related killings of women and girls, challenging the silence of state institutions and the normalisation of male violence. Their activism continues to drive visibility, accountability, and policy change at local, national, and international levels.

Collecting reliable and comparable data on femicide remains one of the most significant challenges for both governments and civil society. The lack of conceptual clarity directly affects how data are gathered, classified, and reported, making it difficult to measure the full scale of the problem or to compare figures across countries. Most countries record data on homicide rather than femicide. Where gender is noted, it is often only as a demographic variable, not as a motive or contextual factor. As a result, many killings of women that are clearly gender-related remain invisible in official statistics. In some contexts, only intimate partner or family-related homicides are counted as femicide, while in others, even these cases are recorded without reference to gender. This inconsistency limits the accuracy of national and regional estimates and obscures the broader social patterns of male violence against women (VAW).

Across Europe, feminist organisations have developed a wide range of initiatives to document femicide and push for systemic responses. Many collect and verify data on women killed by men, often drawing on media reports, court records, and direct information from women’s specialist services (WSS). Their efforts go beyond counting deaths. They analyse patterns of coercive control, identify failures in protection, and link individual cases to broader

institutional and social inequalities. They publish statements, hold press conferences, run media campaigns and organise protests to draw attention to all the systemic failures that often precede the individual cases of femicide. This approach understands systematic data collection as a feminist act of resistance and remembrance, a way to restore visibility to women’s lives, holding institutions accountable, and driving prevention efforts.

## International obligations

In Europe, there has been growing recognition that femicide must be named, measured, and prevented as a distinct form of GBV. The European Union’s ratification of the Council of Europe Convention on preventing and combating violence against women and domestic violence (Istanbul Convention) in 2023 and the adoption of the European Union Directive (EU) 2024/1385 of 14 May 2024 on combating violence against women and domestic violence (EU Directive) in 2024 mark significant progress. These instruments require EU Member States to strengthen prevention, protection, and prosecution, and to improve the collection and sharing of data. Although the Istanbul Convention does not explicitly use the term femicide, it is implicit in its definition of GBV as violence directed against a woman because she is a woman. The Istanbul Convention obliges Member States to take all necessary legislative and policy measures to ensure the right of women to live free from violence, including through effective risk assessment, coordinated institutional response, and accountability for failure to protect women. The Council of Europe’s monitoring body, Group of Experts on Action against Violence against Women and Domestic Violence (GREVIO), has repeatedly noted that the prevention of femicide must be a core component of Member States’ implementation of the Convention.<sup>152</sup>

The European Observatory on Femicide (EOF) serves as a central hub for research, monitoring, and data exchange on gender-related killings of women across Europe.<sup>153</sup> Its aim is to build a comparative knowledge base on femicide, promote shared methodologies, and strengthen collaboration between academic institutions, women’s organisations, and policy actors. The EOF develops both quantitative and qualitative research tools and facilitates the exchange of national data and good practices to support the creation of femicide watches and observatories at the national level. Within this framework, the FEM-UnitED project (2020–2022)<sup>154</sup> provided an important foundation for developing harmonised indicators and guidelines for data collection and analysis, enabling a more systematic understanding of femicide in Europe.

Globally, the UN Special Rapporteur on Violence against Women and Girls continues to promote the establishment of national femicide watches or observatories. These mechanisms are meant to record and analyse every case of gender-related killing of women and girls, identify risk factors, and ensure accountability of state institutions. The call to “count femicides so that counting counts for women”<sup>155</sup> remains as urgent as ever. In her 2021 report, the UN Special Rapporteur set out what a femicide watch/observatory should be: mainly a mechanism that records and analyses every case of gender-related killings of women and girls, disaggregates data by sex, age, perpetrator-victim relationship, motive, and uses the findings to strengthen prevention and ensure accountability.

## WAVE framework for collecting data on femicide

For the Country Report 2025, WAVE collected information on whether state institutions used the term femicide in legislation, policy, or data systems. Respondents reported what types of data were collected, who collected them, and whether victim characteristics and relationships with perpetrators were recorded. The questionnaire also gathered numbers of femicide victims in 2024, information on victims’ previous contact with authorities or specialist services, and whether systematic reviews or femicide analyses were conducted.

## Findings on femicide in Europe

According to information provided by WAVE delegates from 35 out of 46 European countries, at least 2,871 women were victims of femicide in 2024.<sup>156</sup> This figure includes estimates supplied by national experts and feminist organisations where official data were missing. No data on femicide were available from nine countries,<sup>157</sup> and in several others, only partial or unofficial information could be collected. Of the total, 969 femicides were recorded in EU Member States and 1,902 in European countries outside the EU. In many cases, these figures represent minimum estimates, as systematic monitoring of femicide remains uneven across Europe. The data were gathered from a combination of official sources, media reports, research findings, and tracking by WSS.

Only 23 out of 46 countries reported any disaggregated information in these subsections, meaning that the figures below represent partial totals based on available data, not the full 3,982 femicides recorded across Europe in 2024. Among the 1,120 femicide cases where such information was available:

* 843 women (76%) were killed by a current or former intimate partner<sup>158</sup>

* 217 women (19%) were killed by a family member other than a partner<sup>159</sup>

* 36 women (3%) were killed by an acquaintance<sup>160</sup>

* 24 women (2%) were killed by other perpetrators, including strangers or unknown offenders<sup>161</sup>

These findings reaffirm that femicide is most often committed by men with a close personal relationship to the victim. However, the limited number of countries providing detailed breakdowns highlights persistent gaps in systematic, gender-sensitive data collection across Europe. Besides these numbers, Spain additionally reported that in 2024, 36 children were killed by fathers/current or former intimate partners of the mother.

Information on whether femicide victims have previously received specialist support, from women’s organisations or state-run services, remains extremely limited across Europe. Information on this question was available in only 16 of 46 countries. Among them, 13 countries reported that *some* victims had received support, two reported that *most* victims had done so, and one stated that *none* had. In contrast, 22 countries indicated that they *did not know*, while eight countries provided no data at all. This indicates that in nearly half of European countries, there is no systematic information about whether women killed by men had prior contact with WSS, shelters, or other forms of specialist support. The lack of linkage between femicide data, service records, and law enforcement systems severely limits the ability to identify missed opportunities for protection and to learn from fatal cases.

Overall, these findings underscore a critical weakness in national monitoring systems: the absence of mechanisms that systematically record and analyse victims’ prior contact with protection and support services. Addressing this gap is essential for understanding institutional failures and for developing effective prevention measures against femicide.

Across Europe, many women killed by men had previously reported violence to the police, prosecutors, or other public authorities, yet their search for help did not prevent their deaths. Out of 46 countries, 24 reported that *some* or *most* femicide victims had earlier contacted institutions, most often the police. In contrast, 15 countries stated that this information is not known, and the remaining countries provided no data. This suggests that while evidence of prior reporting exists in more than half of the countries, it remains fragmented, inconsistent, and poorly integrated into official data systems.

For example, in **Belgium**, most victims reported their perpetrators (in the vast majority of cases, their current or former partner) to the police; however, these reports were not adequately followed up by the police and/or judicial authorities. In **Hungary**, NANE’s Silent Witness cases rely on information from police and media reports, meaning the available data depends on what is publicly disclosed. In several femicide cases in 2024, authorities had prior knowledge of the violence, such as situations where victims unsuccessfully requested restraining orders or where perpetrators had been released from prison shortly before the killing. In **Iceland**, victims reported the violence to social services.

In the **Netherlands**, media reports and testimonials from relatives of women who have been murdered indicate that there were early warning signs. Police, healthcare services and other public bodies could have followed up if they had had enough knowledge and awareness of red flags and would have connected incidents to possible patterns of intimate terror or stalking. Across countries, respondents emphasised that information is fragmented among police, courts, and WSS and is rarely analysed collectively. In **Republika Srpska**, in two of the three femicide cases, the domestic violence had previously been reported to the police, and both victims had left the shared household before the murder was committed. In **Spain**, more specific data are available, showing that 15 of the 48 women had previously reported their perpetrators to the police.

## CASE STUDY: the Netherlands – the story of Gea

On 15 May 2020, Barbara Godwaldt’s only sister, Gea, was killed by her husband, who then took his own life. A relationship that seemed to start happily—despite early signs that he had been violent with a former girlfriend—gradually turned into a nightmare of intimate terror for her and her daughter, who lived in what initially appeared to be a large, blended family and a dream come true. Over time, arguments became more frequent and more abusive. After fights, he bombarded her with messages, sometimes threatening to harm himself. He made it difficult for her to meet friends. As the violence escalated, she told him she questioned whether the relationship could still be saved. The dynamic shifted: he would cry and apologise. His regrets and promises to return to how things once were convinced her to give him another chance, but her gut feeling that something was terribly wrong remained.

After a long period of abuse, threats, intimidation, and insults, she decided she had to end the relationship—for herself, and to show her daughter that no one should be treated so badly.

She tried to leave the house, but he stopped her. Gea was found dead in the living room, and although the police could not identify the order of events, it was clear she had endured a bloody fight and suffocation. Her husband had hanged himself in the stairwell.

After the murder, Barbara, Gea’s sister, and their family were thrown into a rollercoaster of distressing events. Minutes after learning how her sister had died, Barbara had to contact the perpetrator’s family to arrange picking up clothes so Gea could be buried in something clean. She was interrogated for hours at the police station. She had to identify her sister; it took her 20 minutes to recognise her. The officer assigned to support her had little experience and began talking about his deceased grandmother—the only dead body he had ever seen. Her niece, who still lived with her mother but had not been home that night, had no clothes, study materials, or letters from her mother, as everything was inside the house, now a crime scene. They had to sneak in to retrieve them. The house had not been cleaned after the murder, so they cleaned the blood and other traces themselves. The police refused to acknowledge that Gea had been killed by her husband. Out of sympathy for his family, they repeatedly called it a ‘family tragedy’. Then came disputes over inheritance rights: the aftermath seemed endless.

The guilt, the lack of recognition for what had been done to her sister, and the pain and injustices she witnessed in her own family and among other survivors drove Barbara to become one of the most active and visible advocates against femicide in the Netherlands. Her goal: to prevent this loss for others. After an intense period of traumatic grief, she wrote the Femicide Action Plan and submitted it to the government. Her plan—and the support she mobilised—formed the basis of the Dutch National Action Plan (NAP) *Stop Femicide!*. To this day, campaigning against femicide and advocating for more effective measures has become her daily work. She is one of the leading women and spokespersons of the Federation of Relatives of Victims of Violence ([https://www.nabestaandengeweld-slachtoffers.nl/](https://www.nabestaandengeweldslachtoffers.nl/)). She advises several organisations, supports survivors, and tirelessly advocates to improve femicide policies at both national and regional levels. She appears regularly in the media and as a keynote speaker at conferences.

## The use of the term ‘femicide’

According to information provided by respondents from 46 European countries, in 2024, the term femicide was officially used in nine countries, was under development or legislative consideration in four, and was used only informally or in public discourse in 22. Respondents from 11 countries reported that the term was not used at all by the state or other authorities.

Where femicide is officially recognised, it appears in law, public policy, or national data systems. In **Croatia**, the 2023 amendments to the Criminal Code introduced femicide as a specific aggravated criminal act of murder when the crime is committed against a woman because of her gender. The reform was the result of long-term advocacy by women’s organisations, particularly the Autonomous Women’s House Zagreb and the Women’s Network Croatia, who pushed for legal recognition of gender-related killings as part of the continuum of VAW.

In **Belgium**, a law adopted in June 2023 formally recognised femicide in the Penal Code, introducing legal terminology and state-level monitoring of gender-related killings. The law followed years of feminist campaigning led by the Stop Femicide (*Stop Féminicide*) collective, and it established obligations for the government to collect and publish disaggregated data on femicides annually.

In **Cyprus**, the term was incorporated into legislation in 2022, criminalising femicide as a distinct offence and mandating prevention and awareness measures. France

**WAVE COUNTRY REPORT 2025**
95



---

also uses *féminicide* in legal and statistical practice, while **Italy** records ‘killing of women for gender-related reasons’ (*omicidio di donne per motivi di genere*) in official reports by the Ministry of the Interior.<sup>162</sup> **Spain** officially uses the expression ‘fatal victims of gender violence’ or ‘macho murders’ in legislation (LO 1/2004 and its development) and in judicial reports. However, in the Statistical Portal of the Government Delegation against Gender Violence, there is a section entitled ‘Feminicides’, where the annual records of fatal victims are grouped. In the NGO and media sphere, the term femicide is used with some frequency to refer to the gender-related murder of women.

In the **Netherlands**, the term femicide has been officially endorsed since 2024, following the launch of the National Plan Stop Femicide! by three ministers, and while it is not yet embedded in the legal system, it is now used in national and local policies as well as by the Public Prosecutor’s Office. Since August 2024, the term femicide has been included in **Moldovan** legislation through its definition in the Law on the Prevention and Combating of Violence against Women and Domestic Violence (Law No. 45 of 01.03.2007). However, it has not yet been incorporated into the Criminal Code as a specific offence.

In most European countries, however, the term femicide is not officially recognised, even if it is increasingly visible in society. In 22 countries, respondents noted that while the state does not use the term, it has become part of public, academic, or media discourse, often promoted by women’s rights organisations. Feminist NGOs and activists continue to lead in naming femicide, using it to highlight the gendered patterns behind killings of women and to demand stronger prevention and accountability measures. In **Hungary** and the **Czech Republic**, women’s organisations such as NANE and proFem monitor cases and organise public awareness campaigns that explicitly name femicide, while official institutions continue to record these cases as homicides or domestic violence. In **Malta**, the term femicide is formally recognised but not a separate offence; instead, since 2022, the Criminal Code treats ‘femicidal circumstances’ as aggravating factors requiring maximum sentences and excludes ‘crime of passion’ defences in gender-motivated killings. Malta has also established a Femicide Research and Advocacy Observatory, led by the Women’s Rights Foundation with the national Commission on Gender-Based Violence, to improve data collection, awareness, and policy responses.

Finally, 11 countries reported that the term is not used at all, either by the state or within public debate. In these contexts, killings of women remain classified under general homicide or domestic violence categories.

<sup>162</sup> On 25 November 2025, Italy passed a law introducing the crime of femicide and making it punishable by life imprisonment. The law defines femicide as causing the death of a woman as an act of discrimination or hatred because she is a woman, or with the view to repress her rights, freedoms, or expression of personality.

## CASE STUDY: Belgium – the #StopFéminicide law and initiative

In October 2023, Belgium’s Law of 13 June 2023 on the prevention and combating of femicide and gender-based homicides,<sup>163</sup> commonly referred to as the #StopFéminicide Law, entered into force. It establishes legal definitions of femicide, gender-based homicide, GBV, sexualised violence, and coercive control.

The #StopFéminicide Law sets out four distinct categories of gender-related killing:

* ~~Intimate femicide, such as the killing of a partner~~ or former partner

* Non-intimate femicide, such as the killing of a woman in prostitution networks

* ~~Indirect femicide, including deaths resulting from~~ forced abortion or female genital mutilation

* ~~Gender-based homicide, encompassing killings of~~ trans, gender-fluid, or non-binary persons committed in the context of GBV

The law establishes an obligation for the annual publication of an official report on femicides in Belgium. This report must include:

* The number of complaints to the police

* The number of femicides recorded

* ~~The characteristics of victims and perpetrators~~

* ~~The relationship between victim and perpetrator~~

* The number of convictions of perpetrators

The report is to be reviewed by a consultative committee, which analyses the data and makes recommendations for state action to prevent femicide. However, at the time of reporting, no official report has yet been published. Currently, femicide data in Belgium continue to be collected primarily by civil society initiatives, most notably the Stop Feminicide platform, which has long documented cases and advocated for official recognition of the problem.

This legislative progress represents the outcome of sustained feminist mobilisation, particularly through the Stop Feminicide initiative, which has been instrumental in pushing for state accountability and legal recognition of femicide.

## Data collection on femicide

According to information provided by respondents from 46 European countries, only six countries reported that the state officially collects data on femicide. These are **Croatia**, **France**, **Italy**, **Spain**, **Albania**, and the **Republic of Moldova**. In these countries, the collection of data on

96
**WAVE COUNTRY REPORT 2025**



---



FEMICIDE

gender-related killings of women is embedded within state institutions, usually involving the police, justice or equality bodies, as well as national statistical offices.

In 29 countries, respondents reported NGOs collect or compile data, often maintaining national femicide data- bases or annual reports. Police collect data in 21 coun- tries, usually under general homicide or domestic violence statistics, without identifying the killings as gender related. Other state bodies, including ministries, ombudspersons, and statistical offices, collect related data in 19 countries, but rarely under a specific femicide category. Media mon- itoring is an important source in 10 countries, while aca- demic research is cited in 12 countries.

In **Hungary**, NANE systematically compiles data each year on women killed by partners or family members, drawing on police reports and media sources. More recently, NANE has also begun recording cases of children killed in the context of domestic or intimate partner violence. Each year, during the 16 Days of Activism campaign, NANE organis- es the *Silent Witness March* to honour victims and demand more decisive state action to prevent femicide. The march features life-sized red silhouettes representing victims, each inscribed with the woman’s name, date and place of death, relationship to the perpetrator, and brief details of the case, including prior violence and institutional respons- es. In parallel, PATENT Association and the independent online newspaper *Mérce* launched a joint initiative to in- crease visibility and public accountability: a public femi- cide counter, displayed on social media under the hashtag #MercePatentCounter (#MercePatentSzámláló). Updated regularly, the counter tracks every woman and child killed by gender-based or domestic violence, while also exposing systemic misogyny and state inaction that enable these crimes. Together, these initiatives combine data collection, public awareness, and commemoration, keeping femicide in Hungary visible as both a personal and political issue.

In the **Czech Republic**, the organisation proFem docu- ments femicide cases and uses them to advocate for legal and policy reform. In **Serbia**, the Women Against Violence Network systematically monitors media reports, verifies cases through partners, and publishes annual reports that are recognised by the state as the most reliable national source. In **Austria**, the Association of Austrian Autono- mous Women’s Shelters (*Autonome Österreichische Frau- enhäuser – AÖF*) operates a femicide watch that collab- orates with shelters and specialist services. In **Germany**, the initiative *One Billion Rising Deutschland* and academic researchers publish femicide data and commentary, filling the absence of state reporting. Similar initiatives exist in **Greece**, **Türkiye**, **Kosovo**, and **North Macedonia**, where feminist groups monitor killings and raise public aware- ness. In several of these contexts, media outlets now also use the term femicide in their reporting, showing that feminist advocacy is reshaping the public understanding of gender-based killings even in the absence of state rec- ognition.

Only **Belgium** and the Republic of **Moldova** reported col- lecting data on suicides linked to GBV. In **Belgium**, femi- cide and gender-based homicide data collection frame- works also cover indirect femicides, including deaths by suicide resulting from coercive control, forced marriage, or other forms of GBV. This inclusion follows the adoption of the #StopFéminicide Law (2023), which recognises indi- rect femicide as a category of gender-related killing. While official implementation is still in progress, the law man- dates the gathering and publication of data on all forms of gender-based killing, including suicides related to gen- dered violence.

### Systematic analysis and review of femicide cases

Only a minority of European countries have mechanisms in place to analyse femicide cases and identify lessons for prevention systematically. Out of 46 countries, 12 re- spondents reported that such processes exist or are under development. This means that only about one-quarter of European states have taken any steps towards institution- alising femicide reviews or analytical mechanisms, de- spite long-standing international calls to establish national femicide watches.

In most countries, femicides are still treated as isolat- ed criminal incidents, investigated case by case without broader institutional learning. Respondents highlighted that authorities rarely assess how victims interacted with services before their deaths or whether intervention could have prevented the killing. This lack of systematic review prevents the identification of recurring patterns of institu- tional failure, such as ineffective police response, poor risk assessment, or the absence of inter-agency coordination.

Some positive examples show gradual progress. In **Spain**, the Ministry of Equality conducts ongoing monitoring and publishes detailed annual reports on femicide, distinguish- ing between intimate partner, family-related, and other gender-related killings. **France** has developed the Nation- al Observatory on Violence Against Women (*Observatoire national des violences faites aux femmes*), which produces thematic analyses of femicides and issues recommen- dations for policy improvement. **Croatia** has a state-led femicide watch coordinated by the Ombudswoman for Gender Equality, which analyses cases and publishes statistics in cooperation with the police. **Belgium**’s 2023 #StopFéminicide Law obliges the government to publish an annual report on femicide and to review the data through a consultative committee. In **Poland**, the Women’s Rights Centre runs a feminist-led Femicide Observatory project that monitors killings of women and advocates for strong- er state accountability. In **Finland**, the NGO Women’s Line collects information to contribute to the internation- al Femicide Watch initiative. These examples show that while only a handful of countries have established dedicat- ed observatories, feminist organisations remain the main drivers of femicide monitoring across Europe.

**WAVE COUNTRY REPORT 2025**

97


---

In **Malta**, a Femicide Research and Advocacy Observatory was established, led by the Women’s Rights Foundation in collaboration with the National Commission on Gender-Based Violence and Domestic Violence. The Observatory collects data, raises awareness, and contributes to policy responses to femicide and gender-related killings.

In **Albania**, the Femicide Observatory records key indicators such as the number of cases, prior reporting to authorities, protection orders, age, gender, marital status, education level, relationship between victim and perpetrator, and municipality. However, data on ethnicity, disability, and socioeconomic status of the victims are still missing, leaving significant gaps in understanding intersecting risk factors. The People’s Advocate (Ombudsman), with support from UN Women Albania under the Joint UN Programme End Violence against Women (funded by the Government of Sweden), published the report “Murder of Women and Girls – Femicide in Albania (2021–2023)”.<sup>164</sup> The report analyses femicide cases nationwide, evaluates the role of key institutions, including police, prosecutors, courts, municipalities, and health services, and assesses the effectiveness of protective measures, support services, and rehabilitation programs. It provides detailed municipal-level data and information on cases involving protection orders or prior police reports, contributing valuable insight into institutional responses and prevention gaps.

In the Republic of Moldova, the Commission for Monitoring and Analysing Cases of Domestic Violence Resulting in Death or Serious Bodily Injury was recently renamed the Commission for the Analysis of Femicide and Domestic Violence Cases Resulting in the Victim’s Death or Serious Bodily Injury or Health Damage (Commission).<sup>165</sup> The Commission uses a comprehensive data collection form to document all cases of domestic violence leading to death or serious harm. The police provide most of the information, though the Commission is authorised to gather data and to request cooperation from other relevant authorities and institutions. The form collects detailed information on the act itself, including the legal classification and circumstances of the offence, as well as on the victim’s background, such as citizenship, nationality, sex, age, education, means of subsistence, and whether the victim had dependents or owned a firearm. It also includes data on any addictions or harmful habits (for adult victims), information about past violations of protection orders within the previous five years, and criminal records. Where applicable, details on minor victims are also recorded. In addition, the form captures information about the relationship between the victim and the perpetrator, the circumstances surrounding the commission of the offence, post-incident information about both parties, and the history of their relationship or other relevant background details. Medical data and social

assistance information related to the case and the individuals involved are also included.

Despite these advances, the majority of countries lack formal, legally mandated femicide review mechanisms. In many cases, feminist organisations, shelters, and researchers have stepped in to fill this gap, conducting independent analyses of femicide cases using media monitoring and court data. These initiatives, such as those led by women’s rights networks in **Serbia**, **Hungary**, and **Austria**, provide critical insight into systemic failures and have been instrumental in pushing governments toward recognising femicide as a structural problem rather than an individual crime. However, without official status or access to state-held information, their findings often remain outside policy and institutional reform processes.

### CASE STUDY: Bosnia and Herzegovina – livestreamed femicide

On 11 August 2023, 35-year-old Nermin Sulejmanović livestreamed the murder of his former partner, Nizama Hećimović, from the town of Gradačac. In the videos posted to Instagram, he announced viewers would “see a murder live”, then shot her on camera. He went on to kill two other people and wound several more before taking his own life. The incident triggered immediate national and international outrage, with authorities confirming the sequence of killings and the use of Instagram Live.

The case quickly raised questions about failures in state protection. Media and officials reported that Hećimović had previously reported harassment and violence, and within days, authorities said they would investigate why a restraining order had not been issued and whether police and a local judge failed to act on risks. A year on, observers argued that Bosnia and Herzegovina still had not delivered the legal reforms needed to recognise and prevent femicide, underlining gaps between public pledges and concrete change.

Public reaction was swift and sustained. Thousands marched in cities across Bosnia and Herzegovina, demanding better protection for women, effective police action, and recognition of femicide in law - carrying banners such as “Stop femicide” and “Silence is approval”. UN officials condemned the livestreamed killing as horrifying, while national leaders called for stricter penalties and systemic improvements. These mobilisations kept the case on the political agenda, linking it to broader patterns of GBV in the region.

The Gradačac femicide also exposed gaps in social

media platform accountability. Civil society groups wrote to Meta, asking why the video remained online for hours and urged stronger content-moderation protocols to prevent the amplification of GBV, avoid causing distress to viewers and the retraumatisation of survivors. Combined with the state’s own failures, this case underscored how both online platforms and public authorities must act swiftly and responsibly to protect women’s lives and dignity, including through legal recognition of femicide and systematic post-homicide reviews.

## Conclusion

The findings in this chapter demonstrate that femicide is neither isolated nor inevitable: it is the most visible expression of unequal power relations, enabled by institutional gaps and sustained by social norms that tolerate male control over women and girls. While feminist organisations have made femicide visible, naming it, counting it, and insisting on its political meaning, state recognition and response remain uneven. Although legal frameworks have advanced in Europe, the absence of harmonised definitions and gender-sensitive recording practices continues to obscure the scale and patterns of these killings.

WAVE’s findings underline three structural weaknesses. First, visibility: only a minority of states collect femicide data in a way that captures gendered motives and relationships, leaving WSS and feminist NGOs to fill critical evidence gaps. Second, protection: many women killed by men had previously reported the violence to public authorities, and some of them sought help from WSS and state-run services, yet weak risk assessment, inadequate inter-agency coordination, and poor enforcement resulted in missed opportunities to prevent escalation. Third, accountability and learning: most countries still lack mandated femicide reviews, which means institutional failures are neither systematically examined nor remedied.

Progress is possible and already underway. Where states partner with WSS, adopt clear definitions, and institutionalise data systems, the picture becomes sharper and prevention more plausible. Country experiences highlighted in this chapter, alongside emblematic cases that mobilised public outrage, demonstrate that reform follows when civil society evidence meets political will. Yet scattered initiatives are not enough; Europe needs consistent, comparable, and legally binding responsibilities to protect women and girls.

Overall, the findings indicate that femicide is foreseeable and preventable when state systems respond adequately to women’s reports of violence. Establishing mandatory femicide reviews and integrated national data systems, linking police, judicial, and support service information, would allow governments to identify failures in protection and strengthen preventive responses across Europe.

## Recommendations

* States should explicitly integrate femicide into national strategies and policies addressing VAWG, recognising gender-related killings and suicide linked to domestic abuse as femicides, ensuring such cases are addressed in data collection and accountability mechanisms, and concrete actions are identified to eliminate such preventable deaths.

* States should establish and sustain femicide watch mechanisms to monitor and highlight femicide as a fatal manifestation of the continuum of VAWG, in line with the recommendation of the UN Special Rapporteur on VAWG. This should involve close collaboration with the European Observatory on Femicide through sustained funding, sharing of relevant data and strengthened cooperation with national authorities and women’s specialist organisations to facilitate effective international collaboration and inform policy.

* Governments should establish mandatory, gender-sensitive review mechanisms for all killings of women, with coordinated intervention and real-time data exchange between WSS, law enforcement, health and judicial institutions to systematically analyse each case, identify risk factors, learn from institutional failures, and support consistent classification of femicide where applicable.

* EU institutions should ensure that minimum comparable homicide data is collected in official statistics of all European countries, including disaggregation by sex of victims and perpetrators and their relationship, to ensure identification of femicide. Additionally, data on complaints and reports of violence previously raised by the victims to the authorities should be recorded, as well as information on which statutory and voluntary agencies were previously involved in supporting the victim to ensure accountability of all involved support agencies and to guarantee the effective protection of women experiencing violence.

* Governments and international institutions should support public awareness and commemoration initiatives led by feminist organisations, recognising the social and symbolic power of naming femicide and remembering women killed by men as a political act against gender inequality.

* States should ensure training and capacity-building on femicide prevention is mandatory for police officers, prosecutors, judges, and healthcare as well as social service professionals, focusing on recognising patterns of coercive control, escalating violence, and early warning signs.

## SUMMARY

There is a national women’s helpline in Albania, operating 24/7 and free of charge, offering multilingual support. Additionally, there are other regional helplines and apps supporting survivors of violence against women. There are 26 women’s shelters with at least 153 beds, and at least 12 women’s centres. One rape crisis centre is available in the capital, and two “one-stop-shop” services for cases of sexualised violence have been integrated in hospitals. Primary prevention is included in the National Strategy for Gender Equality, which has a specific budget allocated to it. The state collects data on primary prevention and on women’s specialist services, but data collection is not comprehensive and accurate. Data is available upon request.

## WOMEN’S SPECIALIST SERVICES

### 1. NATIONAL WOMEN’S HELPLINES

*1 The latest available population data on Eurostat is from 2023.

*2 Ibid.

*3 Number of beds from the WAVE Country Report 2023.

Albania has one official state-wide women’s helpline, the National Counselling Line for Women and Girls (*Linja Kombëtare e Këshillimitpër Gra dhe Vajza*, tel.: 116117). This helpline operates 24/7, is free of charge, and therefore, meets the standards of the Istanbul Convention. It is operated by Hotline Albania and offers multilingual support according to the availability of the counsellors. It provides psychological and legal counselling services to women and girls who are survivors of domestic violence, gender-based violence, or sexual abuse, as well as referrals to shelters and protection services. The helpline receives state funding, donations and international funding, and in 2024, it received 4,658 calls, representing a 12% increase compared to the previous year. The most common forms of violence reported by callers were domestic, physical and psychological violence.

In addition to the national helpline, several local organisations across Albania operate regional helplines and provide support services. For instance, the Psycho-Social Centre “Vatra”, a non-profit organisation which supports survivors of human trafficking and violence, provides legal and psychosocial counselling through a helpline available 24/7 and free of charge (*Qendra Psiko-Sociale “Vatra”*, tel.: +355 699333523). Digital tools like the Bright Sky Albania and Find Your Voice (*GjejZa*) apps also help women identify abuse and access help. There is also a National Child Helpline for children and adolescents, including survivors of violence (116111), an Anti-Trafficking Helpline managed by the Ministry of Interior (+355 8001212) and a Green Line for Elderly People, which provides referrals and social support.

## 2. SHELTERS ACCESSIBLE TO WOMEN

<table>
<tr><td>Total number of women-only shelters</td><td>N/A</td></tr>
<tr><td>Total number of all shelters accessible to women</td><td>26</td></tr>
<tr><td>Existing number of beds</td><td>153</td></tr>
<tr><td>24/7 access</td><td>All</td></tr>
</table>

There are 26 shelters in Albania, offering at least 153 beds.<sup>3</sup> These include two state-run shelters (one for survivors of domestic violence and one for survivors of trafficking), eight long-term shelters for survivors of gender-based violence, and 16 emergency shelters, which offer accommodation up to 72 hours. The number of beds available in Albania does not meet the country's needs. All shelters offer 24/7 access, and women are not expected to pay for their accommodation. The length of stay depends on the type of shelter, with limited time in emergency shelters and up to one year in shelters managed by NGOs.

According to law no. 121/2016 "On social care services in the Republic of Albania", in-house services provided by shelters include specialised support, housing, physical security, food, health care, legal assistance, psychosocial

106

COUNTRY PROFILES
A

rehabilitation, employment empowerment, and reintegra- tion services. According to Law 22/2018 "On Social Hous- ing", the state must provide survivors of domestic violence with specialised housing, along with specialised social workers and guaranteed protection from the State Police for high-risk cases. Nevertheless, the specialised housing programme foreseen in this law has not been implement- ed yet.

In terms of accessibility, all shelters can accommodate women with uncertain residence permits and undocu- mented women, refugee women, transgender women, women with children with disabilities and unaccompanied minor girls. Most shelters can be accessed by and are accessible to women with physical disabilities, homeless women, women with substance abuse issues and older women, while some shelters are also equipped to support women with cognitive and sensory disabilities. There are also several specialised shelters in supporting survivors of trafficking (e.g., in Tirana, Elbasan, Vlora) offering hous- ing, legal aid, healthcare and vocational support. The *Vatra* Psycho-Social centre specialises in supporting both sur- vivors of trafficking and specific forms of violence, such as forced marriage and honour-based violence, while the shelter *Edlira Haxhiymeri* in Tirana provides support for lesbian, bisexual, and transgender women, in collabora- tion with the Streha Centre. The Albanian Disability Rights Foundation (ADRF) offers specialised support (including technology-based tools and peer mentoring) for women with disabilities and partners with shelters to improve accessibility. While no shelters are exclusively for older women, some social centres provide support groups and services for older survivors of domestic violence.

While the state-operated shelters are financed directly by the ministry, other shelters rely on multiple sources of funding: state funding, donations, international funding, funds from religious institutions and crowdfunding. Wom- en’s NGOs with a feminist and gender-specific approach run seven shelters in Albania, while the others are run by other NGOs and faith-based organisations. Shelters are lo- cated in urban areas except for the shelter in Lezhë "*Shpija Rozalba*", which is in a rural area. The reasons why shelters had to decline referrals were the lack of space and capaci- ty to support the survivor, the shelter not being adequately equipped to support women and children, if the survivors had severe mental health issues or if no protection order had been issued. The most common forms of violence re- ported by survivors in 2024 were domestic violence, phys- ical violence and psychological violence.

In Albania, besides women-only shelters, there are oth- er types of shelters that support survivors of violence against women. These include mixed-gender shelters that provide assistance to women, men, children, and LGBTQI+ individuals, particularly in cases involving trafficking or displacement. Municipal social centres across various cit- ies offer emergency housing, legal aid, and psychosocial support to survivors of domestic violence, serving people

of all genders. Additionally, anti-trafficking shelters, such as those operated by the National Coalition of Anti-Traf- ficking Shelters (NCATS), provide comprehensive services to all survivors of trafficking, many of whom have experi- enced gender-based violence. Some faith-based and char- ity-run shelters also offer support to women in crisis, often collaborating with NGOs to provide specialised care. While these are not exclusively women-only shelters, they do as- sist survivors of violence against women and often refer them to more specialised services when necessary. Most of these shelters offer 24/7 access.

### 3. WOMEN’S CENTRES

<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Total number of centres</th><th>12</th></tr>
<tr><th>Entities running women’s centres</th><th>Women’s NGOs <br />State <br />Faith-based organisations</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
</tbody>
</table>

There are at least 12 women’s centres in the country, some of which are part of the Women’s Empowerment Network in Albania (AWEN), while others are part of the Monitoring Network Against Gender-Based Violence. Five of these centres are exclusively for women, five are open to all survivors of gender-based violence, and two engage in advocacy activities or social services, supporting broad- er gender equality efforts. Women’s centres offer various types of support, including counselling and psychological support, legal advice, financial and social welfare support, housing advice, employment counselling, referrals and collaboration with other services, representation at court and other institutions, and residential support services, al- though the capacity for this is limited. Women’s centres also provide specialist support for survivors of sexualised violence, such as specialist forensic and medical care, needs assessment, specialist psychological care, special- ist advocacy services, community awareness and educa- tion for prevention and legal advice.

Women’s centres in Albania are accessible to various groups of survivors: women with uncertain residence permits, undocumented women, refugee women, women with physical and cognitive disabilities, older women, un- accompanied girls and transgender women. The Albania Disability Rights Foundation provides specialised support to people with disabilities, and two centres are specialised in supporting transgender women. The Streha Centre offers specialised services for LGBTQI+ individuals who face violence, family rejection, and housing insecurity, and besides emergency accommodation, it also provides psy- chosocial counselling, guidance and referrals to special- ised services, as well as support in accessing education, employment, and healthcare.

Women’s centres in Albania are run by women’s NGOs, the state, and religious institutions, and are funded through state funds, donations, international funding and religious institutions. They are only located in major cities.

# Umbrella 4. SPECIALIST SERVICES FOR SURVIVORS OF SEXUALISED VIOLENCE

There is one rape crisis centre in Albania, the Lilium Centre, based in Tirana, which provides medical, psychological, and legal support to survivors of sexualised violence. This centre also handles forensic evidence collection within a hospital setting. The centre is funded by the state and provides support to women, young women and children, and other survivors. Additionally, there are two new services in the regional hospitals in Fier and Shkodër, dealing with cases of sexualised violence and applying a “one-stop-shop” approach. Besides this, women’s centres and specialist NGOs play a crucial role in supporting survivors of sexualised violence, especially outside of the capital.

## 5. PRIMARY PREVENTION SERVICES

Public authorities in Albania collect data on primary prevention activities related to gender-based violence through surveys, monitoring referral mechanisms, and UN-supported programmes. However, such data collection is not comprehensive and systematic. Albania includes primary prevention activities in key documents such as the National Strategy for Gender Equality 2021–2030, and various municipal Gender Equality Action Plans. These documents focus on education, awareness, and community engagement to prevent gender-based violence, but the focus on evidence-based primary prevention measures, beyond general awareness raising, is still developing. The National Strategy for Gender Equality 2021–2030 emphasises reducing harmful practices and gender-based violence before they occur, using gender mainstreaming as a key prevention tool. Albania regularly finances various primary prevention activities against violence towards women and girls, including awareness-raising campaigns, education, community engagement, and capacity building. In 2023, approximately 9.6% of the national budget was directed to gender equality initiatives, covering both prevention and support services. The activities conducted in the country include feminist self-defence trainings, empowerment activities for women and girls, primary prevention activities specifically targeted to men and boys, training for primary prevention practitioners, self-care activities and awareness-raising campaigns or programmes. Albania has conducted evaluations of primary prevention activities against violence toward women and girls. These evaluations have been funded by both international organisations and public authorities, including national ministries, to help measure the effectiveness of prevention programmes and guide improvements in policies and services.

## SUMMARY

Armenia does not have a national women’s helpline, although there are regional helplines supporting women survivors of violence in every region of the country and there is a process underway to launch a national helpline. There are two women-only emergency shelters in Armenia with 24 beds for women and their children, and at least two other shelters which are accessible to women survivors, although the total number of beds is unknown. There are 11 women’s centres operating as domestic violence support centres as well as one sexual assault crisis centre for survivors of sexualised violence. Measures related to primary prevention are included in the country’s Strategy and Action Plan but there is no specific budget allocated to such activities. The state does collect data on women’s specialist services, including primary prevention activities, and this information is available upon request. The Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs partially subsidises domestic violence support centres. These centres are required to provide information on survivor demographics and other relevant information, such as the type of service provided.

## 1. NATIONAL WOMEN’S HELPLINES

There is no national women’s helpline in Armenia although there is a process underway to launch a national helpline. The Ministry of Social Affairs runs a national helpline (tel.: +374 114 and +374 119) which is not specialised but can refer domestic violence cases to regional helplines, according to the location of the survivor. Therefore, Armenia does not meet the Istanbul Convention standards for the provision of a national women’s helpline.

There are 12 regional helplines specifically supporting survivors of domestic violence in Yerevan and across the 10 regions in Armenia. The helplines run by the registered domestic violence support centres are as follows: Women’s Rights House (tel.: +374 77570870); Martuni Women’s Community Council – Martuni (tel.: +374 94876502), Gavar (tel.: +374 94876505); Family Without Violence (tel.: +374 98092094); Sose Women’s Issues (tel.: +374 98848453), Resource Center for Women’s Empowerment (tel.: +374 77380053); You Are Not Alone – Vayots Dzor (tel.: +374 98886077), Ararat (tel.: +374 77802700); For Equality Human Rights Defender (tel.: +374 099788770); Youth Avanguard (tel.: +374 93574657); Talin-Huys (tel.: +374 91482035); and Women’s Support Centre (tel.: +374 99887808). The helplines are funded through donations and international funding. In 2024, the helplines recorded a total of 3,877 calls, of which 1,980 were received by the Women’s Support Centre. The most common forms of violence reported by callers to the helplines in 2024 where domestic violence, physical violence, and psychological violence.

## 2. SHELTERS ACCESSIBLE TO WOMEN

<table>
<tr><td>Total number of women-only shelters</td><td>2</td></tr>
<tr><td>Total number of all shelters accessible to women</td><td>4</td></tr>
<tr><td>Existing number of beds</td><td>24<sup>4</sup></td></tr>
<tr><td>24/7 access</td><td>All</td></tr>
</table>

There are two women-only shelters in Armenia with a total of 24 beds run by the Women’s Support Centre (WSC), a women’s NGO with a feminist and gender-specific approach, which operates as emergency shelters for survivors of domestic violence.<sup>5</sup> Both women-only shelters offer 24/7 access, and women are not expected to pay for their accommodation in women-only shelters. On average, women and their children stay in women-only shelters for

4 This number only includes the beds in the two women-only shelters run by the Women’s Support Centre (WSC).

5 A transitional shelter for survivors of domestic violence opened in early 2025. This shelter is fully funded by one foundation grant.

a period of two or three months, which WSC has found to be sufficient for survivors to begin the process of rehabilitation and reintegration into society. However, if there is a serious security concern that warrants a longer stay, WSC offer the service for as long as it is needed. The types of in-house services most often provided by the women-only shelters are casework, counselling/psychological support, referrals/collaboration with other services, practical advice, legal advice, and therapy. Shelters also offer self-help groups, life and parenting skills training.

The number of beds in Armenia is far below the Istanbul Convention standards. However, given the social norms around utilising emergency shelters, as opposed to relocating with relatives or finding other options, at the moment the number of shelter spaces is sufficient. The WSC has never had to turn away any women or children. However, as reporting patterns change and more women seek shelter accommodation, this may become an issue in the near future.

Both women-only shelters can be accessed by and are accessible to women with uncertain residence permits/ undocumented women, refugee women, women with physical, cognitive or sensory disabilities, older women (65 years and above), women with older sons (14 years and above), women with children with disabilities, and unaccompanied girls under the age of 18. Neither of the women-only shelters can accommodate women with substance abuse issue, women with psychiatric diagnoses, or transgender women. For safety reasons and taking into consideration cultural norms and attitudes, WSC works with a partner organisation that can provide shelter support for transgender survivors. There is also a shelter for unmarried women with children up to the age of two, and one shelter for survivors of trafficking. These shelters can also offer accommodation to all survivors if the other shelters do not have availability.

Funding for the two women-only shelters primarily comes from foundation grants, international funding, and individual donors, as state funding only covers roughly 10% of the budget. The women-only shelters are located in Yerevan, meaning that there are no women-only shelters outside of the capital city and in other regions of Armenia. The main reason why women-only shelters had to decline referrals was the survivor being ineligible for support. The most common forms of violence reported by survivors to women-only shelters in 2024 were domestic violence, with psychological violence being the most prevalent. A large percentage of survivors had also experienced physical and economic violence, and a smaller percentage had experienced sexualised violence. A total of 274 women and children were accommodated in the women-only shelters in 2024.

There are other shelters in Armenia, that can provide support to women survivors of domestic violence. However, these shelters are for vulnerable families and survivors of trafficking and are not specifically intended to support women affected by violence. These shelters are available to all survivors.

## 3. WOMEN’S CENTRES

<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Total number of centres</th><th>11</th></tr>
<tr><th>Entities running women’s centres</th><th>Women’s NGOs (11 centres)</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
</tbody>
</table>

There are 11 women’s centres in Armenia which operate as domestic violence support centres and provide services to all survivors of gender-based violence, primarily women and their children. All women’s centres provide counselling/psychological support, legal advice, financial and social welfare support/advocacy, housing advice, employment, referrals/collaboration with other services, and representation at court/police/social services. In addition, women’s centres also provide hygiene products and medical help. Only one of the domestic violence centres (Women’s Support Centre) provides emergency shelter support, and all centres refer to this organisation. However, some of the other centres offer financial support to women for their temporary housing needs. Additionally, all centres also offer specialised support to survivors of sexualised violence in the form of specialist psychological care, community awareness and education for prevention, and legal advice. All women’s centres in Armenia can be accessed by and are accessible to women with uncertain residence permits/undocumented women, refugee women, women with physical, cognitive or sensory disabilities, older women (65 years and above), transgender women, and unaccompanied girls under the age of 18. There are no specialised centres supporting particular groups of survivors nor women survivors or those at risk of specific forms of violence in Armenia. However, women’s centres do have experience working with women with disabilities, refugee women, undocumented women, transgender and non-binary people.

Women’s centres are all run by women’s NGOs, and the majority of funding comes from foundation grants and international funds. Some funding for women’s centres also comes from national authorities. There is one registered domestic violence support centres in each region of Armenia. In 2024, a total of 1,939 women were supported by women’s centres.

In addition to the 11 domestic violence support centres, there are other centres providing support to women, although not specifically survivors of domestic violence, as well as centres supporting LGBTQI+ survivors of violence.

## 4. SPECIALIST SERVICES FOR SURVIVORS OF SEXUALISED VIOLENCE

There is one sexual assault crisis centre in Yerevan, the Sexual Assault Crisis Centre (SACC), which provides crisis support and also runs a helpline (tel.: +374 77991280). When needed, the SACC can also provide healthcare services. The centre provides needs assessment, specialist psychological care, specialist sexualised violence advocacy services, community awareness and education for prevention, as well as legal advice. Funding for the SACC comes from projects financed by international organisations and donors. Besides the centre in Yerevan, SACC also has focal point NGOs in different regions of the country where specialists are trained to provide support to survivors of sexualised violence. The sexualised violence service is available to all survivors of sexualised violence, including women, men, children, LGBTQI+ individuals, and people with disabilities.

## 5. PRIMARY PREVENTION SERVICES

Public authorities do collect data on primary prevention activities and provisions on primary prevention are included in the 2025–2028 Strategy and Action Plan for the Implementation of Gender Policy in the Republic of Armenia. Section five of this Strategy and Action Plan does include a definition of primary prevention and focuses on creating a safer and more secure environment and society for all women and girls. However, there is no specific budget allocated to primary prevention activities. Available activities include feminist self-defence trainings, empowerment activities for girls and women, school-based primary prevention programmes, training for primary prevention practitioners, self-care activities, and awareness-raising campaigns or programmes. There is no evaluation of the impact of primary prevention activities in Armenia.

## SUMMARY

There is one national women’s helpline in Austria that operates 24/7, is free of charge and offers multilingual support. There are 32 shelters in the country offering 505 beds in total (including 369 in shelters and 136 in temporary flats). The Network of Austrian Counselling Centres for Women and Girls has 65 counselling centres in all nine Austrian federal states as of 2025. There are at least 17 additional independent women’s counselling centres in Austria. Currently, a new National Action Plan (NAP) is being developed, including primary prevention actions, and there is a specific budget allocated to such activities. There is no comprehensive and centralised data collection mechanism on these activities. According to the financial agreement between the State and the NGOs, the women’s specialist services are required to collect data. All the statistics are published on the website of the National Coordination Office for Violence Against Women.

There is one state-wide women’s helpline in Austria called Women’s Helpline Against Violence (Frauenhelpline gegen Gewalt, +43 800222555). It is free of charge and available 24/7, offering support in German, English, Arabic, Romanian, Spanish and Turkish. Bosnian-Serbian-Croatian was available until 2024. The helpline complies with the standards of the Istanbul Convention. The helpline is run by the Association of Autonomous Austrian Women’s Shelters (AÖF-Verein Autonome Österreichische Frauenhäuser), and is funded by the state, as well as by private donations. The helpline provides support for all types of gender-based violence against women, including physical violence, psychological violence, sexualised violence, sexual harassment, cyber violence, stalking, and economic violence. In 2024, it received 5,425 calls/contacts from 4,805 callers. The most common forms of violence reported by callers were domestic violence, sexualised violence and psychological violence.

There are other regional helplines supporting survivors of violence against women in the country, such as the 24-hour Women’s Helpline of the City of Vienna (Frauennotruf der Stadt Wien, +43 1 71719), the gender-neutral Hotline of the victim protection centres (Gewaltschutzzentren, tel.: +43 800700217) and a gender-neutral Victim’s helpline for victims of all crimes (Opfernotruf +43 800112112).

## 2. SHELTERS ACCESSIBLE TO WOMEN

<table>
<tr><td>Total number of women-only shelters</td><td>32</td></tr>

There are 32 women-only shelters in Austria with 505 beds, including 369 in shelters and the remaining 136 in temporary flats, according to data from 2023. Sixteen of these shelters are part of the AÖF Network. Most women-only shelters offer 24/7 access. Based on the federal state, women who have an income can be expected to pay a small amount for their stay in a shelter, whereas women with lower financial income are not expected to pay. The length of the stay in the shelters depends on individual circumstances and ranges between three and six months. Based on 2023 data of the women’s shelters in the AÖF Network, most women stay in the shelters for no longer than 90 days (61%). The in-house services most frequently provided by the women-only shelters in the country are casework and psychological support/counselling.

In terms of accessibility, all shelters can accommodate older women, most can accommodate women with uncertain residence permits, undocumented women and refugee women. Some shelters can be accessed by and are accessible to women with physical, cognitive and sensory disabilities. There are other shelters in the country specialised in supporting specific groups, such as the women’s counselling centre “Orient Express” in Vienna, which runs a shelter/emergency apartment to accommodate girls and women between the ages of 16 to 24 who have been


**WAVE COUNTRY REPORT 2025**


A


**111**

---

affected by forced marriage, and a shelter for women survivors of trafficking run by the NGO LEFÖ. These shelters do not offer 24/7 services. In 2023, a special women’s shelter for young women aged 16 to 25 was opened in Vienna, offering 28 bed spaces.

The funding of women’s shelters is a responsibility of the respective federal state and the local government. Therefore, the funding differs in each federal state. Additionally, shelters receive donations. Women’s NGOs with a gender-specific and feminist approach run 31 of the women-only shelters. The women’s shelter in Salzburg was closed in 2021, and a new concept has been implemented by the associations VIELE and *Jugend am Werk*. Women-only shelters are available in all regions of Austria; however, their presence in more remote areas varies according to the regional government. According to data from the 16 shelters of the AÖF Network, in 2023, approximately 200 women were unable to find support due to a lack of space in the shelters, which corresponds to 58% of the rejections. Of these, 7% of the referrals were declined due to homelessness, and another 7% because of the place of residency being in another federal state. The most common forms of violence reported by survivors to the women-only shelters in 2024 were domestic, physical and sexualised violence.

There are no other shelters in Austria, besides the women-only shelters, that can provide support to survivors of violence against women.

## 3. WOMEN’S CENTRES

<table>
<tr><td>Total number of centres</td><td>65</td></tr>
<tr><td>Entities running women’s centres</td><td>N/A</td></tr>
</table>

Due to the lack of public data on women’s centres, there are no consolidated statistics on their numbers. According to the Federal Ministry for Women, Science and Research, there are currently 164 counselling centres for women and girls throughout Austria, but some centres are counted twice if they offer different services. The Network of Austrian Counselling Centres for Women and Girls (*Netzwerk Österreichischer Frauen- und Mädchenberatungsstellen*) had 65 counselling centres in all nine federal states in 2025. There are an additional 17 women’s counselling centres in Austria that operate independently of the network. These centres offer psychological assistance, legal advice, financial and social welfare support, employment, residential support services, housing advice and referrals to other services. The counselling is confidential, free of charge and takes place at the centres, by phone or online. Some of the centres of the Network of Austrian Counselling Centres for Women and Girls accompany clients to courts, police and social services. Some women’s centres in Austria can also offer residential support. Additionally, they also provide specialised support for survivors of sexualised violence, offering psychological care, advocacy services, legal advice, community awareness and education for prevention.

Most women’s centres can be accessed by women with uncertain residence permits/undocumented women, refugee women and older women. Some centres can be accessed by and are accessible to women with cognitive, physical and sensory disabilities, as well as transgender women and unaccompanied girls under the age of 18. Many centres also offer specialised support to survivors of specific forms of violence. For instance, at least four centres are specialised in supporting survivors (at risk) of female genital mutilation: the African Women Organisation with the project “Bright Future” in Vienna, FEM SÜD-Frauengesundheitszentrum at Kaiser Franz Spital in Vienna, Orient Express in Vienna and DIVAN in Graz. The new Austria-wide FGM/C Coordination office offers advice, information and support on all issues related to female genital mutilation. Some members of the Network of Austrian Counselling Centres for Women and Girls are specialised in supporting survivors of forced marriage (e.g., Orient Express and LEFÖ in Vienna). The counselling centre DIVAN offers support to survivors of honour-based violence, and LEFÖ has an intervention centre for survivors of trafficking, offering psychological and legal assistance to women and children. The centre Ninlil specialises in supporting women with cognitive and physical disabilities. Some centres provide counselling for migrant women. According to the law, since 2016, all counselling services in Austria that are recognised women’s service centres must be barrier-free. This requirement must also be continuously supported with adequate financial resources. The majority of women’s centres are welcoming to transgender women and non-binary people, and at least five centres explicitly express this inclusion in the name of the centre.

The majority of women’s centres are run by women’s NGOs. Women’s centres are funded by the state and local governments, donations, international funding and religious institutions. Women’s centres often rely on multiple funding sources and must apply every year, making it difficult to ensure long-term financial stability. Funding is often project-based and bureaucratic and does not consider inflation. In terms of geographical coverage, women’s centres are located in all regions of Austria.

## 4. SPECIALIST SERVICES FOR SURVIVORS OF SEXUALISED VIOLENCE

There are currently nine counselling centres for survivors of sexualised violence available in all regions of Austria, which belong to the association BAFÖ (Federation of Autonomous Women’s Counselling Centres Against Sexual Violence Austria). These counselling centres also engage in prevention, public awareness-raising campaigns, and advocate for socio-political change against sexism/sexualised violence. Furthermore, there are three Violence Intervention Clinics (*Gewaltambulanzen*) located in Graz, Vienna and Innsbruck; however, they are not specialised in the care of survivors of sexualised violence. Women’s centres also provide support to survivors of sexualised violence and refer them to specialised services and medical

112

WAVE COUNTRY REPORT 2025

COUNTRY PROFILES
A

professionals. Hospitals have specialist victim protection groups (*Opferschutzgruppen*), which require adequate funding and resources to ensure comprehensive care and effective support. There are also specialised helplines in the country (e.g., *Frauen gegen Vergewaltigung* and *Frauenberatung Notruf bei sexueller Gewalt*). Services for survivors of sexualised violence provide needs assessment, specialist psychological care, advocacy services, community awareness and education for prevention, as well as legal advice. They are funded by the state/local government and donations from individuals and small businesses, and support both women and young women and children under the age of 18.

## 5. PRIMARY PREVENTION SERVICES

Public authorities partially support primary prevention activities. However, there is no comprehensive data collection mechanism on these activities. In Austria, a new National Action Plan is being developed at the time of writing, and it will include some aspects related to primary prevention, although details on its scope are not available yet. There is no official definition of primary prevention in the country, and there are small regional funding programmes for primary prevention offered and managed by different ministries and projects. However, there is no unified or comprehensive overview of these budget lines. In the country, there are several primary prevention activities offered (e.g., empowerment activities for girls and women, school-based primary prevention programmes, training for primary prevention practitioners, awareness-raising campaigns and primary prevention activities targeted at boys and men). One example is the Austria-wide project “StoP – Neighbourhoods without partner violence”, which is managed by the Association of Austrian Autonomous Women’s Shelters and funded by the Ministry of Social Affairs, and is externally evaluated. Moreover, women’s and girls’ counselling centres often integrate primary prevention activities into their work, offering workshops and educational programmes in schools and community spaces. Some women’s organisations conduct their own evaluations of these prevention efforts, focusing on issues such as gender-based violence, sexual harassment, and digital violence. There is no comprehensive evaluation of the impact of primary prevention activities at the national level. Some individual projects and initiatives may include internal or external evaluations, but these are not consistently funded or coordinated by public authorities at the national, regional, or local levels. Currently, there is a comprehensive Austria-wide study being prepared of the impact of the StoP projects in Austria, which should be released in 2026.

## SUMMARY

There is one national women’s helpline in Azerbaijan, which is free of charge, available 24/7 and offers multilingual support. There are also other helplines supporting survivors of violence. There are two women-only shelters accessible to women in Azerbaijan, offering 85 beds in total, as well as eight other shelters accessible to women survivors of violence. There are also 11 Family and Child Support Centres operating in various regions of the country and offering a range of support services. There are no rape crisis centres or sexual violence referral centres in Azerbaijan. State authorities do collect data on primary prevention activities, but not in a centralised or fully standardised way, and there is no specific budget allocated to such activities. The National Action Plan on Combating Domestic Violence for 2024-2027 has been drafted but not yet approved. Apart from primary prevention activities, the state does not collect data on women’s specialist services.
